aristotle-eudaimonia: Eudaimonia is the central aim of Aristotle's ethics, often rendered as happiness but better understood as flourishing or living well over the course of a whole life. It is not a passing feeling of pleasure but the condition of a human being who fully realizes their nature by acting excellently in accordance with reason and virtue. Aristotle argues that eudaimonia is the final end sought for its own sake, to which all other goods are ultimately directed, and that it depends chiefly on the exercise of the virtues, supported by adequate external goods and good fortune. Achieving it is thus a matter of lifelong activity and character, not of momentary satisfaction.
aristotle-golden-mean: The golden mean is Aristotle's doctrine that moral virtue lies between two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the person and the situation. Courage, for instance, stands between the vices of recklessness and cowardice, and generosity between wastefulness and stinginess. The mean is not a mechanical midpoint but the response that practical wisdom judges to be appropriate, hitting the right feeling and action at the right time, toward the right people, for the right reason. This framework gives content to the virtues and explains why acting well requires discernment rather than the mere following of a formula.
aristotle-virtue-ethics: Virtue ethics, in the tradition stemming from Aristotle, locates the moral life in the cultivation of good character rather than in obedience to rules or the calculation of consequences. Its central notion is arete, or excellence, a stable disposition to feel and act well that is developed through habit and practice over time. On this view the key ethical question is what kind of person one should become, and virtues such as courage, temperance, and justice are the traits that enable a human being to live and function well. Aristotle sets out this approach in the Nicomachean Ethics, tying virtue to the fulfillment of our nature as rational, social beings.
care-ethics: The ethics of care is a moral approach that treats responsiveness to the needs of particular others, and the relationships in which we are embedded, as central to ethical life, rather than treating morality primarily as a matter of impartial rules or abstract rights. It grew out of Carol Gilligan's psychological research, which suggested that many people, and women in particular, reason morally in a distinct voice oriented toward care, connection, and the concrete circumstances of relationships, alongside the more familiar ethic of justice and rights. Care ethicists argue that dependence and caregiving are basic features of human life that traditional theories have marginalized. The approach reframes moral maturity around sustaining relationships and meeting real needs rather than applying universal principles.
care-ethics-noddings: Nel Noddings developed an ethics grounded in caring, holding that the fundamental moral relation is the encounter between the one-caring and the one cared-for, in which the carer attends to and is moved by the other's needs. She distinguished natural caring, which flows from inclination as a parent cares for a child, from ethical caring, which we summon out of a remembered ideal of ourselves as caring when inclination fails. For Noddings, ethics is rooted in receptivity and engrossment in the particular other rather than in the application of universal principles, and moral education should cultivate the capacity and disposition to care. Her work gave care ethics a systematic foundation and influenced thinking about moral education.
das-man: The they-self, or das Man, is Heidegger's name for the anonymous "one" that governs much of everyday life—as in what "one" does, says, or thinks—into which individuals typically dissolve. In this mode people conform to averaged expectations, letting public opinion decide their choices and thereby covering over their own responsibility for existence. Heidegger regards this as the ordinary, largely inauthentic condition of Dasein, from which authentic selfhood must be won back rather than presupposed.
eternal-recurrence: Eternal recurrence is Nietzsche's thought that one's life, and indeed the whole of existence, repeats identically an infinite number of times. He offers it less as a cosmological claim than as a test of one's attitude toward life: could you will to live this same life, with all its pain and triviality, over and over forever? To embrace the prospect joyfully rather than with despair is, for Nietzsche, the mark of a life fully affirmed, and the idea is closely tied to his call to love existence exactly as it is.
existence-precedes-essence: "Existence precedes essence" is Jean-Paul Sartre's slogan for the core of atheistic existentialism: there is no fixed human nature given in advance, so a person first exists and only afterward defines what they are through their choices. Unlike a manufactured object whose purpose is set before it is made, the human being arrives without a predetermined role and must create meaning and value through action. This places the full weight of self-definition, and hence responsibility, on the individual.
existentialism: Existentialism is a nineteenth- and twentieth-century philosophical movement centered on the concrete situation of the individual human being, insisting that existence precedes essence, so that people first exist and then make themselves through their choices. Associated with thinkers such as Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and de Beauvoir, it stresses freedom, responsibility, and the anxiety that comes from confronting a world without given meaning. Rather than seeking a fixed human nature, existentialists explore how individuals create value and identity through authentic commitment in the face of finitude and uncertainty.
feminism: Feminism is a broad range of intellectual and political movements united by the conviction that women have been unjustly subordinated and that the sexes deserve equal rights, opportunities, and standing. As philosophy it examines how gender shapes knowledge, power, ethics, and social institutions, and it critiques assumptions that have treated the male as the human norm. Spanning successive waves and diverse schools—liberal, socialist, radical, intersectional, and more—it shares the aim of analyzing and dismantling structures that disadvantage women.
kierkegaard-despair: Despair, in Søren Kierkegaard's analysis in The Sickness unto Death, is a spiritual condition of the self that fails to be rightly related to itself and to God, rather than a mere passing mood. He describes it as a misrelation within the self, expressed either as not willing to be oneself or as defiantly willing to be a self on one's own terms, and he regards it as a condition many people harbor without recognizing. For Kierkegaard the cure lies in faith, in which the self, grounding itself in the power that established it, finds its true relation.
kierkegaard-stages: The stages on life's way is Søren Kierkegaard's account of three fundamental modes of existence through which a person may live: the aesthetic, the ethical, and the religious. The aesthetic life pursues immediacy, pleasure, and novelty but drifts toward boredom and despair; the ethical life commits to duty, responsibility, and moral seriousness; and the religious life involves a faith that transcends universal ethical norms in relation to God. Kierkegaard presents these not as a smooth progression but as distinct existential outlooks between which the individual must choose.
language-games: A language game, in Ludwig Wittgenstein's later philosophy, is a rule-governed activity in which words gain their meaning from the way they are used within a shared form of life, such as giving orders, telling jokes, or reporting an event. Wittgenstein introduced the idea to counter the view that words function chiefly by naming objects, arguing instead that meaning is inseparable from practice and context. The notion underlies his claim that many philosophical confusions arise from taking language out of the settings in which it actually works.
leap-of-faith: The leap of faith is the idea, associated with Søren Kierkegaard, that religious belief cannot be reached by reason or objective proof but requires a decisive personal commitment made in the face of uncertainty. For Kierkegaard, faith involves embracing what cannot be rationally guaranteed, a movement beyond evidence in which the individual stakes their life on God despite the risk. It expresses his conviction that the deepest truths of existence are grasped through passionate inward choice rather than detached speculation.
moral-psychology: Moral psychology studies the mental features that underlie moral life — character and its virtues and vices, moral motivation, and the failures of self-control that the tradition calls weakness of will, or akrasia. A central puzzle, posed since Socrates and Aristotle, is how a person can judge one course of action best yet knowingly do otherwise, revealing tensions among reason, desire, and habit. The field asks how traits are formed, how far character is stable across situations, and what role emotion plays in perceiving and doing what is right.
parmenidean-being: Parmenides of Elea, active in the early fifth century BCE, argued through a rigorous chain of reasoning that whatever truly is must be one, eternal, indivisible, and changeless, since to speak of what is not is to speak of nothing at all. From this he concluded that change, plurality, and coming-to-be are illusions of the senses, and that reason alone reveals genuine reality. His radical denial of change set the terms for much later Greek metaphysics, forcing successors to reconcile the evidence of the senses with the demands of logic.
plato-cave: The allegory of the cave, from Plato's Republic, imagines prisoners chained since birth so they see only shadows cast on a wall, mistaking these projections for reality. One prisoner is freed, painfully ascends to the sunlit world outside, and comes to understand that the shadows were mere images of true things. The story dramatizes Plato's distinction between the world of appearances and the world of the Forms, and it pictures education as a turning of the soul toward truth rather than a filling of it with facts. It also suggests why the enlightened person, returning to explain what they have seen, may be met with hostility.
plato-forms: Plato's theory of Forms holds that the changing, imperfect things we perceive are imitations of eternal, unchanging archetypes that exist independently of the physical world. A particular just act or beautiful object is such only by participating in the Form of Justice or Beauty, which is perfectly and always what its instances are only partially and temporarily. The theory responds to the problem of how stable knowledge is possible in a world of flux: genuine knowledge is of the Forms, grasped by reason, while sensory experience yields mere opinion. It also anchors Plato's ethics and metaphysics, with the Form of the Good as the highest object of understanding.
socratic-ignorance: Socratic ignorance is the recognition that one does not possess the wisdom one might be tempted to claim, captured in the idea that Socrates was wisest because he alone knew that he knew nothing of real importance. Rather than a pose of false modesty, it names an honest awareness of the limits of one's understanding, which Socrates took to be the necessary starting point for genuine inquiry. Those who mistakenly believe they already know cannot learn, whereas acknowledging ignorance opens the way to seeking truth. This stance underlies his relentless questioning of experts who claimed authority they could not justify.
teleological-suspension: The teleological suspension of the ethical is Kierkegaard's provocative claim that faith can, in rare cases, require setting aside universal moral duty for the sake of a higher relation to the divine. His central example is Abraham, commanded to sacrifice Isaac, whose obedience makes no sense within ordinary ethics and can be justified only by a private, absolute duty to God. The idea dramatizes the gap between the ethical, which is universal and communicable, and faith, which is singular and cannot be fully explained to others.
the-look: The Look is Sartre's analysis of what happens when another person's gaze turns me into an object in their world, revealing that I exist not only for myself but also for others. Being seen can bring shame or self-consciousness, because the other apprehends me as a fixed thing over which I have no control, and I in turn objectify them. This conflict of freedoms lies behind the famous line "hell is other people," expressing how our being is perpetually contested in the presence of other subjects.
the-tao: The Tao, or the Way, is the central notion of Daoism: the nameless, formless source and ordering principle from which all things arise and to which they return. In the Daodejing, associated with Laozi, the Tao is said to be beyond full description or definition—"the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"—yet it can be sensed and followed by those who cultivate stillness and simplicity. Living well means aligning oneself with this natural course rather than resisting it through force, ambition, or excessive contrivance.
unexamined-life: The unexamined life is the phrase from Socrates's defense at his trial, where he declared that a life without self-scrutiny is not worth living for a human being. He held that reflecting on one's beliefs, values, and conduct is essential to living well, and refused to give up philosophy even under threat of death. The claim elevates critical self-examination from an optional pursuit to a defining feature of a properly human existence. It expresses Socrates's conviction that the care of the soul, through honest reflection, matters more than comfort or survival.
wu-wei: Wu wei, often translated as effortless action or non-forcing, is the Daoist ideal of acting in accordance with the natural flow of things rather than against it. It does not mean doing nothing, but acting without strain, coercion, or self-assertive striving, so that one's conduct arises spontaneously and fits the situation, as water finds its own path around obstacles. Associated with Laozi and the Daodejing, wu wei holds that the most effective and harmonious results come from restraint and responsiveness rather than aggressive control.
aristotle-practical-wisdom: Phronesis, usually rendered as practical wisdom or prudence, is for Aristotle the intellectual virtue that governs good action in particular circumstances. Unlike theoretical knowledge, which concerns unchanging truths, practical wisdom is the capacity to perceive what the situation requires and to deliberate well about how to achieve worthwhile ends. In the Nicomachean Ethics it is the master virtue of conduct, since without it the moral virtues lack direction, and it cannot be reduced to rules but is acquired through experience and habituation.
brain-in-a-vat: The brain-in-a-vat scenario imagines that your brain has been removed and kept alive in a vat, fed electrical signals by a computer so that your entire experience of an external world is an elaborate illusion. It is a modern version of Descartes's skeptical doubt, raising the worry that you could never rule out such a predicament from the inside and so cannot be certain anything you perceive is real. Hilary Putnam gave the puzzle a notable twist, arguing on grounds of the theory of reference that the sentence "I am a brain in a vat" is self-refuting and cannot be true if uttered by an envatted brain.
cartesian-doubt: Methodological doubt is the procedure by which René Descartes deliberately suspended belief in everything that could possibly be false, in order to find whatever might survive as certain. He pushed this doubt to its extreme by imagining an all-powerful evil demon bent on deceiving him about mathematics, the senses, and the external world, so that no ordinary belief could be trusted uncritically. The exercise is not skepticism for its own sake but a purifying method: by discarding all that is dubitable, Descartes aims to isolate a foundation, the thinking self, secure enough to ground the rest of knowledge.
cartesian-dualism: Mind–body dualism is René Descartes's view that reality contains two fundamentally different kinds of substance: mind, whose essence is thought and which is non-extended, and body, whose essence is extension in space. On this account a human being is a union of an immaterial thinking soul and a material, mechanical body, each intelligible without the other. The position sharpens the enduring problem of how two such distinct substances can causally interact, and it set much of the agenda for later philosophy of mind, which has largely wrestled with the difficulties it bequeathed.
commodity-fetishism: Commodity fetishism is the concept, introduced in the first volume of Capital, that under capitalism the social relations between people take on the appearance of relations between things. Goods seem to possess value as a natural property of their own, obscuring the human labor and social arrangements that actually produced them. Marx uses the religious language of "fetishism" to capture how market exchange makes economic relations look like objective facts about objects, mystifying the labor that lies behind prices and commodities.
eliminative-materialism: Eliminative materialism is the radical view that our everyday way of describing minds — in terms of beliefs, desires, and choices — is a primitive folk theory that neuroscience may turn out to be wrong about, the way alchemy was abandoned. If so, these concepts would not be refined but eliminated and replaced by brain science. Many find this too strong, but it poses how much common sense must survive.
experience-machine: The experience machine is a thought experiment introduced by Robert Nozick to challenge hedonism, the view that pleasure or pleasant experience is all that ultimately matters. He asks us to suppose a machine that could give us any experiences we desired, indistinguishable from reality, for the rest of our lives, while our bodies floated in a tank. Nozick argues that most people would refuse to plug in permanently, revealing that we care about actually doing certain things, being certain kinds of people, and staying in contact with reality—not merely about how our lives feel from the inside. The example is a standard objection to purely experiential accounts of the good life.
fate-vs-free-will: Fate and foreknowledge name a cluster of problems about whether the future's being settled or known in advance is compatible with human freedom. If events are fated to occur, or if an omniscient God already knows what a person will do, it can seem that the person could not have done otherwise, undermining genuine choice and moral responsibility. Philosophers from the Stoics and Boethius through medieval theologians and modern thinkers have proposed various resolutions: distinguishing foreknowledge from causation, arguing that God stands outside time so that knowledge does not precede the act, or holding that freedom requires only acting from one's own will rather than the ability to do otherwise. The debate remains central to discussions of divine providence, determinism, and the nature of free will.
free-will-determinism: The free will problem asks whether human beings can act freely and be morally responsible if every event, including our choices, is fixed by prior causes. Determinism holds that the state of the world at any moment, together with the laws of nature, necessitates exactly one future, which seems to leave no room for genuine alternatives. Hard determinists conclude that free will is therefore an illusion, while libertarians insist that we do possess a freedom incompatible with determinism and so deny that determinism is true of our choices. The dispute bears directly on praise, blame, punishment, and desert.
ghost-in-the-machine: 'The ghost in the machine' is Gilbert Ryle's mocking phrase for the Cartesian doctrine that a person consists of a physical body inhabited by a distinct, immaterial mind. In The Concept of Mind he argued that this dualism rests on a category mistake, wrongly treating mental life as a hidden inner theater causally driving bodily movements. In its place Ryle urged that talk of mind refers to patterns of behavior and dispositions rather than to a private ghostly substance, a view that helped shape philosophical behaviorism.
hard-problem: David Chalmers coined the "hard problem of consciousness" to distinguish it from the comparatively easy problems of explaining cognitive functions such as perception, memory, and behavioral control. The easy problems concern how the brain performs tasks and can in principle be answered by ordinary science; the hard problem asks why there is subjective experience at all—why any physical process should be accompanied by an inner, felt quality rather than proceeding in the dark. Chalmers argues that even a complete functional account would leave this question of why experience exists unanswered, posing a deep challenge to purely physicalist theories of mind.
higher-lower-pleasures: The distinction between higher and lower pleasures is John Stuart Mill's refinement of utilitarianism, arguing that pleasures differ not only in quantity but in quality. Mill held that intellectual, aesthetic, and moral pleasures are higher in kind than merely bodily or sensual ones, and that competent judges who have experienced both would prefer the higher even at some cost in comfort. This move was meant to answer the charge that utilitarianism is a crude doctrine fit only for swine, by grounding the superiority of a cultivated life in the informed preferences of those acquainted with both sorts of enjoyment.
hume-bundle: The bundle theory of the self denies that there is any persisting, unified substance underlying our mental life. Examining his own experience, David Hume found only a succession of particular perceptions—sensations, feelings, and thoughts—but no impression of a simple, continuous ego to which they belong. He therefore proposed that the self is nothing more than a bundle or collection of these fleeting perceptions, held together by relations such as resemblance and causation, a conclusion that unsettles ordinary assumptions about a stable inner subject.
intentionality: Intentionality is the feature of consciousness by which every mental act is directed at or about something: perceiving is perceiving of an object, believing is believing that something is the case. Revived by Franz Brentano and made central by Edmund Husserl, the notion holds that this "aboutness" is the essential mark distinguishing the mental from the merely physical. For phenomenology it becomes the guiding thread of analysis, since to study consciousness is to study the structured ways it intends its objects.
knowledge-argument: The knowledge argument, framed by Frank Jackson through the thought experiment of Mary the color scientist, challenges physicalism about the mind. Mary knows every physical fact about color vision while confined to a black-and-white room; the argument contends that when she finally sees red she learns something new—what the experience is actually like. If she gains new knowledge, the reasoning goes, then not all facts are physical facts, and subjective conscious experience (qualia) escapes a purely physical description. Physicalists have replied that Mary gains a new ability or mode of acquaintance rather than a new fact.
marx-ideology: For Marx, ideology refers to the system of ideas, beliefs, and values that reflects and reinforces the interests of a society's dominant class, often while presenting itself as natural, universal, or simply true. Closely linked is false consciousness, a condition in which subordinate groups misunderstand their real situation and accept beliefs that work against their own interests. Together these concepts explain how prevailing worldviews can obscure exploitation and sustain existing power relations, so that the ruling ideas of an age tend to be the ideas of its ruling class.
philosophy-of-humor: Why do we laugh, and what makes something funny? Three classic theories compete: humor as felt superiority, humor as the delight of perceiving an incongruity that suddenly snaps into sense, and humor as the release of nervous tension. Philosophers also ask whether jokes can be morally judged — whether laughing at a cruel joke makes you complicit in it — and many hold that it can.
plato-euthyphro: The Euthyphro dilemma comes from Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, where Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or is pious because it is loved by the gods. Generalized beyond its religious setting, it poses a sharp question about the foundation of morality: are actions good because a divine will commands them, or does that will command them because they are already good? If goodness depends only on divine command, morality seems arbitrary; but if the gods approve things because they are independently good, then their approval is not what makes them so. The dilemma remains central to debates about the relationship between religion and ethics.
punishment-theory: The philosophy of punishment asks what, if anything, justifies the state in deliberately imposing hardship on those who break the law. Retributive theories hold that punishment is deserved as a response to wrongdoing, repaying guilt in proportion to the offense regardless of future benefit, whereas rehabilitative and other consequentialist theories justify punishment by its results, chiefly reforming the offender and reducing future crime. The debate turns on whether we punish because a wrong was done or in order to bring about better outcomes, and many modern accounts try to combine both aims.
skepticism: Philosophical skepticism is the view, or family of views, that questions whether we can have knowledge at all, or knowledge of some particular domain such as the external world, other minds, or the past. It responds to the problem that our beliefs might be systematically mistaken in ways we could never detect, as dramatized by scenarios like the dreaming argument or the deceiving demon. Ancient skeptics such as Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus recommended suspending judgment to attain tranquility, while modern skepticism, sharpened by Descartes and Hume, became a challenge that theories of knowledge must answer. Skeptical arguments are often used less to advocate doubt than to probe what justification and certainty actually require.
socratic-method: The Socratic method, or elenchus, is a form of cooperative inquiry in which a claim is tested through a disciplined series of questions rather than asserted or refuted directly. Socrates would draw out a person's definition of some notion such as justice or courage, then expose contradictions among the beliefs they held alongside it, leading them to abandon or refine the original view. Its aim is less to win an argument than to clear away false confidence and move both parties closer to a defensible understanding. The method treats knowledge as something arrived at through examination, not received ready-made.
virtue-ethics: Virtue ethics is an approach to morality that centers on character and the traits that make for a good and flourishing human life, rather than on rules or the calculation of consequences. Descending from Aristotle, it holds that virtues such as courage, justice, honesty, and temperance are stable dispositions cultivated through habit, and that the ethical question is less "what should I do?" than "what kind of person should I be?" Revived in the twentieth century, it responds to the sense that duty-based and outcome-based theories neglect the emotions, motives, and lived shape of a whole life.
web-of-belief: The web of belief is Quine's metaphor for the way our beliefs form an interconnected system that faces experience as a whole rather than one claim at a time. Observations impinge on the periphery of the web, while logical and mathematical principles sit near the resistant center; when evidence conflicts with the system, we may revise it at many different points, and no belief is in principle immune to revision. The picture rejects a sharp line between analytic and synthetic truths and reframes knowledge as a holistic, revisable structure.
what-is-it-like: In his 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", Thomas Nagel argues that consciousness has an irreducibly subjective character: for any conscious creature there is something it is like to be that creature, experienced from its own point of view. Because a bat perceives the world through echolocation, we cannot genuinely imagine its inner life from the inside, only picture what it would be like for us to behave as a bat does. Nagel uses this to press a limit on objective, physical accounts of the mind, which describe things from no particular perspective and so seem to leave out the very feature—subjective experience—that makes a state conscious.
ahimsa: Ahimsa is the principle of nonviolence or non-harm toward all living beings, deeply rooted in the Jain, Hindu, and Buddhist traditions of India. It calls not only for the avoidance of physical injury but for restraint in thought and speech, resting on a sense of the kinship and value of all life. In the twentieth century Mahatma Gandhi made ahimsa the ethical and political core of his campaigns, fusing it with satyagraha, or the disciplined pursuit of truth, to resist injustice without inflicting harm. In his hands the ancient ideal became a practical method of collective, nonviolent action.
atman-brahman: Atman and Brahman are the twin poles of much of classical Indian metaphysics: atman is the innermost self or consciousness, while Brahman is the ultimate, unconditioned ground of all reality. In the Advaita Vedanta system articulated by Shankara, the deepest teaching of the Upanishads is that these two are not different but identical, so that the true self is nothing other than the absolute. Ordinary experience of a separate, individual self is traced to ignorance, and liberation comes through the direct realization of this underlying unity. The position is a rigorous nondualism, holding that plurality and separateness are ultimately appearance rather than final truth.
atomism: Ancient atomism, developed by Leucippus and especially Democritus in the fifth century BCE, holds that reality consists of countless indivisible particles, atoms, moving through empty space, or void. All apparent qualities and changes are explained by the arrangement, motion, and combination of these unchanging bodies, so that nothing exists but atoms and the void. This thoroughly materialist and mechanistic picture offered an early way to reconcile the reality of change with a stable underlying substance, and it profoundly influenced later thinkers such as Epicurus.
authenticity: Authenticity, in Heidegger's sense, names a way of existing in which one takes ownership of one's own possibilities rather than drifting along in the anonymous patterns dictated by "the they." It is achieved not by escaping the social world but by resolutely owning one's finitude and choosing in light of it, as against the inauthentic tendency to lose oneself in conventional expectations. The term is descriptive rather than moralistic, marking a difference in how existence is enacted rather than a code of correct behavior.
bad-faith: Bad faith is Sartre's term for the self-deception by which we flee from our own freedom, pretending to be fixed things rather than the free beings we are. A person in bad faith might treat their social role, past, or circumstances as an unchangeable essence in order to disown the responsibility of choosing. Sartre illustrates it with figures like the waiter overplaying his role, showing how we lie to ourselves to escape the anxiety of radical freedom.
buddhism: Buddhism is a family of traditions arising from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in ancient India, aimed at understanding and ending suffering. It diagnoses ordinary existence as marked by dissatisfaction rooted in craving and ignorance, and it offers a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and insight leading toward liberation, often described as nirvana. Rejecting reliance on a creator deity for salvation, Buddhism emphasizes practices such as meditation and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and it has developed into diverse schools across Asia and beyond.
buddhist-compassion: Karuna, usually translated as compassion, is the wish that all sentient beings be free from suffering, and it stands as one of the central virtues cultivated on the Buddhist path. It arises in response to the pervasive fact of dukkha, or unsatisfactoriness, that the Buddha identified at the heart of ordinary existence, and it is meant to be extended without limit to every being rather than reserved for kin or allies. In the Mahayana tradition especially, karuna is paired with wisdom and embodied in the bodhisattva, who vows to work for the liberation of others. Cultivated through meditation and ethical practice, it is understood not as mere sentiment but as an active, disciplined orientation of the mind.
buddhist-impermanence: Impermanence, or anicca, is the Buddhist teaching that all conditioned things are in constant flux, arising and passing away without any stable, lasting essence. Nothing—no object, feeling, thought, or self—remains fixed, and clinging to what is inherently changing is a central source of suffering. Recognizing impermanence is meant to loosen attachment and foster acceptance, and it stands alongside suffering and non-self as one of the three marks of existence in Buddhist thought.
buddhist-karma: In Buddhist thought, karma is the principle that intentional actions carry moral consequences that shape one's future experience and, across the cycle of rebirth, one's future existences. Wholesome intentions and deeds tend toward better outcomes while harmful ones lead to suffering, so character and circumstance are understood as the ripening of past choices rather than the decree of a judging deity. Bound up with rebirth, karma explains the continuity of moral cause and effect through successive lives, until liberation frees one from the cycle altogether.
buddhist-non-self: Non-self, or anatman, is the Buddhist claim that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul underlying our experience. What we take to be a fixed "I" is, on this view, a shifting bundle of physical and mental processes that continually arise and dissolve, held together only by habit and craving. Understanding non-self is intended to undercut the self-centered grasping that drives suffering, and it distinguishes Buddhism from traditions that posit an enduring soul.
faith-vs-reason: The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.
four-noble-truths: The Four Noble Truths form the core framework of the Buddha's teaching about suffering and its resolution. They state that life is pervaded by suffering or unsatisfactoriness (dukkha), that this suffering arises from craving and attachment, that it can cease when craving is extinguished, and that there is a path—the Noble Eightfold Path—leading to that cessation. Presented like a physician's diagnosis and cure, they set out both the problem of human dissatisfaction and a practical program for overcoming it.
immortality: Questions of immortality and the soul concern whether some part of a person, often called the soul or mind, survives bodily death, and what such survival would consist in. Dualist traditions, from Plato onward, treat the soul as a distinct immaterial substance capable of existing apart from the body, while materialists deny any such separable entity and tie personal existence to the living organism. The topic bears on religious hopes for an afterlife, on debates about personal identity over time, and on what it would even mean for the same person to persist beyond death.
kant-autonomy: Autonomy of the will is Immanuel Kant's idea that the moral law is one that a rational agent gives to itself rather than receives from any external source. To be autonomous is to legislate universal principles through one's own reason and to act from them out of duty, so that genuine freedom consists in self-governance according to moral law rather than in doing whatever one is inclined to do. Kant contrasted this with heteronomy, in which the will is determined by desires or outside authority, and made autonomy the basis of both moral obligation and human dignity.
meaning-of-life: The question of the meaning of life asks whether human existence has a point, purpose, or significance, and if so, what makes a life meaningful. Answers divide between those who locate meaning in something beyond us, such as God or an objective moral order, and those who hold that meaning is created by human beings through their projects, relationships, and values. The question gained special urgency in modern thought as traditional religious frameworks were questioned, prompting responses ranging from nihilism to existentialist affirmations of self-created purpose.
nihilism: Nihilism is the view that life, values, and meaning lack any objective grounding: there are no genuine purposes, no binding moral facts. Nietzsche, its most famous analyst, saw nihilism as the crisis following the death of God, the collapse of the frameworks that once gave life meaning. Responses range from despair to Nietzsche's call to create new values and Camus's defiant embrace of the absurd.
philosopher-king: The philosopher king is Plato's proposal, argued in the Republic, that political power should be held by those who have genuine knowledge of the Good rather than by the wealthy, the popular, or the ambitious. Because rulers guided by true understanding rather than self-interest would govern for the benefit of the whole community, Plato concludes that a just city requires that philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers. The idea reflects his distrust of democracy, which he thought vulnerable to demagogues and the untutored desires of the many. It ties legitimate authority to wisdom and to a rigorous education aimed at grasping the Forms.
religious-pluralism: Religious pluralism is the view that more than one religion can offer a genuine path to ultimate reality, so no single tradition holds an exclusive claim on truth. It contrasts with exclusivism, which says only one religion is true, and inclusivism, which says one is fullest though others are partially valid. Philosophers like John Hick defend pluralism, while critics argue it flattens real doctrinal differences and may be self-undermining.
second-order-desires: Harry Frankfurt proposed that what distinguishes persons from other creatures is the capacity for second-order desires: desires about which of one's first-order desires one wants to be effective in moving one to act. A drug addict who wants to quit but also craves the drug has conflicting first-order desires; whether the addict is a person in the full sense depends on which desire he identifies with at the second order. When someone wants a particular desire to be his will, Frankfurt calls this a second-order volition, and having such volitions is the mark of free and responsible agency. This account grounds freedom of the will in a hierarchical structure of the self rather than in the ability to have done otherwise.
stoicism: Stoicism is a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE and later developed by figures such as Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius. It teaches that virtue—living in accordance with reason and nature—is the only true good, and that a flourishing life comes from mastering one's judgments rather than external circumstances. Because emotions like fear and anger arise from mistaken beliefs about what is good or bad, the Stoics sought to cultivate reason and equanimity in the face of whatever fortune brings.
the-absurd: For Albert Camus, the absurd names the collision between the human craving for meaning, order, and clarity and a universe that offers no such answers in return. It is not a property of the world alone or of the mind alone but the confrontation between them, arising when a person who demands significance meets a silent, indifferent cosmos. Camus treats this recognition as the honest starting point for thought, and his central question becomes how to live fully once one no longer expects the world to justify existence.
transcendental-idealism: Transcendental idealism is Immanuel Kant's view that the objects of experience are conditioned by the structures of the human mind, so that space, time, and the categories are not features of reality in itself but the necessary forms through which any experience is possible. It answers the question of how we can have certain, universal knowledge that nonetheless applies to the world: such knowledge is possible because the mind actively organizes sensory input rather than passively receiving it. Kant called his position a 'Copernican revolution,' shifting the focus from objects conforming to our knowledge to knowledge conforming to the constitution of the subject. The doctrine is 'transcendental' because it concerns the a priori conditions of experience, and 'idealist' because appearances depend on the mind, though Kant maintained that things in themselves exist independently.
utopia-dystopia: Utopia and dystopia are contrasting ways of imagining society in order to reflect on politics and human possibility. A utopia depicts an ideal or perfected community—an image of how life might be justly and harmoniously arranged—while a dystopia portrays a nightmarish future in which such aspirations curdle into oppression, surveillance, or dehumanization. Since Thomas More coined "utopia," whose name puns on "good place" and "no place," both forms have served as thought experiments, using an imagined elsewhere to criticize present arrangements or warn against dangerous tendencies. Together they explore what social ideals promise and what their pursuit may cost.
zen: Zen is a school of Mahayana Buddhism, known as Chan in China and Zen in Japan, that emphasizes direct insight into one's own nature over reliance on scripture or doctrinal analysis. Growing from the meeting of Indian Buddhism with Chinese Daoist sensibilities, it stresses seated meditation, disciplined everyday practice, and transmission from teacher to student outside of written texts. Certain lineages employ the koan, a paradoxical question or story designed to exhaust discursive thinking and provoke a sudden shift in understanding. The aim throughout is awakening to reality as it is, unmediated by conceptual overlay.
class-struggle: Class struggle is Marx and Engels's claim, announced in the opening of The Communist Manifesto, that the history of society is a history of conflict between classes with opposing economic interests. In capitalism this conflict centers on the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who must sell their labor to survive. Marx held that this antagonism is built into the structure of production itself and that it would ultimately drive revolutionary change, making class conflict the engine of historical development.
culture-industry: The culture industry is a concept developed by Theodor Adorno, with Max Horkheimer, to describe how mass-produced entertainment—film, popular music, radio, and the like—is manufactured on industrial and commercial lines much like any other commodity. On their account this standardized, profit-driven culture promotes conformity and passivity, offering the appearance of choice while delivering more of the same and dulling audiences' capacity for critical thought. Rather than liberating, popular culture thus helps reconcile people to an unjust social order. The idea was central to the Frankfurt School's critique of modern capitalism and mass media.
epistemological-anarchism: Epistemological anarchism is the provocative position advanced by Paul Feyerabend, summarized in his slogan 'anything goes,' that there is no single fixed method or set of rules to which all good science must conform. Drawing on the history of science, Feyerabend argued that major advances often occurred precisely because researchers broke prevailing methodological norms, and that rigid prescriptions would have stifled progress. The phrase is less a positive rule than a rejection of universal method, defending theoretical pluralism and the freedom of inquiry against attempts to impose one privileged standard of rationality.
falsification: Falsificationism is Karl Popper's proposal that what distinguishes genuine science from pseudoscience is not verifiability but falsifiability: a theory is scientific only if it forbids something and can in principle be refuted by observation. Popper rejected the idea that we confirm theories by piling up supporting instances, arguing instead that we can never prove a universal law true but can decisively show it false. On this account science advances through bold conjectures exposed to severe testing, with theories provisionally accepted only so long as they survive sincere attempts to refute them.
hegel-dialectic: The dialectic is G.W.F. Hegel's method for tracing how thought, and reality itself, develops through contradiction and its resolution. A concept or condition generates a tension or opposition within itself, and this conflict is overcome in a higher stage that both cancels and preserves what came before—a movement Hegel captured with the term Aufhebung, or sublation. Often popularized as a triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, the dialectic for Hegel describes an immanent, self-driven unfolding rather than an external formula imposed on its subject matter. It underlies his account of logic, history, and spirit as processes that advance toward greater self-understanding and completeness.
hegemony: Cultural hegemony, a concept developed by Antonio Gramsci, describes how a dominant class maintains power not mainly through force but by shaping the shared beliefs, values, and common sense of a society. When the worldview that serves ruling interests comes to seem natural, obvious, or simply the way things are, subordinate groups consent to arrangements that disadvantage them. Gramsci saw this consent as produced through institutions such as schools, churches, and media—what he called civil society—rather than through the coercive state alone. Countering hegemony therefore requires cultural and intellectual struggle, not just political or economic confrontation.
kant-phenomena-noumena: In Immanuel Kant's critical philosophy, phenomena are things as they appear to us, structured by the mind's forms of intuition (space and time) and its categories of understanding, while noumena are things as they are in themselves, independent of any observer. Kant argued that human knowledge is confined to phenomena, because we can only know objects insofar as they conform to the conditions of our experience. The noumenal realm remains thinkable but strictly unknowable, a boundary Kant drew to curb metaphysical overreach while preserving room for freedom, morality, and faith. This distinction responds to disputes between rationalists and empiricists by relocating the source of order from the world itself to the knowing subject.
male-gaze: The male gaze names the way visual culture, and film in particular, tends to present the world from a heterosexual masculine point of view, positioning women as objects to be looked at rather than as active subjects. The concept was crystallized by film theorist Laura Mulvey, who drew on psychoanalysis to argue that classical cinema structures pleasure around a male spectator and a passive, eroticized female image. It has become a widely used tool for analyzing how images shape and encode relations of power between the sexes.
marx-alienation: Alienation is Karl Marx's term for the estrangement workers experience under capitalist production, developed especially in his early Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. Because laborers do not own what they make and sell their activity for wages, Marx argues they become separated from the products of their work, from the act of laboring itself, from their own human potential, and from one another. Work, which should express human creativity, instead becomes an external compulsion, and the theory grounds Marx's critique of how capitalism distorts human life.
master-slave-morality: In On the Genealogy of Morality, Nietzsche distinguishes two contrasting sources of moral valuation. Master morality arises among the strong and self-affirming, who call their own qualities "good" and see weakness as merely "bad"; slave morality arises among the oppressed and resentful, who first brand the powerful as "evil" and then define themselves as "good" by contrast. Nietzsche argues that much of modern Western morality, especially values like humility and pity, descends from this reactive slave revolt in ethics, and he uses the distinction to question the origins and worth of our inherited moral concepts.
objectification: Objectification is the treatment of a person as a mere object or instrument rather than as a being with dignity, autonomy, and a subjectivity of their own. In feminist philosophy it names especially the reduction of a person, most often a woman, to a body or a set of parts valued for the use or pleasure of others, denying full agency and moral standing. Philosophers such as Martha Nussbaum have analyzed it into distinct elements—like instrumentality, denial of autonomy, and fungibility—to clarify when and why treating someone as an object is wrong.
paradox-of-fiction: We can be moved to tears by characters we know do not exist — yet philosophers like Colin Radford argued this is paradoxical. We seem to feel genuine emotions only about things we believe real, we know fictional characters are not real, and still we grieve for Anna Karenina. The puzzle challenges what beliefs our emotions actually require.
philosophy-of-love: The philosophy of love examines the nature, varieties, and value of love, asking what it is to love another person and why love matters to a good life. Drawing on distinctions inherited from the Greeks — eros as desire, philia as friendship, agape as selfless care — it explores whether love is a response to a beloved's qualities or a commitment that bestows value, and how it relates to reason, autonomy, and morality. Central puzzles include whether love can be justified, whether it is under our control, and what it means to love someone for who they are.
plato-ring-of-gyges: The Ring of Gyges is a thought experiment in Plato's Republic in which a shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible and uses it to seize power without fear of being caught. Posed by the character Glaucon, it presses the question of why anyone would act justly if they could escape all consequences, suggesting that people behave morally only because they lack the means to get away with wrongdoing. The challenge forces Plato to argue that justice is worth having for its own sake, as a right ordering of the soul, and not merely for the reputation and rewards it brings. It remains a classic statement of the problem of why one should be moral.
plato-tripartite-soul: The tripartite soul is Plato's account, chiefly in the Republic, of the human psyche as composed of three parts: reason, which seeks truth and can grasp what is best; spirit, the seat of anger, ambition, and the love of honor; and appetite, the desires for food, drink, sex, and material goods. He argues for the division by noting inner conflict, as when a person is thirsty yet refuses to drink, showing that one part can oppose another. Justice in the individual consists in these parts fulfilling their roles under the rule of reason, mirroring the ordering of classes in the just city. The model grounds Plato's psychology, ethics, and political theory alike.
pragmatism: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition, largely American in origin, that judges the meaning and worth of ideas by their practical consequences rather than by their correspondence to a fixed reality. Emerging in the late nineteenth century through the work of Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, it holds that beliefs are tools for coping with experience and that a theory's value lies in how well it guides action and inquiry. Against the search for absolute, timeless truths, pragmatists treat knowledge as provisional, revisable, and continuous with everyday problem-solving.
ressentiment: Ressentiment, a French term Nietzsche adopts, names a smoldering resentment felt by those who are powerless to act on their hostility and instead turn it inward, reimagining their weakness as virtue. In his account of the origins of morality, this reactive feeling drives the "slave revolt" in ethics: unable to triumph directly, the aggrieved condemn the strong as evil and elevate meekness and restraint into moral ideals. Nietzsche treats ressentiment as a psychological engine that quietly reshapes values, generating morality from frustrated hostility rather than from strength.
scientific-realism: The debate between scientific realism and anti-realism concerns whether our best scientific theories should be understood as true descriptions of a mind-independent reality, including the unobservable entities they posit such as electrons and genes. Realists hold that the predictive success of science would be a miracle unless its theories were at least approximately true, so we have good reason to believe in the entities they describe. Anti-realists, including instrumentalists and constructive empiricists like Bas van Fraassen, counter that theories need only be empirically adequate—accurate about what we can observe—and point to the history of discarded but once-successful theories as reason for caution about deeper claims. The dispute turns on how much metaphysical commitment scientific success actually warrants.
simulacra: In Simulacra and Simulation, Jean Baudrillard argued that in a media-saturated society signs and images increasingly detach from any underlying reality and begin to circulate on their own. A simulacrum is a copy without an original: a representation that no longer refers to a real thing but only to other representations. Baudrillard called the resulting condition the "hyperreal," a world in which models, maps, and images feel more real and more authoritative than whatever they were once supposed to depict. The concept diagnoses a culture where the distinction between the real and its simulation has effectively collapsed.
terrorism-violence: The ethics of political violence asks when, if ever, the use of force outside ordinary law is morally justified in pursuit of political aims, and what distinguishes legitimate resistance from terrorism. Central questions include whether violence can be excused by the justice of a cause, whether the deliberate targeting of civilians is ever permissible, and how to weigh oppression, self-defense, and the prospects for peaceful change. Traditions such as just war theory, pacifism, and revolutionary thought offer competing answers, and terrorism—typically defined as violence against noncombatants to spread fear for political ends—poses an especially hard case. The debate concerns both the ends invoked and the moral limits on the means used to reach them.
thrownness: Thrownness, Heidegger's Geworfenheit, captures the fact that we always find ourselves already delivered into a situation we did not choose: a time, place, body, language, culture, and set of circumstances. We do not create the conditions of our existence but are "thrown" into them, and this facticity is the background against which any freedom or projection of possibilities takes place. The notion emphasizes that human existence is finite and situated, never a blank starting point.
ubermensch: The Übermensch, or "overman," is Friedrich Nietzsche's image of a human being who creates values out of their own strength rather than inheriting them from tradition, religion, or the crowd. Introduced in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, it responds to the collapse of inherited moral certainties: with old sources of meaning discredited, Nietzsche imagines a figure who affirms life and legislates new purposes for existence. It is an ideal or aspiration rather than a biological type, and Nietzsche presents it as the goal humanity might set for itself once it stops looking beyond this world for value.
utilitarianism: Utilitarianism is the moral theory holding that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall balance of well-being, or happiness, considered impartially across everyone affected. It emerged in Britain through the work of Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill as a reforming answer to moral systems grounded in tradition, intuition, or divine command, offering instead a single measurable standard for evaluating laws and conduct. Because it judges acts by their consequences rather than by intentions or rules, it counts each person's happiness equally and treats the good of the many as the aim of morality.
will-to-power: The will to power is Friedrich Nietzsche's proposed principle for understanding the deepest drive in living beings—not merely a wish to survive or to feel pleasure, but a striving to grow, overcome resistance, expand, and impose form on the world. Nietzsche developed the idea partly against Schopenhauer's blind will to life and against theories that reduced life to self-preservation, suggesting instead that organisms and individuals seek to discharge and enhance their strength. He extended the notion, in his notebooks especially, toward a broader interpretation of nature, knowledge, and value, though he never systematized it into a finished doctrine. It became central to his critiques of morality and to his vision of self-overcoming and the creation of new values.
amor-fati: Amor fati, Latin for "love of fate," is Nietzsche's formula for the highest affirmation of life: not merely to endure what happens but to love it, wanting nothing to be different in the past, present, or future. It stands opposed to resentment and to the wish that reality were other than it is, treating even suffering and necessity as things to be embraced rather than merely tolerated. Nietzsche presents this loving acceptance of one's whole existence as a sign of psychological greatness and a companion to his idea of eternal recurrence.
animal-rights: The subjects-of-a-life account of animal rights, developed by the American philosopher Tom Regan in The Case for Animal Rights (1983), holds that many animals are not mere resources but conscious beings with beliefs, desires, memory, and a welfare that matters to them. Because such creatures are subjects of a life, Regan argues, they possess inherent value and a right not to be harmed or used merely as means to human ends. This deontological position differs from utilitarian animal ethics by grounding protection in rights rather than in the calculation of overall pleasure and pain.
applied-ethics: Applied ethics brings moral theory to bear on concrete practical problems, working out what we ought to do in specific domains such as medicine, business, the environment, and emerging technology. In bioethics it addresses issues like consent, euthanasia, and the allocation of scarce care; in the ethics of technology and artificial intelligence it examines privacy, algorithmic bias, autonomy, and responsibility for machine decisions. Rather than defending a single grand theory, it tests principles against hard cases and aims at reasoned guidance that practitioners and policymakers can use.
aristotle-friendship: Aristotle devotes two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to philia, the bond of affection and goodwill that he counts among the goods essential to a flourishing life. He distinguishes three kinds: friendships of utility and of pleasure, which last only as long as the advantage or enjoyment does, and friendships of virtue, in which each person wishes the other well for the other's own sake. This last, complete form is rare and enduring, and for Aristotle it is both a school of good character and one of life's greatest goods.
binary-oppositions: Binary oppositions are the paired, contrasting terms—such as speech and writing, presence and absence, nature and culture, or reason and emotion—through which Western thought has often organized meaning. Jacques Derrida observed that such pairs are rarely equal: one term is typically privileged as primary or natural while the other is treated as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction targets this hierarchy, showing that the favored term secretly depends on the one it subordinates, so the opposition cannot hold as cleanly as it claims. Exposing this instability was central to Derrida's critique of how philosophy establishes and enforces value.
categorical-imperative: The categorical imperative is Immanuel Kant's supreme principle of morality, a command of reason that binds unconditionally rather than depending on any desired end. In its central formulation it directs one to act only on that maxim which one could at the same time will to become a universal law, testing whether the principle behind an action could be consistently adopted by everyone. Kant contrasted it with hypothetical imperatives, which tell us what to do only if we happen to want some goal, and made it the rational ground of moral duty.
consequentialism: Consequentialism is the family of ethical theories holding that the moral rightness of an action depends solely on its outcomes, so that one ought to act in whatever way produces the best overall results. It contrasts with deontological views, which judge acts by conformity to duties or rules, and with virtue ethics, which centers on character; utilitarianism is its most familiar version. Central debates within consequentialism concern what counts as a good outcome, whether to assess individual acts or general rules, and how to weigh consequences impartially across all affected parties.
death-of-god: "God is dead" is Nietzsche's diagnosis, most famously voiced by a madman in The Gay Science, that belief in the Christian God and the moral and metaphysical order it underwrote has lost its hold on Western culture. He does not mean it as a triumphant slogan but as an event of enormous consequence: without a divine guarantor of meaning and value, humanity risks sliding into nihilism unless it can create new values for itself. The phrase names both a cultural crisis and an opportunity, marking the loss of an absolute foundation and the task of finding meaning without one.
deconstruction: Deconstruction is a mode of critical reading developed by Jacques Derrida that exposes the tensions, gaps, and unstated assumptions within a text rather than seeking a single settled meaning. It challenges the idea that language transparently conveys fixed truths, showing how meaning always depends on differences and deferrals among signs and can undermine the very distinctions a text relies on. Rather than simply destroying a text, deconstruction reads it closely enough to reveal how it works against itself. The approach became central to poststructuralist thought and reshaped literary theory and philosophy alike.
deep-ecology: Deep ecology, a term coined by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess in the early 1970s, contrasts a superficial environmentalism concerned with pollution and resource management against a deeper view that questions the underlying worldview placing humans above nature. It affirms the intrinsic value of all living things, independent of their usefulness to people, and calls for a fundamental shift toward ecological self-realization and a smaller human footprint. The movement responds to the sense that piecemeal reform cannot address the root causes of environmental crisis.
deontology: Deontology is the family of ethical theories holding that the rightness of an action depends on its conformity to moral duties or rules, not merely on its consequences. Its most influential form is Immanuel Kant's, which grounds duty in the categorical imperative and insists that persons be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means. Deontology responds to the intuition that some acts, such as lying or killing the innocent, are wrong even when they would produce good results, thereby setting itself against consequentialist views that judge actions solely by their outcomes.
dichotomy-of-control: The dichotomy of control, most sharply stated by the Stoic Epictetus, divides everything into what is "up to us" and what is not. Our judgments, desires, and choices lie within our power, while our bodies, reputations, possessions, and outcomes ultimately do not. The practical counsel that follows is to invest our concern only in what we control and to accept the rest with equanimity, since misery arises from trying to command things that were never ours to command.
epicurean-death: The maxim that "death is nothing to us" is the core of Epicurus's argument against the fear of dying. Since Epicurus held that good and evil consist in sensation, and death is the total absence of sensation, he reasoned that death can neither be experienced nor harm the one who dies: where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. The teaching was meant not as cold consolation but as therapy, freeing people from an anxiety Epicurus considered the chief obstacle to a tranquil life.
epicurean-pleasure: Epicurus, founding his school in Athens around 300 BCE, taught that pleasure is the highest good and the natural aim of life, but he understood pleasure primarily as the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance rather than as sensual indulgence. This tranquil state, ataraxia, is best achieved through modest desires, friendship, and freedom from the fears of death and the gods, which he sought to dispel with his atomist physics. Epicurean ethics thus prizes a serene and self-sufficient contentment over intense or fleeting gratifications.
existence-risk: An existential risk is a threat that could cause the extinction of humanity or permanently and drastically curtail its potential for future flourishing. The term was developed by the philosopher Nick Bostrom, who argued that such risks deserve special moral urgency because their outcomes are both irreversible and vast in scale, potentially foreclosing all future generations. Candidate risks include engineered pandemics, nuclear war, runaway artificial intelligence, and certain environmental catastrophes. The concept reframes risk assessment around low-probability but astronomically high-stakes events that ordinary cost-benefit reasoning tends to neglect.
fascism: Fascism is a far-right political ideology that elevates the nation or race above the individual, celebrates strength and struggle, and demands a strong leader and a single party with unchecked power. Historical fascism, as in Mussolini's Italy and Nazi Germany, crushed dissent, attacked liberal democracy, and glorified war. Because regimes vary, many scholars describe it as a cluster of traits rather than one fixed doctrine.
grand-narratives: Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern condition as "incredulity toward metanarratives"—a loss of faith in the sweeping stories that once claimed to give history a single direction and legitimate knowledge. Grand narratives are overarching accounts such as the inevitable progress of reason, the emancipation of humanity through science, or the march toward a classless society, which promise to unify all lesser knowledge under one purpose. Lyotard held that these narratives had lost their credibility, leaving instead a plurality of smaller, local stories and language games with no master framework above them. The claim reframed both the status of knowledge and the character of modern culture.
kant-humanity-formula: The humanity formula is one of Immanuel Kant's expressions of the categorical imperative, requiring that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Because rational beings possess an intrinsic worth, or dignity, that is not exchangeable for any price, they must never be used simply as instruments for someone else's purposes. The principle grounds duties such as honesty and respect and has become a touchstone for arguments about human dignity and the wrongness of manipulation and coercion.
ockham-razor: Ockham's Razor is the methodological principle that, among competing explanations, one should not multiply entities or assumptions beyond necessity, so that the simpler account is to be preferred when it explains the evidence equally well. Named for the fourteenth-century logician William of Ockham, who favored parsimony in his rejection of superfluous metaphysical posits, it functions as a rule of theoretical economy rather than a proof of truth. It responds to the temptation to explain phenomena by inventing unobserved causes, urging that explanatory machinery be justified by what it actually accounts for.
plato-justice: Justice in Plato's Republic is defined as a harmony in which each part performs its proper role without overstepping into another's. In the ideal city this means the producers, the guardians, and the rulers each attend to their own function, and in the individual soul it means reason governs, spirit supports it, and appetite obeys. Plato develops this account to answer the challenge that justice is merely a useful convention, arguing instead that it is the healthy internal order that makes both a state and a person good. On this view justice is intrinsically valuable, since the well-ordered soul flourishes while the disordered one is at war with itself.
problem-of-evil: The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good with the reality of suffering and wrongdoing in the world. In its logical form it alleges an outright contradiction between such a God and any evil at all, while its evidential form argues that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely. Responses, known as theodicies, appeal to free will, soul-making, or the limits of human understanding to explain why a good God might permit evil.
sisyphus: In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus takes the figure condemned by the gods to roll a boulder eternally uphill only to watch it fall as the emblem of the absurd human condition. Rather than despair, he argues that Sisyphus can be imagined happy: by consciously embracing his fate without illusion or hope of reward, he wrests a kind of freedom and dignity from a meaningless task. The essay is Camus's answer to what he calls the only serious philosophical problem, whether life is worth living, and it concludes that one can affirm life precisely in the face of its lack of ultimate meaning.
supererogation: Supererogation refers to acts that go 'beyond the call of duty': morally admirable and praiseworthy, yet not required — like donating an organ to a stranger or running into a burning building. The category raises puzzles: if morality demands only the ordinary, what makes saints and heroes praiseworthy for doing more? Some ethicists doubt the category entirely, holding that if an act is morally best, it becomes obligatory.
thoreau-walden: Walden records Henry David Thoreau's experiment in deliberate living, undertaken during his two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, where he sought to strip life to its essentials and confront what it had to teach. His aim was to live simply and consciously—reducing needs, observing nature closely, and resisting the distractions of a commercial society—so as to discover what is truly necessary for a meaningful existence. The book blends memoir, natural observation, and social criticism into a sustained argument for self-examined, intentional life.
anthropocentrism: Anthropocentrism is the view that human beings are the central or most significant entities in the world, and that value or moral standing belongs primarily or exclusively to them. In environmental philosophy the term often carries a critical edge, naming the assumption that nature matters only insofar as it serves human interests. Critics argue that this outlook licenses exploitation of the nonhuman world, while defenders distinguish a chauvinistic version from a more modest claim that humans can only evaluate the world from a human standpoint.
boethius-consolation: The Consolation of Philosophy is a work written by Boethius while awaiting execution, in which the personified figure of Philosophy visits the imprisoned author to heal his despair through reasoned dialogue. Alternating prose and verse, it argues that true happiness lies not in the transient gifts of Fortune but in the highest good, which is identified with God, and it confronts the problems of evil, providence, and the compatibility of divine foreknowledge with human freedom. Boethius resolves the last of these by distinguishing God's timeless, eternal vision from temporal necessity. Blending classical philosophy with a broadly theistic outlook, the book became one of the most widely read texts of the Middle Ages.
bushido: Bushido, literally 'the way of the warrior', is the code of conduct associated with Japan's samurai class, emphasizing loyalty, honor, self-discipline, and readiness to face death. Later writers, notably Nitobe in 1899, presented it as a moral philosophy comparable to European chivalry, though historians debate how systematic the code was; following the Hagakure, some stress it was a death-ready mode of action rather than an ethics of right and wrong.
communitarianism: Communitarianism is a strand of political philosophy that stresses the role of community, shared traditions, and social ties in shaping individuals and grounding moral and political life. It arose partly as a critique of liberal theories, associated with thinkers like Rawls, that picture people as freely choosing individuals abstracted from their attachments. Michael Sandel, a leading communitarian voice, argues that we are 'encumbered' selves constituted in part by loyalties and memberships we did not choose, and that justice cannot be defined independently of a community's shared understandings of the good. Communitarians therefore emphasize civic participation, common purposes, and the moral significance of belonging.
constitutive-rules: Constitutive rules are rules that create an activity in the first place, rather than regulating behavior that exists independently. The rules of chess do not restrict some pre-existing practice; they define what a bishop is and what counts as checkmate, and without them there is no game at all. Philosophers such as Searle used this contrast to explain how institutions like money and marriage are built from shared rules.
democracy-theory: Democracy is a form of political rule in which authority is grounded in the people, who govern themselves either directly or through elected representatives. Philosophical debate about democracy concerns not only procedures such as voting and majority rule but also the values it is meant to realize—political equality, liberty, and legitimacy through the consent of the governed. Thinkers disagree about its proper scope and limits: whether it is chiefly a method for making collective decisions, a way of protecting rights, or an ideal of shared self-rule, and how it should guard against both tyranny and the domination of minorities. These questions run from ancient Athens through modern liberal and participatory theories.
embodiment: Maurice Merleau-Ponty made the lived body central to phenomenology, arguing against views that treat the body as a mere object or the mind as a detached spectator. On his account we do not merely have bodies but are our bodies, and perception, movement, and understanding all flow from a bodily engagement with the world that precedes reflective thought. This notion of embodiment recasts consciousness as situated and incarnate, so that our grasp of space, other people, and meaning itself is grounded in the way our bodies are already at home in a perceived environment.
greatest-happiness: The greatest happiness principle, as formulated by John Stuart Mill, states that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce its reverse, with happiness understood as pleasure and the absence of pain. It serves as the foundational standard of Mill's utilitarianism, extending Bentham's outlook while insisting that the happiness at stake is that of all affected parties, impartially considered, not merely the agent's own. The principle thus makes the general welfare, rather than any narrower interest, the ultimate criterion of morality.
hegel-geist: Geist, often translated as spirit or mind, is the central concept of Hegel's philosophy: a collective, rational, self-developing reality that expresses itself through human consciousness, culture, institutions, and history. It is neither a mere individual mind nor a supernatural entity but the unfolding of reason as it comes to know itself over time, realizing freedom in the process. Hegel spoke of spirit moving from subjective forms in the individual, through objective forms in law and society, to absolute forms in art, religion, and philosophy. The 'World Spirit' names this larger movement by which the rational structure of reality becomes conscious of itself through the whole course of human development.
hume-sentimentalism: The claim that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions expresses David Hume's view that reason alone cannot move us to act or set our ends. Reason, on his account, discovers facts and traces relations of ideas, but it is desires, feelings, and aversions that supply motivation; reason serves by finding the means to satisfy passions it does not itself generate. This sentimentalist position locates the springs of action and the foundations of morality in human feeling rather than in pure rationality.
invisible-hand: The invisible hand is Adam Smith's metaphor for the way individuals pursuing their own interests in a market can unintentionally promote outcomes that benefit society as a whole. Introduced in The Wealth of Nations, it holds that when people specialize and trade to their own advantage, the resulting coordination of prices and production tends to allocate resources efficiently without any central direction.
