The idea responds to the question of how order and mutual benefit can arise from self-interested action rather than deliberate design, though Smith himself hedged it with concern for justice and the moral limits of commerce.
machiavelli-ends: The phrase 'the ends justify the means,' popularly associated with Machiavelli, expresses the view that in politics the rightness of an action can be measured by whether it secures a necessary and beneficial result, even when the action itself would ordinarily be condemned. Machiavelli argued that a ruler concerned with preserving the state may have to be prepared to act against conventional morality, using deception or cruelty when circumstances demand, because judging politics by private ethics alone can lead to ruin. He did not straightforwardly endorse wrongdoing for its own sake; his emphasis was on effective results and the harsh realities of power. The idea raises the enduring question of whether political necessity can ever license immoral conduct.
machiavelli-virtu: Virtù and fortuna are the paired concepts through which Niccolò Machiavelli analyzes political success and failure. Fortuna is the element of chance, circumstance, and shifting events that no ruler fully controls, while virtù is the skill, boldness, and adaptable resolve by which a leader seizes opportunities and imposes order on them. Machiavelli's point is not that outcomes are fated but that fortune governs perhaps half of what happens, leaving the rest to human effort, so the capable prince prepares against reversals and acts decisively when the moment allows. Virtù here is a hard-edged political competence rather than moral virtue in the Christian sense.
macintyre-tradition: Alasdair MacIntyre sought to revive an Aristotelian account of the virtues by embedding them in the concepts of a practice, the narrative unity of a human life, and a moral tradition. A practice is a cooperative human activity with internal goods, such as medicine or chess, and the virtues are the qualities that enable us to achieve those goods and to sustain the practices and communities that transmit them. On his view, a single life is intelligible as a quest for the good, and that quest is always carried out from within a historically extended tradition of inquiry rather than from a neutral standpoint. MacIntyre argued that modern moral discourse is fragmented precisely because it has lost this teleological and traditional framework.
moral-egoism: Ethical egoism is the normative theory that each person ought to act in his or her own long-term self-interest, so that promoting one's own good is the standard of right action. It is distinct from psychological egoism, which merely claims that people do in fact act selfishly; ethical egoism says that they should. The position responds to the question of why morality should demand sacrifice, but it faces the objection that it cannot coherently guide cases where people's interests conflict, and that it seems to license harming others whenever doing so pays.
moral-relativism: Moral relativism is the view that moral judgments are not objectively true or false but are valid only relative to a particular culture, society, or individual point of view. It responds to the observable diversity of moral codes across times and places, and to the difficulty of finding a neutral standpoint from which to declare one code correct. Critics argue that consistent relativism makes it impossible to criticize practices such as slavery or persecution as genuinely wrong, while defenders see it as a safeguard against dogmatism and cultural arrogance.
pascals-wager: Pascal's Wager is Blaise Pascal's argument that belief in God is the rational bet even under uncertainty about whether God exists. Reasoning that the matter cannot be settled by proof, Pascal frames it as a decision under risk: if one believes and God exists, the gain is infinite, while if God does not exist, the loss is slight; disbelief risks an infinite loss for a small worldly gain. Because an infinite potential reward outweighs any finite stake, he concludes that prudence favors wagering on faith, a move often regarded as an early piece of decision theory as much as theology.
power-knowledge: Power/knowledge is Michel Foucault's thesis that power and knowledge are not opposed but intimately bound together, each producing and reinforcing the other. Rather than treating knowledge as a neutral discovery of truth that stands apart from power, Foucault argues that systems of power generate the categories, institutions, and expertise through which certain claims count as knowledge, while knowledge in turn organizes and justifies the exercise of power. Fields such as medicine, psychiatry, and criminology, on this view, both study and help constitute their objects, defining what is normal, healthy, or deviant. The concept reframes truth as something produced within relations of power rather than existing prior to them.
social-darwinism: Social Darwinism is the late-nineteenth-century application of biological notions of natural selection and "survival of the fittest" to human societies, economics, and politics. Associated especially with Herbert Spencer, who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest," it held that competition among individuals, groups, or nations was natural and beneficial, and it was often used to justify laissez-faire capitalism, social inequality, and, in some versions, imperialism and racial hierarchy. Widely criticized for confusing description with moral justification, it is now generally regarded as a misuse of evolutionary theory rather than a legitimate extension of it.
sun-tzu-strategy: Attributed to Sun Tzu in The Art of War, this approach holds that the highest form of strategy achieves its aims with minimal fighting, ideally subduing an opponent without direct battle at all. It stresses knowledge, preparation, deception, timing, and adapting to circumstances, so that victory is secured through positioning and foresight rather than brute force. Though framed for warfare, its counsel to win by shaping conditions in advance has been widely applied to politics, business, and everyday conflict.
the-uncanny: The uncanny, Freud's das Unheimliche, is the class of frightening things that are strangely familiar: the homely turned unhomely. Freud argued its horror comes from the repressed returning to light, in figures such as doubles, lifelike automatons, and the returning dead. This explains why beings that resemble us too closely, like Frankenstein's creature, can terrify more than obvious aliens.
will-to-believe: The will to believe is William James's argument that in certain cases we are entitled to adopt a belief on faith, before the evidence is conclusive, when the choice is genuine, momentous, and cannot be settled by intellect alone. James responded to the demand that we withhold assent until proof arrives, contending that some truths—especially moral and religious ones—only become available to those willing to commit in advance. Refusing to decide, he noted, is itself a choice with consequences, so passionate belief can be legitimate rather than a lapse in reason.
woman-as-other: In The Second Sex, Simone de Beauvoir argues that man has historically been treated as the default, the essential subject, while woman is defined only in relation to him as the "Other"—the inessential, the object against which he measures himself. This asymmetry, she contends, is not rooted in nature but produced and sustained by culture, myth, and social arrangement, so that femininity becomes a situation imposed rather than a destiny given. Understanding womanhood as Otherness exposes the mechanisms by which one group is cast as secondary and denied full standing as a free subject.
yin-yang: Yin and yang name a pair of complementary forces that, in Chinese thought, underlie all change and balance in the natural and social world. Yin is associated with qualities such as darkness, receptivity, and rest, and yang with light, activity, and assertion, but neither is good or evil; each contains a seed of the other and continually gives way to it. This idea offers a way of understanding reality as a dynamic interplay of opposites that must be kept in harmony rather than a battle in which one side must triumph.
apollonian-dionysian: In The Birth of Tragedy, Nietzsche describes two artistic and psychological impulses through Greek mythological figures. The Apollonian, named for Apollo, stands for order, clarity, individuation, form, and the beauty of measured appearance; the Dionysian, named for Dionysus, stands for ecstasy, intoxication, dissolution of the self, and the chaotic vitality beneath appearances. Nietzsche argues that Greek tragedy achieved greatness by fusing the two, and he uses the pair more broadly to analyze the tension between rational form and elemental energy in art and life.
argument-from-reason: An argument made famous by C. S. Lewis: if naturalism is true — if our beliefs are just products of irrational physical causes — then we have no reason to trust our own reasoning, including the reasoning behind naturalism itself. So, on this view, rational thought cannot be a purely natural process and points to a rational source behind the world. Critics, notably Elizabeth Anscombe, dispute whether this follows.
aristotle-soul: In his treatise On the Soul (De Anima), Aristotle defines the soul not as a separate substance lodged in the body but as its form: the organizing principle that makes a living thing the living thing it is. On this view the soul is the actuality of a body that has life potentially within it, so that soul and body are related as shape is to matter rather than as two independent items. He distinguishes nutritive, perceptive, and rational capacities, arguing that living things possess these powers in ascending degrees, with reason the distinctive mark of the human soul.
augustine-time: Augustine's reflections on time, set out in his Confessions, confront the puzzle that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the present has no duration, so it becomes unclear how time can be real or measured at all. His influential proposal is that time is bound up with the mind's activity: we measure it as a kind of extension or distension of the soul, holding the past through memory, the present through attention, and the future through expectation. On this view time is not an independent container but is tied to the created order and to conscious experience. The discussion remains a touchstone for later philosophy of time and mind.
berkeley-idealism: Subjective idealism, captured in the maxim esse est percipi, to be is to be perceived, is the view that physical objects have no existence independent of being perceived by a mind. George Berkeley argued that we are only ever acquainted with our own ideas and sensations, so it is incoherent to posit unperceived material substance behind them; what we call things are simply stable collections of sensible qualities. To explain why the world persists when no human observes it, he held that all ideas are continuously perceived by the infinite mind of God, making reality fundamentally mental rather than material.
catharsis: Aristotle's term in the Poetics for what tragedy does to its audience: by arousing pity and fear for the suffering hero, a play brings about a catharsis of those emotions — a purging, purification, or clarification (translators disagree) that leaves us unburdened rather than corrupted. This answers Plato's charge that drama merely whips up dangerous feelings. Today the word also names any safe emotional release through art.
compatibilism: Compatibilism is the view that free will and determinism can both be true: even if our actions are causally determined, we can still act freely in the sense that matters for moral responsibility. On this account, an action is free when it flows from the agent's own desires and reasoning without external coercion or compulsion, regardless of whether those states were themselves caused. Associated with thinkers from Hobbes and Hume to contemporary philosophers like Harry Frankfurt, compatibilism reframes freedom as a matter of the right kind of control rather than an ability to have done otherwise under identical conditions. Critics charge that this redefines freedom rather than securing the deeper autonomy people intuitively want.
cosmopolitanism-ethics: Cosmopolitanism, as developed by Kwame Anthony Appiah, is the ethical stance that all human beings belong to a single moral community and owe one another obligations that cross the borders of nation, culture, and creed. Appiah pairs this universal concern with a respect for particular, legitimate differences, arguing that we can take an interest in others' distinct ways of life without abandoning the conviction that some values are shared. His version emphasizes conversation across difference as the practical means by which strangers can come to understand and live with one another.
descartes-cogito: The Cogito is René Descartes's claim, captured in the phrase 'I think, therefore I am,' that the very act of doubting or thinking guarantees the existence of the thinker. Seeking an indubitable foundation for knowledge, Descartes found that while he could doubt the external world and even his own body, he could not coherently doubt that he was doing the doubting. The Cogito thus serves as the first certainty on which he attempts to rebuild a secure system of knowledge, and it places the self-conscious subject at the center of modern epistemology.
extended-mind: The extended mind thesis, proposed by Andy Clark and David Chalmers, holds that the mind is not confined to the brain or even the body but can literally extend into the environment when external tools become integrated into our cognitive processes. Their famous example imagines a man who relies on a notebook to store beliefs the way others rely on biological memory; if the notebook functions in the same role, they argue, it counts as part of his mind. The view challenges the intuitive boundary of skull and skin and has shaped discussions of cognition, technology, and personal identity.
forgiveness: Forgiveness is the philosophical topic of what it is to overcome resentment or blame toward someone who has wronged us, and when doing so is fitting. Typically analyzed as the deliberate letting go of justified negative emotions without denying that a wrong occurred, it raises questions about whether forgiveness must be earned through repentance, whether it can be owed or merely offered as a gift, and how it differs from excusing, condoning, or simply forgetting. It sits at the intersection of moral emotion, personal relationships, and the ethics of holding others accountable.
hegel-master-slave: The master–slave dialectic is a pivotal passage in Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit that depicts how self-consciousness comes to know itself only through another self-consciousness. Two subjects confront one another in a struggle for recognition; one risks death and prevails as master, while the other submits and becomes bondsman. Yet the relationship inverts itself: the master grows dependent on the slave's labor and recognition, while the slave, through disciplined work upon the world, develops genuine self-consciousness and freedom. The episode illustrates Hegel's claim that identity, freedom, and self-knowledge are essentially social, achieved through mutual recognition rather than in isolation.
incongruity-theory-humor: The leading philosophical theory of what makes things funny: we laugh when something violates expectation or fits no familiar pattern — a mismatch between setup and outcome. Kant and Schopenhauer gave it classic form: laughter comes from the sudden collapse of a strained expectation. Critics note it needs supplementing, since a broken expectation can shock rather than amuse, and much humor never gets resolved.
locke-personal-identity: John Locke argued that what makes a person the same individual over time is not the persistence of a soul or a body but the continuity of consciousness, especially memory. On this view, a person is a thinking, self-aware being who can regard itself as the same across different times and places, and identity extends only as far as that consciousness can reach back through remembered experience. The theory reframes selfhood as a psychological rather than a metaphysical fact, and it raised enduring puzzles about lapses of memory, forgotten deeds, and the boundaries of moral responsibility.
logical-positivism: A movement of the 1920s–30s Vienna Circle holding that a statement is meaningful only if it is true by definition or empirically testable. Its verifiability principle dismissed much traditional metaphysics and theology as not merely false but literally meaningless. The principle proved hard to state without destroying itself, and the movement was largely abandoned by mid-century — yet it shaped what analytic philosophy has counted as rigorous ever since.
minimal-state: The minimal state, or 'night-watchman state,' is Robert Nozick's ideal of a government limited to protecting people against force, theft, and fraud and to enforcing contracts. In Anarchy, State, and Utopia he argues that only such a state can be justified without violating individual rights, and that any more extensive state—one that redistributes wealth or imposes broader goals—wrongfully uses some people as means for others' ends. Nozick grounds this in an entitlement theory of justice, on which holdings are just if acquired and transferred through legitimate voluntary steps. His libertarian position stood as a direct rival to Rawls's more egalitarian liberalism.
panopticon: The panopticon is an architectural design for a prison, conceived by Jeremy Bentham, in which a central watchtower can observe every cell while the inmates cannot tell whether they are being watched at any given moment. Michel Foucault took it up as a model for modern disciplinary power: because prisoners may always be under observation, they come to regulate their own behavior, so surveillance produces self-discipline without constant force. For Foucault the panopticon symbolizes how modern institutions—prisons, schools, hospitals, factories—shape docile, self-monitoring individuals. The image has become a touchstone in discussions of surveillance, control, and the effects of being perpetually watched.
personal-identity: Personal identity concerns what makes someone the same person over time despite change, and what the self fundamentally is. Philosophers have offered competing criteria: the body or brain, continuity of memory and psychology, or the persistence of an immaterial soul. Locke's memory-based view, Hume's bundle theory that finds no enduring self behind experiences, and later refinements have all sought to say why the child and the adult, or the person before and after profound change, count as one and the same. The question matters for responsibility, anticipation, survival, and the concern we have for our own futures.
platonic-love: Platonic love, as presented in Plato's Symposium, describes an ascent in which erotic desire is gradually redirected from particular beautiful bodies toward ever higher objects, culminating in the contemplation of Beauty itself. Beginning with attraction to a single person, the lover comes to appreciate beauty in all bodies, then in souls, laws, and knowledge, before glimpsing the eternal Form of Beauty. This ladder of love treats desire not as something to be suppressed but as a force that, rightly guided, draws the soul toward truth. The modern sense of nonsexual affection derives loosely from this vision, though Plato's own account is a metaphysical journey toward the Forms.
political-animal: In the Politics Aristotle famously describes the human being as by nature a political animal (zoon politikon), meaning that we are constituted to live in an organized community and can fully realize our nature only within one. Unlike other social creatures, humans possess speech and reason, which enable them to deliberate about justice and the common good and so to form a city (polis). On this view the state is not an artificial contract imposed on naturally solitary individuals but the natural setting in which human flourishing becomes possible.
possible-worlds: Possible worlds are complete alternative ways things might have been, used in logic and metaphysics to analyze claims about necessity and possibility: a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in at least one. David Lewis defended the striking doctrine of modal realism, on which these worlds are not mere abstractions or fictions but concrete realities as fully existent as our own, spatiotemporally isolated from us. Though few accept Lewis's full realism, possible-worlds talk has become an indispensable tool across philosophy of language, modality, and counterfactual reasoning.
social-contract: The social contract is the idea that political authority and the obligation to obey it rest on an agreement, real or hypothetical, among the people who are to be governed. It responds to the question of what could legitimately bind free individuals to a common power rather than leaving them in a lawless condition. Thomas Hobbes gave the theory its classic modern form, arguing that in a state of nature life would be one of perpetual insecurity, so rational individuals consent to surrender much of their freedom to a sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. Later thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau reworked the terms of the bargain, but the shared move is to ground the state in consent rather than in divine right or brute force.
time-travel: The metaphysics of time travel examines whether travel to the past or future is coherent and what constraints it would impose. The chief puzzle is the grandfather paradox: if you could go back and prevent your own existence, you would undo the very journey that made this possible, so something must stop you. Philosophers such as David Lewis argue that time travel need not be contradictory, provided the past is fixed and the traveler's actions were always already part of it, ruling out any change to what has happened. Related debates concern causal loops, personal versus external time, and which theories of time even permit backward travel.
truth-in-fiction: The question of what counts as true inside a story. Some truths are stated outright ('Robin is Canadian'); many more are implied — we assume Sherlock Holmes has a heart, though Conan Doyle never says so, since background facts of the world carry over unless overridden. Philosophers like Kendall Walton and David Lewis analyze fiction as a game of make-believe whose truths are what the story instructs us to imagine.
augustine-will: The divided will is Augustine of Hippo's analysis of the experience of wanting and not wanting the same thing, in which a person genuinely commands the will to act yet finds it resisting itself. Drawing on his own struggles, he argues that this internal conflict reveals not two natures but a single will fractured and weakened, unable to fully follow what it knows to be good. This condition he traces to the disordering effects of sin, from which the will cannot free itself by its own effort but requires divine grace. His treatment reshaped Western thinking about freedom, motivation, and the limits of self-mastery.
being-toward-death: Being-toward-death is Heidegger's account of how mortality shapes human existence not as a distant event but as an ever-present possibility that structures how we live. Because death is one's own, certain, and cannot be delegated to anyone else, honestly facing it individualizes a person and can pull them out of anonymous everyday distraction. Anticipating death, on this view, is not morbid but a condition for grasping one's life as a finite, unified whole and living it authentically.
dasein: Dasein, literally "being-there," is Martin Heidegger's term for the kind of being that we ourselves are—the entity for whom its own existence is at issue and who has an implicit understanding of what it means to be. Rather than treating the human as a substance or thinking subject, Heidegger analyzes Dasein through the ways it is always already involved in a world, engaged with things and others. The concept reframes the study of the human around care, temporality, and the question of Being itself.
dewey-experience: Experience and education names John Dewey's philosophy of learning, which holds that genuine education grows out of and reorganizes lived experience rather than transmitting inert facts. Reacting against both rote traditional schooling and unstructured permissiveness, Dewey argued that educative experiences must be continuous, connecting to what came before and opening onto further growth, and interactive, engaging the learner with a real environment. Teaching, in this scheme, is the thoughtful arranging of conditions so that students inquire, test ideas, and develop the habits of intelligent reflection.
hegel-history: Hegel held that history is not a random succession of events but a rational, purposive process in which spirit progressively realizes freedom. He famously described world history as 'progress in the consciousness of freedom,' advancing through the rise and fall of civilizations, each embodying a stage in the self-development of reason. Individuals and even great historical figures often serve ends larger than they intend, a dynamic Hegel called the 'cunning of reason.' While this teleological view has been widely criticized as speculative or as rationalizing suffering, it profoundly shaped later philosophies of history, including Marx's materialist reworking of dialectical development.
heidegger-technology: In his reflections on technology, Heidegger argues that its essence is not any particular machine or tool but a mode of disclosure he calls "enframing," in which everything shows up as a stockpile of resources to be ordered and exploited. Modern technology thus reveals nature and even human beings as mere "standing-reserve," narrowing our sense of what things are. Heidegger warns that this way of seeing is dangerous because it threatens to conceal other, richer relations to the world, yet he suggests that recognizing it may also open a path toward a freer relationship with technology.
hume-induction: The problem of induction concerns whether we are ever justified in inferring from observed cases to unobserved ones, such as expecting the future to resemble the past. David Hume argued that such inferences rest on a presumption of the uniformity of nature that can be established neither by logic, since no contradiction follows from denying it, nor by experience, since that would already assume the very principle in question. He concluded that inductive expectation is grounded in habit and custom rather than rational demonstration, a skeptical result that continues to shape the philosophy of science.
just-war-theory: Just war theory is the tradition of moral reasoning about when it is permissible to go to war and how war may rightly be waged. Rooted in thinkers such as Augustine and Aquinas and later secularized, it distinguishes jus ad bellum — conditions like just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, and last resort — from jus in bello, which governs conduct in war through principles of discrimination between combatants and civilians and proportionality of force. It offers a middle path between pacifism, which rejects all war, and realism, which denies that morality applies to it.
kant-aesthetics: In his account of aesthetic experience, Immanuel Kant distinguished the judgment of taste—our claim that something is beautiful—from mere personal liking by arguing that it is disinterested, universal in its demand, and grounded in a free harmony between imagination and understanding. When we call an object beautiful, we speak as if the pleasure should be shared by everyone, even though the judgment rests on feeling rather than a concept. The sublime, by contrast, arises when we confront the vast or overwhelming in nature; our sensibility is overpowered, yet reason's capacity to conceive infinity reveals a dignity within us that exceeds any sensory magnitude. Kant developed these ideas in the Critique of Judgment, linking aesthetic feeling to the wider unity of his philosophical system.
land-ethic: The land ethic, articulated by the American forester and conservationist Aldo Leopold in A Sand County Almanac (1949), proposes that ethical concern should extend beyond individual humans to the whole biotic community of soils, waters, plants, and animals. Leopold famously held that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of that community, and wrong when it tends otherwise. It reframes humans not as conquerors of the natural world but as plain members and citizens of it, responding to the destructive effects of treating land purely as economic property.
monadology: Monadology is Gottfried Leibniz's metaphysics of simple, indivisible, immaterial substances he called monads, which are the true elements of reality. Each monad is a self-contained point of perception with no windows, meaning it does not causally interact with others; instead their states are coordinated by a divinely established pre-established harmony so that the whole universe is mirrored, from its own perspective, within each one. On this view the material world of extended bodies is a well-founded appearance grounded in these mind-like unities rather than in inert matter.
nietzsche-perspectivism: Perspectivism is Nietzsche's view that there is no purely objective, view-from-nowhere knowledge; all seeing and knowing occurs from some particular standpoint shaped by interests, drives, and circumstances. Rather than concluding that anything goes, he suggests that understanding grows by drawing on many perspectives, since the more angles we bring to bear on a matter, the more complete our grasp of it becomes. The idea challenges the notion of a single absolute truth and treats our concepts and values as interpretations rather than neutral mirrors of reality.
noble-lie: The noble lie is a myth that Plato, in the Republic, proposes rulers might tell citizens to promote social harmony and loyalty to the just city. In his example, the people are to be told that they were born from the earth and that a god mixed different metals into their souls, marking each for a particular station. Plato presents this founding fiction as beneficial rather than malicious, intended to bind the community and reconcile people to their roles. The idea raises enduring questions about whether useful falsehoods can be justified in politics and about the tension between truth and stability in a well-ordered society.
ontological-argument: The ontological argument, first formulated by Anselm of Canterbury, attempts to prove God's existence from the concept of God alone, without appeal to observation of the world. Anselm defines God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived and reasons that such a being must exist in reality and not merely in the mind, since a being that existed in reality would be greater. Uniquely among the classic proofs it is entirely a priori, moving from an idea to a conclusion about existence. It has provoked continuous debate, from Gaunilo's early objection through Kant's charge that existence is not a genuine predicate, and continues to attract both defenders and critics.
personalism: Personalism is the family of views holding that the person — unique, self-conscious, capable of free choice and love — is the highest kind of value and must never be treated as a mere thing. Thinkers from Borden Parker Bowne to Max Scheler and Martin Buber developed it, and it informed Martin Luther King Jr.'s social ethics. Institutions, on this view, exist for persons, not the reverse.
phenomenology: Phenomenology is the philosophical study of experience as it is lived and given to consciousness, aiming to describe the structures of appearance rather than to explain them causally. Inaugurated as a rigorous method by Edmund Husserl, it asks us to set aside assumptions about the external world—the so-called bracketing or epoché—so as to attend to phenomena precisely as they present themselves. Later thinkers such as Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty extended it toward questions of existence, embodiment, and being, making it one of the most influential movements of twentieth-century thought.
pragmatic-truth: Truth as what works is the pragmatist account, developed especially by William James, that a belief is true insofar as it proves useful in guiding us successfully through experience. Rather than defining truth solely as a static match between statement and fact, James held that ideas become true through a process of verification—they "work" by leading to reliable expectations and satisfactory dealings with the world. Critics charged that this confuses truth with mere expediency, and James spent much effort insisting that genuine working must answer to reality, not personal convenience.
sophist-relativism: The dictum that man is the measure of all things comes from the sophist Protagoras, active in fifth-century BCE Athens, and expresses a relativist view of truth and value. On this reading things are as they appear to each perceiver, so that what is true, good, or just is relative to individuals or communities rather than fixed by any absolute standard. The position challenged the notion of objective knowledge and provoked lasting responses from Plato and others, who saw in it a threat to the possibility of genuine truth.
speciesism: Speciesism is the term, popularized by Peter Singer, for a bias that gives greater moral weight to the interests of members of one's own species simply because of species membership. By analogy with racism and sexism, the charge is that treating a being's suffering as less important merely because it is not human is an arbitrary prejudice rather than a defensible moral distinction. Singer argues that the morally relevant question is whether a being can suffer, and that consistency requires extending equal consideration of interests across the boundary of species.
stoic-cosmopolitanism: Stoic cosmopolitanism is the idea that every human being, sharing in reason, belongs to a single universal community that transcends city and nation. Voiced by thinkers from Zeno to Seneca and Marcus Aurelius, it holds that we are "citizens of the world" bound to one another by a common rational nature and therefore owed justice and concern regardless of birth or status. This vision widened the scope of moral obligation beyond the local polis and later shaped ideals of universal human dignity.
stoic-present-moment: Living in the present is a recurring theme in Stoic thought, articulated with particular force by Marcus Aurelius. Since the past is gone and the future not yet ours, the Stoics held that only the present moment is truly in our possession and the only thing we can actually lose or use well. Attending fully to the here and now, rather than being dragged by regret or fear, is offered as a path to freedom from disturbance and to right action.
taoism: Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Tao, the underlying pattern and source of all things. Associated with the Daodejing attributed to Laozi and the writings of Zhuangzi, it prizes spontaneity, simplicity, and naturalness over rigid convention, striving, and artificial control. As a philosophy it counsels yielding to the natural course of events rather than forcing outcomes, and it later developed into organized religious forms with their own practices and pursuit of longevity.
turing-test: Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the Turing Test replaces the vague question "can machines think?" with a concrete behavioral test: if a human judge, communicating only through text, cannot reliably tell a machine's responses from a person's, the machine should count as intelligent. The proposal sidesteps disputes about inner experience by treating conversational indistinguishability as the criterion for thought. It has framed decades of debate in artificial intelligence and the philosophy of mind about whether behavior alone can settle questions of genuine intelligence.
williams-integrity: Bernard Williams argued that utilitarianism, by demanding that agents always act to maximize overall good, fails to respect a person's integrity—the coherent web of deeply held commitments and projects that make a life one's own. His famous cases of George the chemist and Jim and the Indians are meant to show that requiring someone to set aside their fundamental convictions whenever the aggregate calculus demands it treats them as a mere channel for producing states of affairs. This assault on integrity, he claimed, alienates people from their own actions and from the ground projects that give their lives meaning. The critique became a central objection to impartial consequentialist ethics and to overly systematic moral theory generally.
animal-liberation: Animal Liberation is Peter Singer's 1975 book arguing that the interests of non-human animals deserve equal moral consideration, and it became a foundational text of the modern animal rights movement. Drawing on a utilitarian concern for suffering, Singer contends that because many animals can feel pain, their suffering counts morally in the same way human suffering does, and that ignoring it is a form of prejudice. The book applies this argument to practices such as factory farming and animal experimentation, urging sweeping changes in how humans treat other sentient beings.
aquinas-double-effect: The doctrine of double effect, whose classic formulation derives from Thomas Aquinas, addresses when it is permissible to perform an action that has both a good and a seriously harmful consequence. It holds that such an act may be justified if the act itself is not wrong, the good effect is what one intends while the harm is merely foreseen and not the means to the good, and the good achieved is proportionate to the harm allowed. Aquinas developed it in discussing self-defense, where preserving one's life is intended and the attacker's death is not. The principle remains central to debates in medical ethics, warfare, and moral philosophy about the difference between intending and merely foreseeing harm.
aristotle-four-causes: Aristotle's doctrine of the four causes holds that a full explanation of anything requires answering four distinct questions about it: what it is made of (the material cause), what form or structure makes it the kind of thing it is (the formal cause), what brought it into being (the efficient cause), and what end or purpose it serves (the final cause). He developed this scheme in the Physics and Metaphysics as a response to earlier thinkers who, he argued, had grasped only fragments of true explanation. Because it treats purpose as a genuine kind of cause, the theory undergirds Aristotle's broadly teleological view of nature.
benjamin-aura: Walter Benjamin used the notion of "aura" to name the unique presence and authority that a traditional work of art possesses by virtue of its singular existence in a particular time and place. In his essay on the work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction, he argued that technologies such as photography and film, by producing endless copies, strip artworks of this aura and detach them from ritual and tradition. Benjamin viewed this loss with ambivalence: it diminished a certain reverence, yet it also opened art to mass audiences and to new political possibilities. The concept remains influential in thinking about art, media, and authenticity.
black-skin-white-masks: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) is Frantz Fanon's psychological and philosophical study of how colonialism and racism deform the inner life of the colonized. Drawing on psychoanalysis, phenomenology, and his own experience, Fanon analyzed how a racist world can lead Black people to internalize inferiority and to strive to assume the values, language, and self-image of the white colonizer. The work is a foundational text of anticolonial thought, examining the alienation imposed by a society that fixes people within a devalued racial identity.
confucian-li: Li refers to the rituals, manners, and forms of proper conduct that structure social and ceremonial life in Confucian thought. Ranging from religious rites to everyday etiquette, li provides the concrete patterns through which people express respect, mark relationships, and harmonize their communities. Confucius held that observing li was not empty formality but a means of cultivating inner virtue, so that outward propriety and genuine moral feeling reinforce one another.
dewey-democracy: Democracy as a way of life is John Dewey's conviction that democracy is not merely a form of government but a mode of shared, cooperative living rooted in communication, inquiry, and mutual respect. For Dewey, self-rule means people continually participating in the associations that shape them—workplaces, schools, communities—and reconstructing those institutions through intelligent, experimental problem-solving. On this view voting and elections are only the outer machinery; the deeper substance is a culture in which individuals grow by contributing to and learning from a common life.
food-ethics: Food ethics is the study of the moral questions surrounding how food is produced, distributed, and consumed, spanning the treatment of animals in agriculture, the environmental impact of farming, fair labor and trade, and personal choices such as vegetarianism. It asks whether practices like factory farming are justifiable, how responsibility for hunger and food waste should be understood, and what a just food system would look like. The field connects individual eating habits to large-scale ethical, ecological, and economic concerns.
hegel-recognition: The struggle for recognition is Hegel's thesis that a person achieves self-consciousness and freedom only by being acknowledged as a self by others who are themselves recognized as free. Recognition cannot be one-sided or coerced; genuine selfhood requires reciprocity, a mutual acknowledgment among equals. Where recognition is denied or distorted, as in the domination of master over bondsman, both parties are diminished and the relationship is inherently unstable. This idea, developed in the Phenomenology of Spirit, has become foundational for later social and political theory concerned with identity, respect, and the harms of misrecognition.
heraclitean-flux: Heraclitus of Ephesus, writing around 500 BCE, is remembered for the doctrine that everything is in ceaseless change, captured in the saying that one cannot step into the same river twice. Beneath this flux, however, he posited the logos, a unifying rational principle or measure that orders the world's constant transformations and holds opposites in tension. His view that reality is a dynamic balance of strife and change stands as an early counterpoint to those who sought a stable, unchanging foundation for things.
kant-respect: Respect for persons is the Kantian idea that every rational being possesses an unconditional worth, or dignity, that must never be treated merely as a means to someone else's ends. It follows from Kant's formulation of the categorical imperative requiring that we act so as to treat humanity, in ourselves and others, always also as an end in itself. Because persons are capable of setting their own ends and legislating moral law through reason, they command a form of regard categorically different from the price we attach to mere things. This principle grounds much of modern rights discourse and the moral prohibition on using, deceiving, or coercing people in ways that bypass their rational agency.
kingdom-of-ends: The kingdom of ends is Immanuel Kant's ideal of a moral community in which all rational beings are united under common laws that each of them legislates and to which each is subject. Every member is at once a lawgiver and one who obeys, and each is treated as an end in themselves possessing dignity rather than a mere means. Kant offered this vision as a further formulation of the categorical imperative, inviting us to act as though we were always legislating for such a systematic union of rational agents.
memetics: Richard Dawkins coined the 'meme' in 1976 as a unit of culture — a tune, catchphrase, belief, or practice — spread by imitation, mutating and competing for minds much as genes compete under natural selection. Memetics treats cultural change as an evolutionary process; critics question whether 'memes' are real, well-defined units, so the idea remains controversial.
mill-liberty: On Liberty is John Stuart Mill's 1859 essay defending individual freedom against the coercive power of the state and the pressure of majority opinion. Its central claim, the harm principle, is that society may restrain a person only to prevent harm to others, leaving self-regarding conduct free. Mill argues at length for freedom of thought and discussion, contending that even false opinions serve truth by testing it, and he warns against the stifling conformity he called the tyranny of the majority.
paradigm-shift: A paradigm shift, a notion made central by Thomas Kuhn in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), is a fundamental change in the framework of assumptions, methods, and exemplary problems that guides a scientific community. Kuhn argued that science proceeds not by steady accumulation but through long periods of 'normal science' under a reigning paradigm, punctuated by crises when mounting anomalies force a revolutionary switch to a new one. Because rival paradigms can be 'incommensurable,' the transition involves a wholesale reorientation of how practitioners see the world, not merely the addition of new facts.
parfit-teleportation: The teleporter and fission cases, developed by Derek Parfit, test what personal identity really consists in. If a machine scans and destroys you, then builds an exact replica elsewhere, is the replica you or merely a copy—and does the answer change if the original is not destroyed, or if two replicas are made? Parfit argues that in such fission scenarios there is no determinate fact about which future person is you, and concludes that identity is not what matters for survival. What matters instead is psychological continuity and connectedness, and recognizing this, he suggests, should loosen our fixation on the persistence of a single self.
pragmatic-method: The pragmatic method, first sketched by Charles Sanders Peirce, is a rule for clarifying the meaning of a concept by tracing the practical effects we would expect if it were true. To grasp what an idea signifies, one asks what observable differences it would make in experience and conduct; if two rival notions imply no such difference, they mean the same thing. Peirce intended this as a discipline for settling otherwise interminable metaphysical disputes by tying meaning to conceivable consequences.
racial-contract: In The Racial Contract (1997), Charles W. Mills argued that the familiar social-contract tradition of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau conceals an unspoken agreement among those classified as white to establish and maintain a global order of racial domination. On this reading, the abstract 'persons' of contract theory were tacitly restricted to white men, while nonwhite peoples were excluded from full personhood and subjected to conquest and exploitation. Mills used the idea to expose how a supposedly neutral political philosophy has underwritten and normalized white supremacy.
rousseau-natural-goodness: This is Rousseau's claim that human beings are naturally good, or at least innocent, and that vice, inequality, and misery arise not from our nature but from the development of society and its institutions. In the imagined state of nature people are self-sufficient and compassionate, but the growth of property, comparison, and dependence corrupts them, breeding pride, envy, and injustice. The thesis reverses the older view that civilization tames a naturally wicked animal, and it frames Rousseau's political and educational projects as attempts to recover or protect that original goodness. It shaped Romanticism and modern debates about whether social conditions or human nature is the deeper source of our ills.
rousseau-social-contract: The general will is Jean-Jacques Rousseau's term for the collective will of a political community aimed at the common good, as distinct from the mere sum of individuals' private interests. Rousseau argued that a legitimate state is one whose laws express this general will, so that in obeying them citizens are in effect obeying themselves and remain free even while bound. The idea addresses how a people can be governed without being subjected to any particular person's domination, locating sovereignty in the citizen body as a whole. It remains influential and controversial, since deciding what the general will actually requires, and who speaks for it, is far from straightforward.
sartre-freedom: For Sartre, human beings are radically free and therefore wholly responsible, "condemned to be free" because we cannot avoid choosing even when we try. Since no God, nature, or external authority determines our values, every action is a self-defining commitment, and in choosing for ourselves we implicitly affirm an image of what a human being should be. This freedom is not liberating comfort but a heavy burden, inseparable from anguish and the impossibility of blaming circumstances for who we become.
ship-of-theseus: The Ship of Theseus is a puzzle about identity over time, reported by the biographer Plutarch, who noted that the Athenians preserved Theseus's ship by gradually replacing its decaying planks. This raises the question of whether the ship remains the same object once every original part has been swapped out, and whether identity resides in matter, form, or continuity. The thought experiment has become a standard way of probing what makes something persist as one and the same thing despite the replacement of its parts.
state-of-nature: The state of nature is a philosophical thought experiment imagining human life before or without political authority, used to justify the origins and limits of government. In Thomas Hobbes's version, set out in Leviathan, the absence of a common power leaves people in a condition of insecurity and mutual fear — a "war of all against all" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" — which rational individuals escape by contracting to submit to a sovereign. Later thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau reimagined the state of nature quite differently, but each used it to argue what legitimate political power must secure.
watchmaker-argument: The watchmaker argument, given its most famous form by the English clergyman William Paley in Natural Theology (1802), reasons that just as finding a watch on a heath would lead one to infer a designer, the intricate order and apparent purpose of living things point to an intelligent designer of nature. It is a version of the teleological, or design, argument for the existence of God. The argument was influentially challenged by David Hume before Paley and later undercut by Darwin's account of how natural selection can produce apparent design without a designer.
aquinas-natural-law: Natural law, as systematized by Thomas Aquinas, is the theory that there is an objective moral order accessible to human reason and grounded in the rational nature that all persons share. Aquinas holds that natural law is the rational creature's participation in the eternal law by which God governs creation, and that its first precept is to do good and avoid evil, from which more specific duties follow by reflecting on natural human goods such as life, knowledge, and society. Because it rests on reason rather than revelation, it is meant to bind all people regardless of faith or culture. The theory has profoundly shaped Western ethics, jurisprudence, and ideas of human rights.
aquinas-virtues: In the ethics of Thomas Aquinas, human excellence is organized around two sets of virtues. The four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—are acquired through habit and reason and were inherited from classical antiquity, governing how a person deliberates and acts well in ordinary life. The three theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—are, by contrast, held to be infused by grace and to orient the person toward God as the ultimate end. Together they express Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotelian moral psychology with Christian theology, in which natural virtue is completed rather than replaced by the supernatural.
becoming-woman: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" is Simone de Beauvoir's most famous line, marking her insistence that gender is not a biological given but a social and historical construction. On this view the traits taken to define femininity are instilled through upbringing, expectation, and constraint rather than dictated by anatomy, so that being a woman is a role one is shaped into rather than an essence one possesses. The claim helped separate sex from gender and became a foundational move for later feminist thought.
berlin-two-liberties: In his 1958 lecture Two Concepts of Liberty, Isaiah Berlin distinguishes negative liberty, the absence of interference by others, from positive liberty, the capacity for self-mastery or self-rule. Negative liberty asks how wide the area is within which a person may act unobstructed; positive liberty asks who or what governs one's choices. Berlin warned that the ideal of positive liberty, however attractive, can be twisted into justifications for coercion when authorities claim to know a person's 'real' self or true interests better than the person does, and he defended the priority of leaving individuals a protected sphere of noninterference.
camus-revolt: Rebellion, for Camus, is the constructive response to the absurd: rather than surrendering to nihilism or false hope, the rebel says no to injustice and suffering while affirming a value shared with others. In The Rebel he distinguishes this metaphysical and moral revolt—which asserts human solidarity and sets limits—from revolution that sacrifices present lives to an abstract future and thereby betrays its own origin. Revolt thus becomes a way of creating meaning and holding to human dignity without appealing to any transcendent guarantee.
civil-disobedience: Civil disobedience, as argued by Henry David Thoreau in his 1849 essay, is the deliberate, nonviolent refusal to obey unjust laws or support an unjust government, accepting the legal penalty as a form of moral protest. Prompted by his opposition to slavery and the Mexican–American War, Thoreau insisted that individual conscience outranks the dictates of the majority and that a just person may be obliged to withdraw cooperation from wrongdoing. His argument later influenced figures such as Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. in shaping mass movements of principled resistance.
cynicism: Cynicism was an ancient Greek philosophical movement, epitomized by Diogenes of Sinope in the fourth century BCE, that urged living in accordance with nature and in defiance of social convention. The Cynics held that virtue is the only good and that happiness comes from freedom, self-sufficiency, and the rejection of wealth, status, and artificial desires, which they regarded as sources of servitude. Diogenes dramatized these ideas through a deliberately austere and provocative way of life, making the movement as much a practice as a set of doctrines.
discipline: Michel Foucault used the paired ideas of discipline and docile bodies to describe how modern power shapes individuals not chiefly through spectacular force but through routine, minute training of the body. In institutions such as schools, prisons, factories, and armies, techniques of timetabling, surveillance, ranking, and correction organize movement and habit so that people internalize control and regulate themselves. The result is the "docile body": one made both more useful and more obedient. Foucault argued that this quiet, productive form of power, rather than sovereign command, is characteristic of modern society.
emerson-self-reliance: Self-reliance is the ideal Ralph Waldo Emerson championed in his 1841 essay of that name: the summons to trust one's own intuition and conscience rather than conform to society's expectations, traditions, or the opinions of others. Emerson urged that each person carries an original relation to truth and that imitation is a kind of suicide of the soul, so integrity means acting from inner conviction even at the cost of appearing inconsistent. The doctrine celebrates individual nonconformity as the wellspring of genuine thought and moral courage.
epistemology-of-testimony: Much of what we know — history, science, geography — comes from what other people tell us. The epistemology of testimony asks when accepting such secondhand claims is rational: Hume argued we need evidence of each speaker's reliability, while Thomas Reid held that we are naturally inclined to trust others and they to be truthful. Most recent work seeks flexible, case-by-case rules.
freud-civilization: In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Sigmund Freud argues that human happiness is fundamentally at odds with the demands of civilized life. To live together, individuals must renounce or redirect their aggressive and sexual instincts, and this enforced restraint produces a lasting, guilt-laden dissatisfaction. Freud locates the price of order in the internalized conscience, or superego, which turns aggression back against the self, so that the more successful a civilization becomes at securing peace, the more discontent it may breed in those who sustain it.
gender-performativity: Gender performativity is Judith Butler's thesis that gender is not the expression of a stable inner essence but is constituted through repeated acts, gestures, and stylizations of the body that produce the illusion of a natural, fixed identity. On this view there is no 'doer behind the deed': the appearance of an underlying gendered self is an effect of the very performances it seems to cause. Developed in Gender Trouble (1990), the idea challenges the assumption that sex grounds gender and opens space for understanding how norms can be subverted through their own repetition.
gettier-problem: The Gettier problem, named for Edmund Gettier's brief 1963 paper, challenges the long-standing definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Gettier presented cases in which a person holds a belief that is both true and justified yet intuitively fails to count as knowledge, because the belief is true only by luck—its justification and its truth are connected in the wrong way. The problem prompted decades of work in epistemology attempting to add a fourth condition or reformulate the analysis so as to rule out such accidentally true justified beliefs.
harm-principle: The harm principle, advanced by John Stuart Mill in On Liberty, holds that the only legitimate ground on which power may be exercised over an individual against their will is to prevent harm to others. On this view a person's own good, whether physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for coercion, so conduct that affects only oneself lies beyond the rightful reach of law or social pressure. The principle marks out a protected sphere of individual liberty and has become a touchstone in debates over paternalism, free expression, and the limits of state authority.
hume-miracles: In his essay on miracles David Hume argued that no testimony can rationally establish that a miracle has occurred. Since a miracle is by definition a violation of a law of nature supported by uniform and extensive experience, the evidence against it is as strong as evidence can be, whereas human testimony is often mistaken or deceptive. Hume concluded that a wise person should believe a miracle report only if its falsehood would be even more improbable than the event it describes, a standard he thought testimony could rarely if ever meet.
institutional-theory-of-art: The institutional theory of art, associated with George Dickie and building on Arthur Danto, holds that something becomes art not by how it looks but through its position in the artworld — created or presented by someone acting within the institutions of art, such as galleries, museums, and criticism. This explains why a signed urinal can be art, though critics ask what it implies about artistic value.
locke-natural-rights: Natural rights are entitlements that individuals possess by virtue of their humanity rather than by the grant of any government. John Locke held that in a state of nature persons hold rights to life, liberty, and property that precede political authority, and that the legitimate purpose of government is to protect these rights by consent of the governed. The idea supplied a standard against which states could be judged and justified resistance to rulers who violated it, deeply influencing later liberal and revolutionary political thought.
metabolic-rift: The metabolic rift is Marx's term, revived by John Bellamy Foster, for the rupture capitalism drives between humanity and nature: soil nutrients travel from farms to cities as food and never return, livestock and crops are severed, and waste flows back faster than the earth can absorb. It names a structural imbalance in how society appropriates nature, not merely a pollution problem.
moral-luck: Moral luck is the puzzle that arises when factors beyond an agent's control seem to affect how much moral praise or blame they deserve, even though a widely held principle says people should be judged only for what is within their control. Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel independently drew attention to it: a reckless driver who happens to kill a child is blamed far more than an equally reckless driver who happens to hit no one, though the difference is sheer chance. Nagel distinguished several varieties, including luck in outcomes, in circumstances, and in the constitution one is born with. The problem is troubling because it suggests that ordinary moral judgment cannot be reconciled with the intuition that responsibility should track only voluntary choice.
public-sphere: The public sphere is a concept associated with Jürgen Habermas, denoting a domain of social life in which private individuals come together to discuss matters of common concern and form public opinion through reasoned debate. Habermas traced its emergence to the coffeehouses, salons, and print culture of early modern Europe, where in principle argument counted for more than social rank. He argued that this space is essential to democratic legitimacy, but warned that commercialization and mass media can degrade it into managed spectacle and manufactured consent. The idea has become a touchstone for debates about media, democracy, and civic discourse.
pyrrhonian-skepticism: Pyrrhonian skepticism, traced to Pyrrho of Elis and systematized by Sextus Empiricus, is a practice of suspending judgment (epochē) about how things really are. Confronted with equally strong arguments on opposing sides of any question, the skeptic withholds assent rather than affirming or denying, holding that the appearances alone can guide daily life. The aim is practical: by giving up the anxious search for certainty, the skeptic hopes to attain ataraxia, a state of untroubled calm.
scientism: Scientism is the view that science — or the methods of the natural sciences — is the only genuine source of knowledge, so that claims in ethics, aesthetics, or religion are mere opinion or nonsense. Critics distinguish it from respect for science: they argue that valuing science itself, and judging how it should be used, requires norms that science alone cannot supply.
standard-of-taste: In 'Of the Standard of Taste,' David Hume asked how judgments of beauty can be more than personal preference if beauty lies in the feeling of the beholder. His answer: some judges are genuinely better — those with practice, wide comparison, freedom from prejudice, and delicacy of sentiment — so taste, while not mathematical fact, is answerable to shared human nature and ideal critics.
veil-of-ignorance: The veil of ignorance is a thought experiment devised by John Rawls to work out principles of justice that fair-minded people could accept. He asks us to imagine choosing the basic rules of society from an 'original position' in which we do not know our own place in it—our class, talents, race, gender, or conception of the good. Deprived of this knowledge, no one can tailor the rules to favor their own situation, so the principles chosen will be impartial and fair to all. Rawls argued that parties behind the veil would prudently choose principles protecting basic liberties and the worst-off, since anyone could turn out to be in that position.
abduction: Inference to the best explanation, also called abduction, is a form of reasoning in which you start from surprising facts and work backward to the hypothesis that, if true, would best account for them. Introduced by the American philosopher Charles Peirce, it differs from deduction, which guarantees its conclusion, and induction, which generalizes from examples. Many hold that everyday reasoning, from medical diagnosis to detective work, runs largely on it.
bergson-laughter: In his 1900 essay Laughter, Henri Bergson analyzed the comic as arising when we perceive "something mechanical encrusted upon the living." We laugh, he argued, at rigidity, repetition, and automatism in what ought to be supple and adaptive—a person behaving like a machine, a stiff gesture, an absent-minded slip into routine. Laughter thus serves a social function, gently correcting the inelastic and demanding that people stay flexibly attentive to life. The account ties his theory of comedy to his broader philosophy of duration, spontaneity, and the difference between the living and the merely mechanical.
double-consciousness: Double consciousness is W.E.B. Du Bois's description, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), of the divided self-awareness produced by living within a society that devalues one's race. He wrote of the sense of 'always looking at one's self through the eyes of others' and of feeling one's 'twoness'—being both American and Black in a nation that grants full recognition to neither together. The concept captures the psychological strain of measuring oneself by the standards of a world that regards one with contempt or pity.
drowning-child: The drowning child is a thought experiment introduced by Peter Singer to argue that affluent people have a strong moral obligation to aid those in dire need far away. Singer asks the reader to imagine passing a shallow pond where a child is drowning: rescuing the child at the cost of muddy clothes is obviously required, since a trivial loss cannot outweigh a life. He then contends that distance and the presence of other potential helpers make no real moral difference, so failing to donate to prevent distant, avoidable death is comparably wrong to walking past the pond.
frankfurt-bullshit: In his essay On Bullshit, Harry Frankfurt offered a philosophical analysis of a familiar but under-theorized form of speech, arguing that the bullshitter differs fundamentally from the liar. A liar knows the truth and deliberately asserts its opposite, thereby still respecting truth as the thing to be evaded, whereas the bullshitter simply does not care whether what he says is true or false and speaks only to serve some other purpose, such as impressing an audience. Frankfurt concluded that this indifference to truth makes bullshit a greater enemy of truth than lying is. The essay is a compact case study in conceptual analysis applied to a phenomenon of everyday communication and public life.
freud-death-drive: The death drive, sometimes called Thanatos, is the concept Sigmund Freud introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) to name a fundamental urge toward dissolution, aggression, and a return to an inanimate state. He proposed it to explain phenomena the pleasure principle could not, such as the compulsion to repeat traumatic experiences and the persistence of self-destructive behavior. Set against Eros, the life drive that binds and preserves, the death drive expresses a countervailing tendency toward discharge, destruction, and the undoing of tension. The idea remains among Freud's most speculative and disputed, yet influential in later psychoanalytic and cultural theory.
freud-unconscious: The unconscious is the cornerstone of Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis: a region of the mind holding thoughts, memories, and desires that are hidden from awareness yet powerfully shape feeling and behavior. Freud held that many such contents are actively repressed because they are threatening or unacceptable, and that they resurface in disguised form through dreams, slips of the tongue, symptoms, and jokes. Interpreting these expressions was, for him, the route to understanding neurosis and the self. The claim that we are not transparent to ourselves—that much mental life is inaccessible to introspection—has been enormously influential and much contested.
golden-rule: The Golden Rule is the ethical principle that one should treat others as one would wish to be treated, often stated as "do unto others as you would have them do unto you." Versions of it appear across many religious and philosophical traditions, from Confucius and the Hebrew Bible to the Christian Gospels, which is part of its appeal as a candidate universal moral standard. It works by asking an agent to reverse perspectives and test a proposed action for reciprocity, though philosophers note that it can mislead when people's preferences or circumstances differ sharply.
historical-materialism: Historical materialism is Marx's theory that the fundamental driver of historical change is the way societies organize material production. On this view, the economic base—the forces and relations of production—shapes a society's political institutions, laws, and dominant ideas, and history advances through transformations in these material conditions and the class conflicts they generate. Developed with Friedrich Engels, it reframes history not as a story of ideas alone but as a succession of modes of production, each carrying the tensions that eventually give rise to the next.
hume-is-ought: The is–ought problem observes that arguments frequently slide from statements about what is the case to conclusions about what ought to be, without explaining how the shift is warranted. David Hume noted that a purely factual or descriptive premise cannot by itself entail a prescriptive or moral conclusion, since the terms of obligation appear only in the conclusion and nowhere in the premises. The point challenges attempts to derive morality directly from natural facts and has framed much subsequent debate in ethics about the gap between fact and value.
kierkegaard-anxiety: Anxiety, in Søren Kierkegaard's analysis, is the peculiar unease that arises when a person confronts their own freedom and the open range of what they might become. Unlike fear, which has a definite object, anxiety has no object; it is the dizziness we feel gazing into the abyss of possibility, aware that we could choose otherwise. Kierkegaard treats it not as a mere pathology but as a defining mark of the self, bound up with the awareness of sin and the demand to become an individual before God.
levinas-face: Emmanuel Levinas placed ethics before metaphysics, arguing that our most fundamental relation is not knowledge of the world but the encounter with another person. In this encounter the "face" of the Other confronts me with an infinite claim that I cannot reduce to my own categories or possess; it commands me and calls me to responsibility before I have chosen it. For Levinas this face-to-face relation is the origin of moral obligation, making responsibility for the Other the first fact of human existence rather than a consequence of contract or calculation.
mackinnon-dominance: Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach reframes sex inequality not as a matter of irrational difference between the sexes but as a system in which men hold power and women are subordinated. On this account sexuality itself is socially constructed around male dominance, so practices like pornography and sexual harassment are not marginal excesses but mechanisms that eroticize and entrench that hierarchy. MacKinnon argued that law should confront this inequality directly, treating pornography as a civil-rights harm rather than protected expression.
natural-kinds: Philosophers distinguish natural kinds from nominal kinds. Natural kinds, like water, gold, or tigers, are held to be genuine divisions in nature, discovered rather than invented, each with an underlying structure explaining why its members share properties. Nominal kinds, like chair or game or zombie, exist only through our classificatory practice. Many hold that nature supplies real differences but never carves itself into kinds, leaving some line-drawing to us.
philosophical-zombies: A philosophical zombie is an imagined being physically and behaviorally identical to a normal human but wholly lacking conscious experience—there is nothing it is like to be it, even as it walks, talks, and reacts exactly as we do. David Chalmers uses the apparent conceivability of such creatures to argue that consciousness cannot be fully explained by physical facts alone, since a complete account of brain and behavior would leave the presence of subjective experience unexplained. The thought experiment sharpens the so-called hard problem of consciousness and remains a central weapon in debates between physicalists and their critics.
plantinga-basic-beliefs: A properly basic belief is one a person is rationally entitled to hold without inferring it from other beliefs or supporting it with argument. The idea challenges classical foundationalism, which restricts the legitimately basic to what is self-evident, incorrigible, or evident to the senses; Alvin Plantinga argued that this criterion is both too narrow and self-refuting, since it does not itself meet its own standard. On his reformed epistemology, beliefs such as the existence of other minds, the reality of the past, and belief in God can be properly basic when they arise in the appropriate circumstances from properly functioning cognitive faculties. The account thus aims to show that religious belief need not rest on evidential proofs to be rational.
pythagorean-harmony: The harmony of the spheres is a doctrine associated with Pythagoras and his followers in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, who held that number and proportion are the ultimate principles of reality. Struck by the discovery that musical intervals correspond to simple numerical ratios, they extended this insight to the cosmos, imagining that the heavenly bodies move according to harmonious mathematical relationships and even produce an inaudible music. The idea expresses the deeper Pythagorean conviction that the order of the universe is fundamentally mathematical.
quine-indeterminacy: The indeterminacy of translation is W. V. O. Quine's thesis that there is no uniquely correct way to translate one language into another, because incompatible translation manuals can each fit all possible behavioral evidence equally well. In his 'radical translation' scenario, a linguist confronting an unknown tongue could never fix, from observation alone, whether a native term means 'rabbit' or 'undetached rabbit part.' Quine drew from this the more radical conclusion that facts about meaning are not fully determined by any facts at all, unsettling assumptions about linguistic and mental content.
schopenhauer-will: In Arthur Schopenhauer's metaphysics, the world we perceive is mere representation, appearance ordered by the mind, while its inner reality is Will—a blind, purposeless striving that underlies all of nature and every living thing. Adapting Kant's distinction between appearance and thing-in-itself, Schopenhauer identified the thing-in-itself with this restless Will, manifest in the drives of animals, the growth of plants, and even the forces of inanimate matter. Because the Will is a ceaseless craving without ultimate aim, existence driven by it is marked by perpetual want and dissatisfaction. He set out this vision in The World as Will and Representation, where art and, more fully, the denial of the will offer relief from its demands.
sense-reference: Sense and reference is the distinction Gottlob Frege drew to explain how expressions relate to the world and to our understanding of them. The reference of a term is the object it stands for, while its sense is the particular mode of presentation, the way that object is given to us. Frege illustrated this with 'the morning star' and 'the evening star,' which share a reference (Venus) but differ in sense, thereby explaining why identity statements can be informative rather than trivial, and laying a foundation for modern philosophy of language.
spinoza-monism: Substance monism is Baruch Spinoza's doctrine that there exists only one infinite substance, which he identifies with God and nature alike in the phrase Deus sive Natura, 'God or Nature.' Everything that exists—minds, bodies, and events—is not a separate thing but a mode or modification of this single substance, expressed through its infinite attributes, of which we grasp thought and extension. Rejecting the idea of a transcendent creator standing apart from the world, Spinoza reconceives God as the immanent, necessary system of reality itself, from which all things follow.
sufficient-reason: The Principle of Sufficient Reason, central to Gottfried Leibniz's philosophy, states that nothing is the case, and nothing happens, without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise. Paired with the principle of non-contradiction, it governs all truths of fact and drives Leibniz's arguments in metaphysics, including his cases for God's existence and for the best possible world. It expresses a deep confidence that reality is thoroughly intelligible: every fact, however contingent, is in principle explicable, and there are no brute, reasonless features of the world.
thomson-violinist: The violinist argument is a thought experiment devised by Judith Jarvis Thomson to defend the permissibility of abortion even granting, for the sake of argument, that a fetus is a person with a right to life. She imagines waking up surgically connected to a famous unconscious violinist who will die unless he uses your kidneys for nine months, and argues that although unplugging yourself causes his death, you are not morally obligated to remain connected. The point is that a right to life does not entail a right to use another person's body, so bodily autonomy can override even an innocent person's claim to survival. The argument shifts the abortion debate away from the moral status of the fetus and toward what one person may be required to do for another.
