trolley-problem: The trolley problem is a thought experiment in which a runaway trolley will kill five people unless it is diverted onto a side track where it will kill one, forcing a choice about whether it is permissible to act so that one dies instead of five. Introduced by Philippa Foot and later elaborated by Judith Jarvis Thomson, it is designed to test intuitions about the difference between killing and letting die, and between harm caused as a means and harm caused as a side effect. Its power comes from contrasting cases that seem numerically identical yet elicit opposite moral judgments, such as diverting the trolley versus pushing a large man off a bridge to stop it. The problem has become a standard tool for examining the doctrine of double effect and the limits of consequentialist reasoning.
anarchism: Anarchism is a political philosophy that regards the state and other forms of coercive, hierarchical authority as illegitimate and unnecessary, and seeks a society organized instead through voluntary cooperation, mutual aid, and self-governance. Anarchists hold that people can order their affairs without rulers, and they differ over means and emphasis, from the mutualism and collectivism of thinkers like Proudhon and Bakunin to the communism of Kropotkin and later individualist and syndicalist currents. The tradition shares a critique of concentrated power—political and often economic alike—as a source of domination. It aims not at chaos but at a stateless order built from the bottom up.
aquinas-five-ways: The Five Ways are Thomas Aquinas's five concise arguments for the existence of God, presented at the opening of his Summa Theologiae. Each begins from a familiar feature of the observable world and reasons toward a necessary first cause: motion requires an unmoved mover, causation a first cause, contingency a necessary being, degrees of perfection a supreme measure, and the order of nature an intelligent designer. Aquinas identifies the terminus of each argument with what people call God. Drawing heavily on Aristotle, the Five Ways became a standard framework for natural theology and remain a focus of philosophical discussion.
banality-of-evil: The banality of evil is a phrase coined by Hannah Arendt in her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a Nazi administrator of the Holocaust. She used it to describe her impression that Eichmann was driven less by fanatical hatred or monstrous depth than by thoughtlessness, careerism, and an unreflective willingness to follow orders and cliché. The provocative claim is that immense evil can be carried out by ordinary people who fail to think about what they are doing, rather than only by demonic villains. Widely debated and often misunderstood, the idea directed attention to the moral dangers of unthinking obedience within bureaucratic systems.
chinese-room: John Searle's Chinese Room is a thought experiment designed to show that running a program is not sufficient for genuine understanding. He imagines himself locked in a room, following a rulebook to manipulate Chinese symbols and produce fluent replies without understanding a word of Chinese; the room as a whole passes for a Chinese speaker, yet no one and nothing inside grasps meaning. Searle uses the case to argue against "strong AI," contending that syntax—the formal manipulation of symbols—can never by itself yield semantics, the actual understanding of what symbols mean.
climate-ethics: Climate ethics is the branch of moral philosophy that studies the ethical questions raised by human-caused climate change, including who bears responsibility for emissions, how burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed, and what is owed to future generations and to the world's poorest people. It grapples with problems of collective action, historical responsibility, and the difficulty of assigning duties when harms are diffuse and long-delayed. The field asks how principles of justice apply when the consequences of present choices fall largely on those who did least to cause them.
ethics-of-belief: The ethics of belief holds that believing is something we can be praised or blamed for. In an 1877 essay, W. K. Clifford argued that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, telling of a ship-owner who silences his doubts and sends an unseaworthy ship to sea. William James famously replied that some commitments are too vital to wait for proof.
functionalism: Functionalism is a leading theory of mind on which a mental state — pain, belief, desire — is defined by what it does, not what it is made of: its causes, effects, and relations to other states. If so, minds need not be built from neurons; anything playing the right causal roles, silicon included, could realize one. This openness to non-biological minds makes functionalism central to debates about artificial intelligence.
i-thou: The I–Thou relation is a central idea of the Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, set out in his 1923 work I and Thou. Buber distinguishes two basic ways of relating to the world: the I–It attitude, in which we treat others as objects to be used, analyzed, or experienced, and the I–Thou attitude, in which we meet another as a genuine presence in a direct, mutual encounter. Authentic existence, for Buber, is dialogical, arising in these moments of meeting, which he saw as ultimately pointing toward relation with the eternal Thou, or God.
informal-fallacies: Informal fallacies are common patterns of bad reasoning identified by content and context rather than broken logical form — attacking the arguer instead of the argument (ad hominem), misrepresenting a position to knock it down (straw man), or treating a contested chain of consequences as inevitable (slippery slope). Naming them sharpens everyday argument, though accusations of fallacy can themselves be misapplied, since a suspect-looking move is sometimes legitimate.
justice-as-fairness: Justice as fairness is the name John Rawls gave to his theory of a just society, developed most fully in A Theory of Justice. Its core is that principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would agree to under fair conditions, modeled by the original position and the veil of ignorance. Rawls proposed two main principles: each person is guaranteed an extensive scheme of equal basic liberties, and social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they attach to positions open to all and work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. The theory offered a systematic liberal alternative to utilitarianism and reshaped political philosophy in the late twentieth century.
locke-labor-property: The labor theory of property holds that a person acquires a rightful claim to a previously unowned thing by mixing their labor with it. John Locke reasoned that although the earth is given to humanity in common, each individual owns their own body and its work, so gathering, cultivating, or fashioning something makes it one's own. He qualified this with provisos that one should leave enough and as good for others and not let goods spoil, offering an early attempt to justify private property from within a framework of natural rights.
maslow-hierarchy-of-needs: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is Abraham Maslow's proposal that human motivation is organized in levels: we generally secure physiological needs and safety before belonging, esteem, and finally self-actualization — becoming all we can be — become our driving concerns. Though widely taught and intuitively appealing, the strict ordering has been empirically questioned, and the model survives more as a flexible picture of what people need than as a rigid law.
nagarjuna-emptiness: Emptiness, or sunyata, is the teaching that all things lack any fixed, independent essence and exist only in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designation. It was developed most rigorously by the Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, who used relentless dialectical arguments to show that positing self-existent entities leads to contradiction. Rather than a claim that nothing exists, emptiness holds that things are real precisely because they are dependently arisen and thus without inherent nature. For Nagarjuna this insight dissolves the grasping and metaphysical confusion that bind beings to suffering.
narrative-identity: Narrative identity is the idea that we make sense of who we are by shaping our lives into stories — selecting events, finding connections, and casting ourselves as characters whose actions follow from a developing plot. Thinkers such as Alasdair MacIntyre and Paul Ricoeur hold that this storytelling is not decoration but partly constitutive of the self. Critics counter that some selves, and some lives, resist narrative form altogether.
one-dimensional-man: In One-Dimensional Man, Herbert Marcuse argued that advanced industrial society pacifies and absorbs dissent by satisfying material desires and manufacturing new ones through consumption and technology. The "one-dimensional" person is one whose critical, oppositional, and imaginative capacities have been flattened, so that thought and behavior no longer reach beyond the existing system to envision genuine alternatives. Even apparent freedoms and comforts, Marcuse suggested, serve to integrate individuals more deeply into the status quo. A member of the Frankfurt School, he offered the book as a critique of how affluent capitalism neutralizes radical possibility.
open-society: The open society is Karl Popper's ideal, elaborated in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), of a political order that permits criticism, tolerates dissent, and holds its rulers and institutions accountable through peaceful reform. He contrasted it with 'closed' societies governed by tribal certainties or grand historical blueprints, and attacked thinkers such as Plato, Hegel, and Marx as intellectual ancestors of totalitarianism. Popper tied the open society to his fallibilism: because no one possesses final truth, political arrangements should be provisional, revisable, and open to correction in light of their consequences.
prisoners-dilemma: The prisoner's dilemma is a game-theory puzzle: two suspects who cannot coordinate each do best by betraying the other, whatever the other does, yet if both betray, both end up worse than if both had stayed loyal. It captures how individually rational choices can produce collectively bad outcomes. The strategy tit-for-tat — cooperate first, then mirror your partner's last move — showed cooperation can emerge when the game is repeated.
private-language: The private language argument, developed in Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations, contends that a language whose words refer to purely private, inwardly known sensations—intelligible in principle to no one but the speaker—is impossible. Because such a language would offer no public criteria for using a term correctly, there could be no genuine distinction between following a rule and merely seeming to, and so no real meaning at all. The argument targets the assumption that mental terms get their sense by private ostension and reshapes debates about the relation between language, mind, and the shared world.
problem-of-other-minds: The problem of other minds asks how we can know that anyone besides ourselves has a mind — that behind outward faces there is real experience rather than unfeeling machines. I have direct access to my own pain but only to others' outward signs. Proposed answers range from analogy to treating belief in other minds as the best explanation of behavior; some argue the question dissolves once language is understood.
reid-common-sense: Common sense philosophy is the position that certain basic beliefs—in the existence of the external world, other minds, and the general reliability of our faculties—are foundational principles we are entitled to accept without proof. Thomas Reid developed it in direct response to the skeptical conclusions of Hume, arguing that a philosophy which ends by denying what everyone unavoidably believes has gone astray in its premises rather than uncovering the truth. He held that these first principles are built into the constitution of the mind and that trusting them is a mark of sound reasoning, not credulity.
reliabilism: Reliabilism is a family of theories in epistemology, associated especially with Alvin Goldman, that ground the justification or knowledge-status of a belief in the reliability of the process that produced it. On this view a belief counts as justified when it is formed by a process—such as accurate perception or sound reasoning—that tends to yield true beliefs, rather than by any evidence the believer can consciously cite. Reliabilism arose partly as a response to Gettier-style cases and shifts the focus of epistemic evaluation from internal reasons to the truth-conducive workings of belief-forming mechanisms.
searle-intentionality: Biological naturalism is John Searle's account of how mind fits into the physical world: consciousness and intentionality are real, higher-level features of the brain, caused by neurobiological processes much as digestion is caused by the stomach. Intentionality is the mind's capacity to be about or directed at things—beliefs are about states of affairs, desires about outcomes—and Searle holds this aboutness to be an intrinsic, biologically grounded feature that cannot be reduced to mere symbol processing. The position aims to take consciousness seriously as a genuine phenomenon while denying both dualism and the claim that computation alone produces a mind.
situationism: Situationism, in ethics, is a challenge from social psychology to the idea of stable character. Studies such as Milgram's obedience experiments and the hurried-seminarian study suggest that small situational pressures — an authority present, being late — predict behavior better than presumed virtues or vices do. If so, the ideal of firmly good character may be empirically shaky, one many philosophers accept only partially, arguing character survives in weakened form.
wilderness-ethics: Wilderness and nature aesthetics concern the value we find in wild places and the appropriate way to appreciate natural beauty. Ethically, debates turn on whether wilderness has worth apart from human use and whether the very idea of pristine, untouched nature is coherent given human history. Aesthetically, philosophers ask how appreciation of a landscape differs from appreciation of art, and whether knowledge of ecology and natural science should inform and deepen our experience of the natural world.
a-series-time: J.M.E. McTaggart distinguished two ways of ordering events in time. The A-series ranks them as past, present, or future—positions that continually shift as what was future becomes present and then past—while the B-series orders them by the fixed relations of earlier-than and later-than. McTaggart argued that the A-series is essential to real change yet incoherent, since any event must possess all three incompatible properties of pastness, presentness, and futurity, and he concluded that time itself is unreal. The distinction has framed modern debate between tensed theories of time, which take the passage of the present seriously, and tenseless theories built on the B-series.
arendt-totalitarianism: Totalitarianism, as analyzed by Hannah Arendt in The Origins of Totalitarianism, names a novel and radical form of domination exemplified by Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia. Unlike ordinary tyranny, it seeks total control not just of politics but of every sphere of life, fusing ideology and terror to remould human beings and abolish spontaneity, plurality, and independent thought. Arendt traced its roots to phenomena such as antisemitism, imperialism, and the rise of atomized mass society, and argued that its concentration camps aimed to render people superfluous. Her account remains a landmark attempt to understand how such regimes arise and why they are distinct from earlier despotisms.
aristotle-potentiality: Aristotle draws a fundamental distinction between potentiality (dynamis) and actuality (energeia or entelecheia) to explain how change and being are possible. A thing is potentially what it can become and actually what it presently is: an acorn is potentially an oak, and becoming an oak is the actualization of that potential. Introduced largely in the Metaphysics, the pair lets Aristotle answer earlier puzzles about whether anything can genuinely come to be, and it grounds his account of motion, growth, and the priority of the actual over the merely possible.
best-possible-world: The doctrine of the best of all possible worlds is Gottfried Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil, holding that a perfectly wise and good God, surveying every possible world, necessarily chose to create the one with the greatest overall balance of goodness. Apparent evils and imperfections are permitted only because they are inseparable from a greater good or a richer, more harmonious whole. Since God could not do less than the best, the actual world, for all its flaws, must be optimal—a claim Voltaire later famously satirized but which Leibniz meant as a serious defense of divine justice.
capabilities-approach: The capabilities approach, developed by Martha Nussbaum in dialogue with the economist Amartya Sen, evaluates human well-being and justice in terms of what people are actually able to do and to be—their real freedoms or capabilities—rather than by resources, wealth, or subjective satisfaction. Nussbaum proposes a list of central human capabilities, such as life, bodily health, the use of the senses and imagination, practical reason, and affiliation, that a just society owes to each person up to a threshold level. The approach insists on treating each person as an end and attends to how circumstances and social arrangements enable or block genuine functioning. It has been influential in development economics, human rights, and theories of social justice.
cartesian-theater: The Cartesian theater is Daniel Dennett's derisive label for a mistaken picture of consciousness in which there is a central place in the brain where everything 'comes together' and is presented to an inner observer, as if on a screen. Dennett argues this image is an incoherent remnant of Cartesian dualism, since it merely relocates the puzzle of experience to a homunculus who would need its own inner theater in turn. In its place he proposes a 'multiple drafts' model, on which mental content is distributed across parallel processes with no single finish line where consciousness happens.
cyborg: A cyborg is a hybrid of organism and machine. Donna Haraway made the cyborg a feminist symbol: a being whose mixed nature dissolves firm boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, undermining 'natural' categories like gender. Many argue we are already cyborgs — vaccines, pacemakers, and phones are part of us — so the boundary was never clean.
difference-principle: The difference principle is the part of John Rawls's theory of justice that governs social and economic inequalities. It holds that such inequalities are just only insofar as they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society; otherwise a more equal distribution is required. The principle does not demand strict equality but permits differences in wealth and position when they raise the prospects of those at the bottom, for instance by providing incentives that increase overall resources. It reflects Rawls's conviction that the natural distribution of talents and starting points is morally arbitrary, so a fair society arranges its institutions to make the worst-off as well off as possible.
ecofeminism: Ecofeminism examines the connection between the domination of women and the domination of nature, arguing that both stem from a shared logic of hierarchy and dualism that ranks culture over nature, reason over emotion, and man over woman. The Australian philosopher Val Plumwood, among its leading theorists, criticized the way Western thought treats nature as a passive, valueless background to human activity. The view seeks to dismantle these interlocking structures of oppression and to recover a relational understanding of humans as embedded in the natural world.
eugenics: Eugenics is the project of improving a human population by controlling who reproduces, encouraging 'desirable' traits and discouraging 'undesirable' ones. Twentieth-century programs included forced sterilization, and the 'eu' (good) in eugenics quietly smuggles in a judgment about which lives count as good stock. The central moral question is who decides which traits count, and by what right.
family-resemblance: Wittgenstein observed that some concepts resist definition by fixed conditions shared by all their instances. 'Game' is his example: board games, ball games, and solitaire share no single common feature, only overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like faces in one family. He argued many words work this way — learned through examples rather than strict definitions.
frankl-meaning: Drawing on his survival of the Nazi concentration camps, Viktor Frankl argued that the deepest human drive is not pleasure or power but the search for meaning, and that a person can endure almost any suffering if they can find significance in it. Logotherapy, the psychotherapeutic approach he founded, holds that meaning can be discovered through work and creation, through love and encounter with others, and through the attitude one takes toward unavoidable suffering. Even in conditions where everything else is stripped away, Frankl insists, the freedom to choose one's stance toward one's circumstances remains.
heteronormativity: Heteronormativity names the web of social norms, institutions, and assumptions that treat heterosexuality as the default, natural, and privileged form of sexuality and organize gender and family life accordingly. It describes how a culture can make opposite-sex desire and the traditional gender binary seem self-evident, marginalizing other orientations and identities as deviations. Associated with Judith Butler and queer theory more broadly, the concept exposes how such norms are produced and enforced rather than simply given by nature.
kant-perpetual-peace: Perpetual peace is Immanuel Kant's proposal, set out in his 1795 essay of that name, for the conditions under which lasting peace among states might be secured rather than merely a temporary truce between wars. He argued that peace requires republican constitutions, a federation of free states bound by international law, and a principle of universal hospitality permitting peaceful interaction across borders. Kant treated peace not as a natural given but as a moral and political task, something reason commands us to pursue and gradually approach. His vision has influenced later thinking about international institutions, cosmopolitan right, and the connection between democratic governance and peace.
last-man: The Last Man is Nietzsche's satirical portrait, drawn in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, of a degraded end-state of humanity: a comfort-seeking creature who has abandoned all high aspiration, striving, and risk in favor of safety, mild pleasure, and contentment. Blinking complacently, the last man asks "What is love? What is creation?" and no longer understands the questions. Nietzsche presents this figure as the opposite of the Übermensch and as a warning about a culture that, having lost its ideals, settles into shallow self-satisfaction.
liar-paradox: The Liar Paradox arises from a sentence like 'This sentence is false': if it is true it is false, and if false then true. It drove major twentieth-century work on truth, suggesting an ordinary notion of truth is inconsistent, and proposed fixes tend to relocate rather than remove the problem.
purity-and-danger: In Purity and Danger, anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that dirt is 'matter out of place' — not an absolute property but a violation of an order we impose. What counts as filthy tracks what a culture counts as orderly, so purity rules express social boundaries. Anxieties about contamination, on this view, often mark a group treated as out of place.
soul-making-theodicy: Soul-making theodicy, developed by John Hick, answers why an all-good God permits suffering: hardship and real choice make the world a 'valley of soul-making,' where free beings grow into virtues like courage and compassion. God keeps an 'epistemic distance' so goodness is never coerced. Critics reply that some suffering seems far beyond what character formation could require.
stoic-indifferents: Preferred indifferents are things the Stoics judged to have no bearing on virtue—and thus on genuine happiness—yet which are still reasonably worth pursuing. Health, wealth, and reputation, for example, are "indifferent" because a good life does not depend on them, but they are naturally "preferred" over their opposites and may rightly be chosen when doing so conflicts with no duty. The distinction lets the Stoic act sensibly in the world while insisting that only virtue is truly good and only vice truly bad.
stream-of-consciousness: Stream of consciousness is William James's term for the continuous, flowing character of mental life, in which thoughts and sensations run together rather than arriving as discrete, separable units. In his Principles of Psychology he argued that experience is felt as an unbroken current, always personal, always changing, and never the same twice, so the mind cannot be analyzed into a mosaic of fixed atoms. The idea reshaped psychology and later gave its name to a literary technique for rendering the movement of inner experience.
twin-earth: In his Twin Earth thought experiment, Hilary Putnam asks us to picture a planet exactly like ours except that the substance there called "water" is not H2O but a different compound, XYZ, indistinguishable in everyday experience. Since a speaker on Earth and an identical counterpart on Twin Earth are in the same internal mental state yet their word "water" refers to different substances, Putnam concludes that meaning is not fixed by what is in the head. This argument for semantic externalism—captured in the slogan "meanings just ain't in the head"—holds that the reference of many terms depends on the actual environment and community, not on inner mental content alone.
underdetermination: Underdetermination of theory by evidence is the claim that data alone never pin down a single theory: several incompatible explanations can fit the same observations equally well. Choice among them must then rest on values like simplicity or explanatory power, which the evidence itself does not dictate. Many hold this makes scientific inference less mechanical than it looks.
vindication-women: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is Mary Wollstonecraft's 1792 treatise arguing that women appear inferior to men only because they are denied education and treated as ornaments rather than rational beings. Writing amid the ideals of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, she contended that reason is not gendered and that granting women the same intellectual and moral cultivation as men would make them better citizens, wives, and mothers. The work is a foundational text of modern feminist thought and an early systematic case for women's equality.
wheel-of-fortune: The wheel of fortune is the image, given lasting form by Boethius, of Fortune as a capricious goddess turning a wheel that raises some to prosperity while casting others down. It expresses the ancient insight that worldly goods such as wealth, power, and reputation are fickle and never truly in our possession. Boethius uses the figure to argue that because these gifts belong to Fortune's changeable nature, staking one's happiness on them guarantees eventual grief. The remedy he proposes is to seek a stable good beyond Fortune's reach. The motif went on to pervade medieval and Renaissance art and literature.
abjection: Abjection, in Julia Kristeva's sense, names our uneasy reaction to things that blur the line between self and not-self, like corpses, blood, and bodily waste: what was once part of us but must be cast out for the self to exist. The 'abject' is thus neither subject nor object, and it provokes both disgust and fascination. Many horror works trade on confronting us with it.
augustine-city-of-god: The doctrine of the two cities is Augustine of Hippo's account of human history as the intertwined story of two communities defined by what they love. The earthly city is formed by love of self carried to the point of contempt for God, while the heavenly city is formed by love of God carried to the point of contempt for self. Written partly to answer the charge that Christianity had caused Rome's fall, the framework distinguishes eternal spiritual allegiance from any particular political order. The two cities remain mingled in this world and are separated only at the final judgment.
confucian-filiality: Xiao, or filial piety, is the Confucian virtue of reverence and care owed by children to their parents and, by extension, to ancestors and elders. It calls for supporting and honoring one's parents in life, mourning and remembering them in death, and continuing the family line and its values. Confucians regarded xiao as the root of all other virtues, reasoning that a person who learns devotion within the family will extend the same loyalty and respect outward into society and the state.
confucian-junzi: In Confucian thought, the junzi is the exemplary or noble person, an ideal of moral maturity that anyone can aspire to through cultivation rather than a status fixed by noble birth. The junzi embodies virtues such as ren (humaneness), yi (rightness), and li (propriety), acting from a settled sense of what is right rather than from calculation of advantage. Confucius offered this figure as a standard for personal conduct and public leadership, contrasting the junzi with the petty person who is guided by profit and self-interest.
confucian-ren: Ren, often translated as benevolence, humaneness, or co-humanity, is the central virtue of Confucian ethics. It names the disposition to care for others and to treat them with the consideration one would wish for oneself, expressed in Confucius's counsel not to do to others what you would not want done to you. For Confucius, ren is the inner moral quality that animates all the virtues and marks the fully realized human being, cultivated through self-discipline and relationships rather than merely followed as a rule.
correspondence-theory-of-truth: The correspondence theory of truth is the familiar idea that a statement is true when it matches how things actually are: the belief that it is raining is true if it really is raining. Its appeal is plain, but philosophers debate what exactly 'corresponds' to what, and critics offer alternatives such as coherence. Many worry that detaching claims from reality corrodes shared truth itself.
dialetheism: Dialetheism is the minority view, associated with Graham Priest, that some contradictions are actually true: there are statements that are both true and false at once. Classical logic resists this, since from one true contradiction everything would seem to follow, so dialetheists build special logics to contain the damage. Most philosophers reject the view, but it targets stubborn puzzles like the liar sentence.
ethics-of-ambiguity: The Ethics of Ambiguity is Simone de Beauvoir's attempt to build a moral philosophy on existentialist foundations, taking seriously the claim that human beings have no fixed essence and must create meaning through their choices. She argues that freedom is the source of all value, but because we are always situated among others whose freedom matters as much as our own, genuine freedom requires willing the liberation of others rather than treating them as means. The ambiguity of the title names the human condition itself—we are at once free consciousness and bound flesh, subject and object—and ethics consists in embracing that tension rather than fleeing it into bad faith.
game-theory: Game theory is the mathematical study of strategic decision-making: situations where the best choice for each participant depends on what others choose. It analyzes scenarios like the prisoner's dilemma, in which individually rational choices leave everyone worse off, and models reputation, repeated play, and negotiation. Though built on idealized rational agents, it is applied widely, from economics to war, and its predictions sometimes clash with actual behavior.
hedonic-calculus: The hedonic calculus is Jeremy Bentham's proposed method for measuring the pleasure and pain likely to result from an action so that its moral value can be weighed. Bentham suggested assessing factors such as a pleasure's intensity, duration, certainty, nearness in time, likelihood of leading to further pleasures, purity, and the number of people affected. The idea was to make morality a quasi-empirical procedure, allowing lawmakers and individuals to compare options and choose whichever promises the greatest net happiness.
impartial-spectator: The impartial spectator is Adam Smith's device for explaining moral judgment in The Theory of Moral Sentiments: an imagined, well-informed and disinterested observer whose approval or disapproval we internalize when we assess our own conduct. On this view, conscience is not a direct perception of duty but the habit of viewing our actions as a fair third party would, correcting for our natural partiality toward ourselves. The concept addresses how creatures moved by sympathy and self-love can nonetheless reach shared and reasonably objective moral standards.
kripke-naming: In Naming and Necessity, Saul Kripke argued that proper names are 'rigid designators,' picking out the same individual in every possible situation in which that individual exists, rather than functioning as disguised descriptions. On this view a name like 'Aristotle' refers to the same person even in counterfactual scenarios where he did none of the things we associate with him, its reference secured by a causal-historical chain reaching back to an initial baptism. Kripke's account overturned the dominant descriptivist theory and introduced influential notions of necessary yet a posteriori truth.
lucretian-nature: On the Nature of Things (De Rerum Natura) is a Latin poem by Lucretius that expounds the atomism and ethics of Epicurus. It argues that everything, including the soul, is composed of atoms moving through void, that natural events have material causes rather than divine ones, and that the gods take no interest in human affairs. From this physics Lucretius draws a moral lesson: understanding nature dispels the fear of the gods and of death, opening the way to a serene life.
mimesis: Mimesis is the Greek term for imitation, central to ancient theories of art. Plato worried that art merely copies appearances, an imitation of an imitation, and so leads us away from truth; Aristotle replied that imitation is natural and valuable, letting us learn and, through tragedy, work through pity and fear. The debate over whether art copies reality, distorts it, or reveals it through representation has run ever since.
ontology-of-fiction: The ontology of fiction asks what kind of thing a fictional character is: does Sherlock Holmes exist in any sense, and what makes the Holmes of one story the same character as the Holmes of another? Some say characters are abstract artifacts created by authors; others, possible people; others, a lesser kind of being without existence. It is a testing ground for questions about creation and identity.
philosophy-of-music: Philosophy of music asks what music is and why it moves us: whether a musical 'work' is the score, a performance, an expression of emotion, or something else, and whether music can carry meaning at all. Thinkers from Plato onward debated its ethical force, while Schopenhauer held that music expresses reality's inner nature more directly than any other art. Cross-cultural examples complicate the Western, score-centered picture.
philosophy-of-play: Philosophy of play asks what play is and why it matters. Thinkers like Schiller and Huizinga argued that play, free, rule-bound activity pursued for its own sake, is not mere idleness but something that completes our humanity; Plato and Aristotle already treated games and leisure as formative of persons and communities. Others probe its shadows, such as games that exclude outsiders.
posthumanism: Posthumanism is a family of views that unsettles the traditional idea of a fixed, unified 'human' at the center of things. Thinkers such as Donna Haraway argue we are already hybrids of flesh and technology, cyborgs whose identities are assembled from bodies, machines, and information. The view tends to dissolve hierarchies, human over animal, machine, and object, while critics warn against losing what makes us human.
rhizome: The rhizome is an image of thought and organization proposed by Gilles Deleuze, with Félix Guattari, as an alternative to the traditional "tree" model of knowledge with its single root and branching hierarchy. Borrowed from botany, a rhizome is a horizontal, decentered network—like crabgrass or a fungal mat—that can connect any point to any other, has no fixed center or origin, and keeps growing even when broken. As a concept it favors multiplicity, heterogeneity, and open-ended connection over rigid, ranked structures. Deleuze and Guattari used it to rethink culture, politics, and thought as sprawling networks rather than ordered systems.
romanticism: Romanticism was a late-eighteenth- and nineteenth-century movement that exalted imagination, feeling, and the individual's encounter with the infinite over Enlightenment rationalism and tidy systems. Romantic thinkers prized mystery, the sublime vastness of nature, and the creative power to 'make the world Romantic', preferring an unresolved, endlessly deepening meaning to a neat solution. Its legacy runs through art, ethics, and the idea that truth may exceed what formulas can capture.
schopenhauer-pessimism: Philosophical pessimism, as developed by Arthur Schopenhauer, is the view that existence is fundamentally characterized by suffering and that, on balance, it would be better not to strive after the endless demands of the will to life. Because life is driven by insatiable craving, satisfaction is fleeting and quickly gives way to new want or to boredom, so that pain outweighs pleasure over the whole of existence. Schopenhauer drew partly on Buddhist and Hindu themes in concluding that liberation lies in quieting the will rather than gratifying it. His pessimism deeply influenced later thinkers and artists, including Nietzsche, who wrestled with it, and Freud, who echoed its picture of the psyche as governed by relentless drives.
the-sublime: The sublime is the overwhelming feeling we get before something vast or terrifying that exceeds our grasp, a storm, a mountain, an abyss, which blends fear with a strange pleasure. Edmund Burke analyzed it as delightful terror at what could harm us, while Immanuel Kant argued it reveals something in us: imagination fails before the immense, but reason can conceive what sense cannot. It remains a key idea in aesthetics.
transhumanism: Transhumanism is the view that we should use technology, from genetic engineering to body enhancement and mind-uploading, to overcome human limits, including disease, aging, and death itself. Advocates like Nick Bostrom frame this as a moral duty; bioconservative critics such as Fukuyama warn that erasing our natural limits may erase our humanity. The debate turns on whether enhancement fulfills or abolishes the person it improves.
zeno-paradoxes: Zeno of Elea, a disciple of Parmenides in the fifth century BCE, devised a series of paradoxes intended to defend his teacher's claim that motion and plurality are illusory. The best known, such as Achilles and the tortoise and the arrow that seems never to move, argue that motion leads to contradictions when space and time are treated as infinitely divisible. Whether or not they succeed, the paradoxes pose deep puzzles about infinity, continuity, and the structure of space and time that have occupied philosophers and mathematicians ever since.
aestheticism: Aestheticism is the view that beauty and artistic value matter in their own right, apart from moral, religious, or practical worth — the creed of 'art for art's sake.' On this view the aesthete takes aesthetic experience, not ethics or utility, as the highest measure of life. Some hold it to its extreme: that art needs no justification beyond the pleasure of contemplating it.
anti-natalism: Anti-natalism is the view that it is morally wrong to bring new people into existence. Its defenders, such as David Benatar, argue that every life contains real suffering, while the nonexistent cannot be deprived of pleasure, so creating someone always harms them — or at least imposes on them risks they never consented to. On this view, adopting existing children is morally preferable to procreation.
art-horror: 'Art-horror' is philosopher Noël Carroll's term for the distinctive emotion aroused by horror fiction: a blend of fear and disgust aimed at monsters. He holds that horror monsters characteristically violate our cultural categories — fusions of species, mixtures of living and dead, formless or incomplete things. This 'categorical impurity' is why revulsion and fascination typically arrive together.
bergson-duration: Duration (durée) is Henri Bergson's name for time as it is actually lived and felt, as opposed to time as measured by clocks. Real duration is a continuous, qualitative flow in which past and present interpenetrate and each moment is genuinely new, unlike the homogeneous, divisible instants that science treats as spatial units laid side by side. Bergson argued that intellect and physics distort time by spatializing it, and that only intuition grasps duration from within. The idea grounds his views on memory, freedom, and creativity, and shaped much of early twentieth-century thought.
bergson-memory: In Matter and Memory (1896), Henri Bergson set out to clarify the relation between mind and body by rethinking perception and recollection. He distinguished habit-memory, the bodily repetition of learned actions, from pure or spontaneous memory, which conserves the past in its entirety and is not stored in the brain like a thing. On his account the brain is an organ of action that filters and channels memory toward present needs rather than a warehouse of images, so mind and matter differ in degree and rhythm rather than being wholly separate substances. The book advanced Bergson's larger claim that consciousness is fundamentally temporal, gathering the past into the living present.
corporate-personhood: Corporate personhood is the idea that a corporation can count as a 'person' — holding rights, entering contracts, and bearing responsibility — even though it is not a human being. Legal systems grant this status by law, and some philosophers argue corporations can also be moral agents whose decisions and responsibilities are not reducible to any individual's. Others insist the label is a fiction that lets real people escape blame.
dharma: Dharma is a foundational term across Indian thought whose meaning shifts with context, generally denoting the order, duty, law, or teaching that sustains both the cosmos and right human conduct. In Hindu ethics it names the moral and social obligations proper to one's station and circumstances, the righteous path that upholds a well-ordered life. In Buddhism the Dharma is the Buddha's teaching and, more broadly, the truth about the nature of things that the teaching points to. Common to these senses is the idea of a normative structure that living in accordance with brings harmony, and departing from brings disorder.
disability-philosophy: The philosophy of disability examines what disability is, how it should be understood, and what justice requires in relation to it. A central debate contrasts the 'medical model,' which locates disability in an individual's bodily impairment, with the 'social model,' which locates it in the way societies are built and organized to exclude people whose bodies or minds differ from an assumed norm. The field also addresses questions of well-being, autonomy, accommodation, and the value of disabled lives, challenging assumptions that treat disability as simply a deficit.
gnosticism: Gnosticism was a family of early religious movements holding that salvation comes through gnosis — direct inner knowledge of the divine — rather than faith, ritual, or church. Many Gnostics taught that the material world was made not by the true God but by a lesser, flawed creator, leaving sparks of the divine trapped in matter and waiting to be awakened.
great-chain-of-being: The Great Chain of Being was the premodern picture of reality as a single ranked hierarchy: God at the top, then angels, humans, animals, plants, and inert matter, each thing with its fixed place. It implied that some beings are naturally higher than others. Evolutionary thinking is widely held to have dissolved the chain — species form a branching tree, not a ladder.
imaginative-resistance: Imaginative resistance is a puzzle about fiction: readers easily imagine impossible physics — faster-than-light travel, flying pigs — yet balk at imagining a world where morality itself is different, such as a story where cold-blooded murder is noble. Many hold that we simply refuse to 'enter into' vicious sentiments, even in imagination. Explaining exactly why we resist, and when, remains debated.
intentional-stance: The intentional stance is Daniel Dennett's term for the strategy of predicting a system's behavior by treating it as a rational agent that has beliefs, desires, and goals. Rather than asking whether a thermostat, animal, or person really has mental states in some deep metaphysical sense, we adopt the stance because doing so yields reliable predictions of what the system will do. For Dennett, the usefulness and success of this interpretive strategy is what it means to have beliefs and desires, offering a deflationary but robust account of mind.
intersectionality: Intersectionality, a term introduced by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, holds that systems of power such as racism and sexism do not operate independently but intersect to produce distinctive forms of disadvantage. Crenshaw showed that Black women, for instance, can face harms that neither antiracist nor feminist frameworks alone capture, because their experience falls at the crossing of multiple axes of identity. The concept has become a central analytic tool for understanding how race, gender, class, sexuality, and other categories combine to shape people's social positions.
neoplatonism: Neoplatonism is the philosophical system developed by Plotinus in the third century CE and elaborated by later thinkers such as Porphyry and Proclus. At its center stands "the One," an utterly simple and ineffable source from which all reality emanates in descending levels—Intellect, Soul, and the material world—so that everything ultimately derives from and yearns to return to this origin. Combining rigorous metaphysics with a mystical goal of union with the One, Neoplatonism profoundly shaped later Christian, Islamic, and Jewish thought.
personhood: In philosophy, personhood is the status of being a being to whom moral consideration is owed — standardly tied to capacities like self-consciousness, rationality, and the ability to see oneself as persisting over time. Many philosophers argue that personhood and biological humanity can come apart: some humans might lack it, and some non-human or artificial beings might have it. Whether that argument succeeds is deeply contested.
political-realism: Political realism is the view that politics is governed above all by power, interest, and the need for order — not by moral ideals. Realists from Machiavelli onward have argued that a ruler who insists on doing only what is morally admirable may lose everything worth protecting. Compromise, deception, and force, on this view, are often not corruptions of politics but its ordinary materials.
schopenhauer-pendulum: The pendulum between pain and boredom is Schopenhauer's memorable image for the predicament of a life driven by the will. So long as a desire remains unsatisfied, we suffer the pain of lack; once it is satisfied, the satisfaction fades and we are left with emptiness and boredom until a new want arises. Human existence therefore swings back and forth between these two poles, never resting in lasting contentment. The image encapsulates his pessimism: because willing has no final term, the very structure of desire makes durable happiness unattainable.
simulation-hypothesis: The simulation hypothesis proposes that our reality might be a computer simulation run by an advanced civilization rather than a base physical world. In a 2003 argument, Nick Bostrom contended that at least one of three claims must hold: civilizations almost always go extinct before reaching the capacity to run such simulations, advanced civilizations rarely choose to run many ancestor simulations, or we are very probably living in one. The reasoning turns on the thought that if sophisticated simulations became feasible and common, simulated minds would vastly outnumber original ones. The hypothesis revives ancient skeptical worries about appearance and reality in a technological form.
spinoza-conatus: Conatus is Baruch Spinoza's term for the striving by which each thing endeavors to persevere in its own being. In his Ethics this striving is not an added desire but the very essence of a thing: to exist is to resist dissolution and to maintain oneself. In human beings the conatus appears as the drive toward self-preservation and flourishing, and Spinoza uses it to ground his account of emotion and value, explaining desire, joy, and sorrow as functions of whether one's power of acting is increased or diminished.
spinoza-determinism: Spinozist necessity is the claim that everything that happens follows with strict necessity from the nature of the one substance, so that nothing in the universe could have been otherwise. Because God or Nature acts solely from the necessity of its own essence, there is no free will in the sense of an uncaused choice, and even human decisions are fully determined by prior causes. Spinoza does not treat this as bleak fatalism but as the basis of freedom rightly understood: liberation comes through understanding the causes that determine us, replacing passive bondage to the passions with active knowledge.
subjective-truth: With the phrase "subjectivity is truth," Kierkegaard argues that for the deepest existential matters what counts is not objective correctness but the passion and inwardness with which one holds and lives a belief. He distinguishes truths that can be established impersonally from truths, especially religious ones, whose meaning depends on how they are appropriated by an existing individual. The claim is not that facts are relative but that certain truths become real only through committed, personal engagement rather than detached observation.
tragedy-of-the-commons: The tragedy of the commons describes how a shared resource gets ruined by individually rational behavior: each herder benefits fully from adding one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is spread across everyone. Multiply that by many users and the common pasture is destroyed — even though no one wanted that outcome. The phrase, from Garrett Hardin, now names this whole family of collective-action problems.
transcendentalism: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American intellectual and literary movement, centered in New England, that emphasized the primacy of intuition, the divinity of nature, and the inherent goodness and self-sufficiency of the individual. Drawing on Romanticism and German idealism, its figures—chiefly Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau—held that a deeper spiritual truth transcends the senses and is accessible directly through personal insight rather than through established institutions or received doctrine. The movement fed reform causes, from abolition to education, and reshaped American letters.
zhuangzi-perspectivism: Zhuangzi is known for a playful perspectivism that questions whether any single viewpoint can capture the truth about reality or value. His famous butterfly-dream story—waking unsure whether he is a man who dreamt he was a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man—dramatizes how our judgments about what is real, right, or beautiful depend on the standpoint we occupy. Rather than settling such disputes, Zhuangzi urges a flexible, open acceptance of the constant transformation of things, loosening our grip on fixed distinctions and rigid certainties.
biopower: Biopower is Michel Foucault's term for a modern form of power that manages whole populations and individual bodies through statistics, medicine, public health, and institutions, rather than simply commanding by law or force. On this view, states decide who is fostered and who is exposed to death, and surveillance leads people to police themselves.
category-mistake: A category mistake, a notion introduced by Gilbert Ryle, occurs when something is placed in a logical category to which it does not belong, as when a visitor shown the colleges and library asks to be shown 'the University' as if it were a further building. Ryle used the idea to diagnose confusions in philosophy, arguing that many puzzles arise from treating concepts of one type as though they were of another. The device is central to his critique of the mind as a separate inner substance.
cicero-duty: Ciceronian duty refers to the account of moral obligation set out in Cicero's De Officiis ("On Duties"), written near the end of the Roman Republic. Drawing on Stoic ethics, Cicero examines how the honorable and the useful relate, arguing that what is truly beneficial can never conflict with what is right, and he analyzes the virtues of wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance as sources of practical duty. Addressed to his son but aimed at public life, the work became one of the most influential treatises on ethics and civic responsibility in the Western tradition.
dirty-hands: The problem of dirty hands, named after Jean-Paul Sartre's play and developed by Michael Walzer, asks what happens when a political leader must do something morally wrong—a lie, a betrayal, even killing—because the situation genuinely demands it. Many hold such acts can be necessary yet still wrong, leaving the leader a guilt that matters.
epistemic-injustice: Epistemic injustice, a concept named by Miranda Fricker, is a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. She distinguished two main forms: testimonial injustice, in which prejudice leads a hearer to give a speaker's word less credibility than it deserves, and hermeneutical injustice, in which gaps in a society's shared interpretive resources leave some group unable to make sense of their own experiences. The idea shows that unfairness can operate not only in the distribution of goods but in whose knowledge and understanding are recognized.
ethics-of-lying: The ethics of lying and deception asks when, if ever, it is wrong to deceive. Kant famously held that lying is always wrong, however well-intentioned; utilitarians judge each lie by its consequences; and philosophers like Sissela Bok start from a strong presumption against lying, since deception robs others of informed choice and corrodes trust.
feminine-mystique: The Feminine Mystique names Betty Friedan's 1963 diagnosis of "the problem that has no name": the pervasive dissatisfaction of educated mid-century American housewives confined to domestic roles and told that fulfillment lay solely in marriage, motherhood, and homemaking. Friedan argued that the culture propagated an idealized image of femininity that stifled women's ambitions and identities, leaving many with an unspoken sense of emptiness. Widely credited with helping launch second-wave feminism, the book urged women to seek meaningful work and self-realization beyond the home.
gadamer-hermeneutics: Philosophical hermeneutics, developed by Hans-Georg Gadamer in Truth and Method (1960), treats understanding not as a method for recovering an author's original meaning but as an event that happens whenever we interpret a text, artwork, or tradition. We always approach what we seek to understand from within our own historically shaped 'horizon' of assumptions, and genuine understanding occurs through a 'fusion of horizons' in which our expectations and the other's meaning are brought into productive contact. Gadamer thus rehabilitated prejudice and tradition as enabling conditions of interpretation rather than obstacles to be eliminated.
jung-archetypes: Archetypes, in the analytical psychology of Carl Jung, are universal, inherited patterns or images that structure human experience and recur across myths, dreams, religions, and art. They are not fixed pictures but predispositions to form certain kinds of images and to respond in typical ways, expressing themselves through figures such as the mother, the hero, the wise old man, and the shadow. Jung held that these forms arise from a shared layer of the psyche, giving a common symbolic vocabulary to peoples widely separated in time and place.
jung-collective-unconscious: The collective unconscious is Carl Jung's term for a deep stratum of the mind that lies beneath the personal unconscious and is shared by all human beings. Unlike Freud's unconscious of individually repressed memories, it consists of inherited structures—the archetypes—that predispose people to experience and imagine the world in recurring patterns. Jung offered it to explain why similar symbols and mythic themes appear across cultures with no historical contact, treating them as expressions of a common psychic inheritance rather than borrowed ideas.
jung-shadow: The shadow, in Carl Jung's psychology, is the part of the personality that a person refuses to recognize in themselves—the impulses, weaknesses, and desires judged unacceptable and therefore repressed or projected onto others. Because it is disowned rather than absent, the shadow retains its energy and can erupt unbidden or be seen distorted in the people one despises. Jung argued that psychological maturity requires confronting and integrating the shadow rather than denying it, since owning one's darker side is a precondition for wholeness and self-knowledge.
korsgaard-constructivism: Kantian constructivism, as developed by Christine Korsgaard, holds that moral principles are not discovered as facts existing independently of us but are constructed from the standpoint of rational agents facing the practical problem of what to do. Drawing on Kant, Korsgaard argues that in acting we must confer value on our ends and take our own rational nature as a source of normativity, and that reflection on the conditions of agency yields binding obligations. Her notion of practical identity explains how the roles and commitments through which we understand ourselves generate reasons, while the shared status of being reasoning agents grounds duties to others. The view seeks to locate the authority of morality in the structure of self-conscious rational willing rather than in external metaphysical facts.
lacan-mirror-stage: The mirror stage is Jacques Lacan's account of a formative moment, roughly between six and eighteen months, when an infant recognizes its reflection and identifies with that unified image. This identification is both enabling and alienating: the child assumes a coherent sense of self from an external picture that seems more whole and controlled than its still-uncoordinated body actually is. For Lacan the episode inaugurates the ego as something constituted through misrecognition, founding identity on an image received from outside rather than on any inner unity.
lacan-symbolic: Jacques Lacan organized psychic life around three interlinked orders. The Imaginary is the realm of images, identifications, and the illusory sense of wholeness first gained in the mirror stage. The Symbolic is the order of language, law, and social structure into which the subject is inducted, where meaning is produced through difference and the rules that govern desire. The Real is what resists symbolization altogether—the excess that cannot be captured in image or word—and the three orders together frame Lacan's rethinking of how the human subject is formed.
legal-positivism: Legal positivism is the view that whether something is law is a separate question from whether it is just. A rule can count as valid law because of who enacted it, even if it is deeply immoral—which, positivists argue, is exactly why we should say unjust laws are laws, but bad ones.
naturalistic-fallacy: The naturalistic fallacy is G. E. Moore's charge that it is a mistake to define moral goodness in terms of any natural property, such as pleasure, desire, or evolutionary fitness. In Principia Ethica he argued that 'good' names a simple, non-natural quality that cannot be reduced to factual descriptions, and offered the 'open question argument': for any proposed natural definition, it remains sensibly open to ask whether things with that property are really good. The claim influenced twentieth-century metaethics and is often linked to the broader worry about deriving values from facts.
oedipus-complex: The Oedipus complex is Sigmund Freud's claim that young children pass through a phase of intense attachment to one parent and rivalry with the other, named for the Greek king who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother. Freud thought resolving it shapes adult personality; the theory is widely criticized today.
physicalism: Physicalism is the view that everything that exists—including minds, thoughts, and feelings—is ultimately physical, or depends entirely on arrangements of physical stuff. Many hold it follows that mental life just is brain activity; dualists disagree, arguing that consciousness or souls cannot be captured in physical terms. The debate tests what we think we are.
rectification-of-names: The rectification of names is the Confucian idea that social and moral order depends on making words match reality, so that a ruler truly rules, a father truly acts as a father, and each role is filled according to its proper meaning. Confucius argued that when names and actualities drift apart, language loses its force, obligations become unclear, and society falls into disorder. The remedy is to align conduct with the standards implied by one's titles and relationships, treating accurate naming as the foundation of good government and ethics.
schopenhauer-compassion: Schopenhauer grounded morality not in reason or duty but in compassion, the immediate participation in another's suffering that moves us to relieve it. He argued that ethical action arises when the ordinary boundary between self and other is momentarily overcome, so that we recognize in another being the same will that constitutes our own inner nature. This metaphysical insight—that at the deepest level all beings are one—explains why genuine kindness is possible and why cruelty and egoism rest on the illusion of separateness. His ethics of compassion, set out in On the Basis of Morality, offered a pointed alternative to Kant's rule-based account of moral obligation.
stoic-premeditation: Premeditatio malorum, the "premeditation of adversities," is a Stoic exercise of deliberately imagining setbacks, losses, and even death before they occur. Practiced by Seneca and others, it is meant to strip misfortune of its power to shock, to loosen our attachment to things we cannot keep, and to remind us that such events lie outside our control. By rehearsing hardship in advance, the Stoic aims to meet it with composure rather than panic when it actually arrives.
stoic-view-from-above: The view from above is a Stoic contemplative exercise in which one imaginatively rises to survey human affairs from a cosmic vantage point. Associated especially with Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, it invites us to picture the vast sweep of time and space so that our quarrels, ambitions, and anxieties appear small and fleeting. The practice is meant to instill perspective and humility, tempering emotion by setting individual concerns against the whole of nature.
tabula-rasa: Tabula rasa, Latin for a blank slate, is the doctrine that the mind at birth contains no innate ideas and that all knowledge derives from experience. John Locke advanced it against rationalists who held that certain principles are stamped on the mind from the start, arguing instead that sensation and reflection furnish the raw materials of thought. The view makes experience the ultimate source of concepts and became a cornerstone of British empiricism, with far-reaching implications for education, moral development, and the shaping of human character.
wolf-meaning: Meaning in life, as developed by the contemporary philosopher Susan Wolf, is a distinct value that lies between self-interested happiness and impersonal morality. Wolf argues that a meaningful life arises when "subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness" — that is, when a person is actively and lovingly engaged in projects that are also genuinely worth caring about. The account responds to the worry that a life could be pleasant or dutiful yet still feel empty, locating meaning in the fit between what we love and what is worthy of love.
addams-settlement: The social ethics of the settlement house is the practical moral philosophy Jane Addams developed through Hull House, the Chicago settlement she co-founded to share the lives of the urban poor and immigrant communities. Addams held that ethics must be lived and reciprocal—learned by association across class lines rather than dispensed as charity from above—and that genuine democracy requires attending to the interdependence of all members of society. Her work fused pragmatist thought with social reform, treating cooperative daily engagement as the school of a broadened, more democratic conscience.
aspect-perception: Wittgenstein used 'aspect perception' or 'seeing-as' for the way we can see the very same thing under different aspects — the famous duck-rabbit figure seen first as a duck, then as a rabbit. Many hold this shows perception is never raw sensation: what we see is shaped by concepts, memory, and practice. Failing to see new aspects is 'aspect blindness,' and moral vision may partly depend on it.
avicenna-floating-man: The Floating Man is a thought experiment devised by the Persian philosopher Avicenna to show that self-awareness does not depend on the body or the senses. He asks us to imagine a person created fully formed but suspended in empty space, blindfolded and touching nothing, so that no sensory information reaches them; even in this condition, Avicenna argues, the person would still affirm their own existence. From this he concludes that the soul knows itself immediately and is distinct from the body, an argument sometimes seen as a distant forerunner of Descartes's cogito.
bacon-idols: The Idols of the Mind are Francis Bacon's classification, set out in his Novum Organum (1620), of the systematic errors that distort human understanding and obstruct genuine knowledge of nature. He named four: the Idols of the Tribe, rooted in human nature itself; the Idols of the Cave, arising from an individual's particular temperament and upbringing; the Idols of the Marketplace, caused by the ambiguities and misuse of language; and the Idols of the Theater, inherited uncritically from received philosophies and dogmas. Bacon urged that recognizing and purging these idols was a necessary preparation for his new inductive, experimental method.
bergson-elan-vital: Élan vital is the vital impetus that Henri Bergson placed at the heart of his 1907 work Creative Evolution. Against mechanistic and strictly Darwinian accounts, which he saw as explaining life only by external causes, Bergson proposed a creative, forward-pushing life force that drives evolution toward novel and unpredictable forms. Life, on this view, is not the unfolding of a preset plan but an ongoing creative surge that continually invents new solutions and diverges into branching lineages. Though influential in its day and admired by many artists and writers, the notion drew criticism for its vagueness and lack of empirical grounding.
birdcage-oppression: Marilyn Frye's birdcage image illustrates why oppression is often invisible when examined one piece at a time. Looking at a single wire of a birdcage, one cannot see why it would confine a bird, which could simply fly around it; only by stepping back to see the whole network of wires does the trap become clear. Frye used this to argue that oppression consists of a systematic, interlocking set of barriers and forces that mutually reinforce one another, so that each restriction on women appears trivial in isolation while together they constrain a whole group.
death-of-the-author: In a 1967 essay, Roland Barthes declared the 'death of the author': once a text is written, the writer's intention no longer fixes what it means. A work is a 'tissue of quotations' from a shared culture, and its unity lies where readers make it. On this view there are as many readings as readers, and the creator holds no final interpretive authority.
dialectic-of-sex: In The Dialectic of Sex (1970), Shulamith Firestone reworked Marx and Engels to argue that the deepest form of oppression is not class but sex, rooted in the biological facts of reproduction and the family structures built around them. She contended that women's subordination originates in the reproductive division of labor and that genuine liberation would require freeing women from biology itself, including through reproductive technology. The book was a founding text of radical feminism, pressing the claim that overturning patriarchy demands transforming, not merely reforming, the family and the sexual order.
film-as-philosophy: Many philosophers hold that films can do philosophy, not merely illustrate it. A film can stage a thought experiment, embody an argument in its plot, or force viewers to feel the force of a problem — personal identity, free will, the good life — in a way abstract prose cannot. On this view, watching attentively can itself be a kind of thinking.
five-faces-oppression: Iris Marion Young argued that oppression is not a single phenomenon but a family of distinct conditions, and she identified five 'faces': exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, and violence. Rather than locating injustice solely in the deliberate acts of a tyrant, she showed how structural relations and everyday practices can systematically disadvantage social groups. The framework lets one recognize that different groups may be oppressed in different ways, and that a group can suffer some faces of oppression without suffering all of them.
mencius-good-nature: Mencius held that human nature is fundamentally good, arguing that everyone is born with incipient moral tendencies he called the four sprouts—compassion, shame, courtesy, and a sense of right and wrong. On this view wrongdoing arises not from an evil nature but from neglect, bad circumstances, or failure to nurture these innate beginnings, much as a plant withers without care. The task of ethics is therefore to cultivate and extend these natural feelings so they mature into the full virtues, a position that shaped later Confucian debates about moral education.
mill-subjection-women: The Subjection of Women is John Stuart Mill's 1869 essay arguing that the legal and social subordination of women is both unjust and a barrier to human progress. Mill contends that the supposed inferiority of women reflects the effects of their upbringing and constrained circumstances rather than any natural fact, and he calls for legal equality, access to education and the professions, and reform of a marriage law that placed wives under their husbands' control. Written partly in collaboration with Harriet Taylor, it became an influential early statement of liberal feminism.
montaigne-skepticism: Que sais-je?—'What do I know?'—is the motto that captures Michel de Montaigne's tempered skepticism, an attitude of habitual questioning rather than dogmatic denial. Writing in the sixteenth century, Montaigne doubted the reach of human reason and the reliability of the senses, noting how custom, perspective, and mood shape what people take to be certain. Rather than despairing, he turned this doubt into a mode of self-examination in his Essays, using suspended judgment as a way to live modestly, tolerantly, and attentively to the shifting realities of experience.
moral-dilemmas: A moral dilemma arises when two or more moral duties bind at once and cannot both be honored — save the drowning stranger or your child, tell the truth or protect someone. Philosophers distinguish negotiable duties, which can be weighed and overridden, from non-negotiable ones, which cannot. Many hold that in genuine dilemmas whichever choice you make, you do something wrong and carry a moral remainder.
moral-particularism: Moral particularists, like Jonathan Dancy, deny that morality runs on fixed universal rules. A feature that counts for acting one way in one situation — a promise, a need — can count differently or not at all in another. Judgment, on this view, means reading each situation's particular shape rather than applying a code; critics worry this leaves too little to guide us.
pacifism: Pacifism is the view that war and violence are morally impermissible, or at least never justified. Versions differ: absolute pacifists refuse lethal force in every case; conditional or realist pacifists oppose war in principle while allowing, as a last resort, defense of the innocent. Many pacifists draw on Gandhi's nonviolence, which holds that means shape ends — violence only begets more violence.
philosophy-of-art: The philosophy of art asks what art is and what makes works of it valuable. Is artistic value beauty, emotional expression, form, or the power to reward attention over time? Can films and video games count as art? Philosophers here try to define the concept, explain how judgment works without rules, and ask why created things can matter to us at all.
relational-autonomy: Traditional pictures of autonomy celebrate the independent self: deciding alone, unencumbered by others. Feminist philosophers of 'relational autonomy' argue this picture is false to human life. On their view, people are partly constituted by their relationships — family, love, culture — so being self-governing is not escaping those ties but competently negotiating them, ideally within relationships that support one's growth rather than crush it.
self-deception: Self-deception is getting yourself to believe something you have reasons to think false — the investor ignoring the collapsing numbers, the lover denying the evident affair. It breeds a puzzle: deceiving requires intending not to know, yet the deceiver and the deceived are one person. Philosophers debate how this is possible; many favor subtler accounts, like managing your own attention, over a literally divided mind.
society-of-the-spectacle: In The Society of the Spectacle (1967), Guy Debord argued that modern life has come to be mediated by images: direct experience gives way to commodities, celebrities, and screens, and social relations become representations of relations. The spectacle is not mere advertising but a way of ruling — even rebellion can be packaged and sold back. Genuine living, he held, must be reclaimed from the image.
stakeholder-theory: Stakeholder theory answers the question 'who is a business for?' It holds that a firm's managers owe consideration to everyone with a stake in it — workers, customers, suppliers, the community — not only the stockholders. Its rival, stockholder theory, holds the corporation's sole responsibility is to maximize shareholder profit within the law. On the stakeholder view, treating employees as expendable cogs is not just bad strategy but a wrong.
tillich-ground-of-being: God as the ground of being is a conception developed by the German-American theologian Paul Tillich, who argued that God should not be thought of as a supreme entity existing alongside other things but as being-itself, the source and ground from which all existence derives. On this view, to call God a being among beings, however great, is to diminish the divine; God is instead the depth and ground of everything that is. Tillich linked this idea to faith understood as ultimate concern, an orientation toward what matters unconditionally in human life.
uncanny-valley: The robotics pioneer Masahiro Mori observed that as machines look more human, our liking rises — until the point where they are almost, but not quite, human. There affinity plunges into revulsion: the moving corpse-like face, the stiff smile. He called this dip the 'uncanny valley,' and he speculated hopefully that well-made robots might cross it, even coming to carry a kind of buddha-nature.
xunzi-bad-nature: Xunzi took the opposing Confucian view that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, since people are born with self-interested desires that, left unchecked, lead to conflict and disorder. For Xunzi goodness is not innate but a deliberate achievement, produced by ritual, education, and the accumulated wisdom of the sages, which reshape raw impulses into virtuous conduct. His emphasis on ritual (li) and conscious effort as the source of morality directly answered Mencius's claim that virtue grows from natural sprouts.
russells-teapot: Russell's teapot is an analogy devised by Bertrand Russell to argue that the burden of proof lies with the person making an unfalsifiable claim, not with those who doubt it. Russell imagined asserting that a china teapot orbits the Sun somewhere between Earth and Mars, too small to be detected by any telescope; the claim cannot be disproved, yet no one is thereby obliged to believe it. He used the image to challenge the idea that skeptics must refute religious or other extraordinary assertions rather than the claimants having to support them.
phil:aristotle: Aristotle was a fourth-century BC Greek philosopher who studied under Plato, tutored Alexander the Great, and founded his own school, the Lyceum. Rejecting Plato's separate realm of Forms, he located the essence of things within the things themselves and built a vast systematic account of the natural and human world across logic, biology, physics, ethics, and politics. He developed the first formal system of logic, argued that the good life consists in the exercise of virtue and reason, and analyzed causation, substance, and change in ways that framed inquiry for two millennia. His works became foundational to medieval Islamic, Jewish, and Christian thought and to the emergence of the sciences.
phil:berkeley: George Berkeley was an Anglo-Irish philosopher and bishop best known for his idealism, the view that material objects have no existence independent of being perceived.
