phil:cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, orator, and philosopher whose works became a principal channel through which Greek philosophy reached the Latin-speaking world. Though not a systematic thinker of one school, he drew on Academic skepticism, Stoicism, and other traditions in dialogues such as On Duties, On the Nature of the Gods, and On the Ends of Good and Evil. He is especially known for his defense of natural law, republican virtue, and a life guided by moral duty, and his polished Latin prose shaped European rhetoric for centuries.
phil:foot: Philippa Foot (1920–2010) was a British philosopher who helped revive virtue ethics in the analytic tradition and grounded morality in facts about human flourishing. She is widely remembered for introducing the trolley problem, a thought experiment probing why it may seem permissible to divert a runaway trolley to kill one person rather than five yet impermissible to kill one person to save several others. In Natural Goodness she argued that moral evaluations are a species of natural evaluation, akin to judging what makes a good specimen of a living thing.
phil:galen-strawson: Galen Strawson (b. 1952) is a British analytic philosopher known for starkly argued positions on the self and free will. He defends the reality of the self against narrative theories of identity, and his 'Basic Argument' contends that no one can be truly responsible for their actions, since we cannot be causa sui — the cause of ourselves.
phil:george-herbert-mead: George Herbert Mead (1863–1931) was an American pragmatist philosopher and social psychologist at the University of Chicago. He argued that the self is not innate but emerges through social interaction — especially by taking the perspective of others — a view that founded symbolic interactionism and reshaped ideas about identity, mind, and language.
phil:gettier: Edmund Gettier (1927–2021) was an American philosopher known chiefly for a brief 1963 paper that upended the long-standing definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Through simple counterexamples, he showed that one can hold a belief that is both true and justified yet still, intuitively, fail to count as knowledge because the justification connects to the truth only by luck. These so-called Gettier cases launched decades of work in epistemology aimed at repairing or replacing the traditional analysis of knowledge.
phil:giorgio-agamben: Giorgio Agamben (b. 1942) is an Italian philosopher who writes on law, power, and politics in the tradition of Heidegger and Foucault. He is best known for the figure of homo sacer and the concept of 'bare life': people stripped of political standing, exposed to sovereign power most starkly in the camp and the state of exception.
phil:goldman: Alvin Goldman (b. 1938) is an American philosopher who has been a central figure in epistemology and the philosophy of mind. He is a leading proponent of reliabilism, the view that a belief counts as knowledge when it is produced by a reliable, truth-conducive process, offered as one response to the Gettier problem. Goldman also helped found social epistemology, the systematic study of how social practices and institutions bear on the acquisition of knowledge, and contributed to debates on simulation theory in the understanding of other minds.
phil:haraway: Donna Haraway (b. 1944) is an American feminist theorist of science and technology. Her 'Cyborg Manifesto' uses the figure of the human–animal–machine hybrid to dissolve rigid boundary concepts like nature versus culture, and her notion of 'situated knowledges' argues that all knowledge is partial and located, never from a neutral god's-eye view.
phil:john-hick: John Hick (1922–2012) was a British philosopher of religion known for two big ideas: a 'soul-making' theodicy, on which evil and suffering exist because a world that builds moral and spiritual character is more valuable than a ready-made paradise, and a pluralism holding that the major world faiths are different culturally shaped responses to one ultimate divine reality.
phil:joseph-campbell: Joseph Campbell (1904–1987) was an American comparative mythologist who drew on Jung's archetypes to argue that the world's myths share one underlying pattern, which he called the monomyth or 'hero's journey' — departure, initiation, and return. His book The Hero with a Thousand Faces became a template for screenwriters and students of storytelling alike.
phil:mackie: J.L. Mackie was an Australian philosopher best known for his defense of moral skepticism and his contributions to metaethics, philosophy of religion, and the theory of causation. In his 1977 book Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, he advanced the "error theory," arguing that ordinary moral judgments presuppose objective values that do not in fact exist, so all such claims are systematically false. He is also remembered for a sharp formulation of the logical problem of evil and for influential work on Locke and Hume.
phil:max-weber: Max Weber (1864–1920) was a German sociologist and political economist, one of the founders of modern social science. His Protestant Ethic thesis traced capitalism's roots to religious ideas, and he analyzed how modernity 'disenchants' the world and how states claim legitimate authority. His debates with Marxist historical materialism shaped twentieth-century social theory.
phil:mctaggart: J.M.E. McTaggart was a British idealist philosopher best remembered for his argument for the unreality of time. He distinguished the "A-series," which orders events as past, present, and future, from the "B-series," which orders them as earlier and later, and contended that the A-series is both essential to time and internally contradictory, concluding that time itself is illusory. His argument continues to frame contemporary debates in the metaphysics of time.
phil:milton-friedman: Milton Friedman (1912–2006) was an American economist, Nobel laureate, and leader of the Chicago school of free-market economics. In business ethics he is known for the 'Friedman doctrine': that a corporation's sole social responsibility is to increase its profits within the rules of the game — a provocative claim that later stakeholder and CSR debates still define themselves against.
phil:nagarjuna: Nagarjuna was an Indian Buddhist philosopher and founder of the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way, school of Mahayana thought. He is best known for the doctrine of emptiness, the claim that all phenomena lack any independent, intrinsic nature because they arise only in dependence on other things. Through rigorous dialectical arguments, developed most famously in his Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, he sought to dissolve metaphysical extremes and fixed views while avoiding nihilism, an approach that profoundly shaped later Buddhist philosophy across Asia.
phil:plutarch: Plutarch was a Greek philosopher, biographer, and essayist of the first and second centuries AD, writing under Roman rule and steeped in the Platonic tradition. He is best known for his Parallel Lives, which pair eminent Greeks and Romans to draw out moral character, and for the Moralia, a wide-ranging collection of essays on ethics, religion, and practical wisdom. More a moralist than a systematic theorist, he used history and biography to illuminate virtue and human conduct. His works profoundly shaped Renaissance and later European literature and thought.
phil:regan: Tom Regan was an American philosopher and a leading theorist of animal rights. In The Case for Animal Rights (1983) he argued that many animals are "subjects-of-a-life"—beings with beliefs, desires, memory, and a welfare of their own—and therefore possess inherent value that entitles them to respectful treatment rather than use as mere resources. Unlike utilitarian approaches, his rights-based view holds that such value cannot be traded away for aggregate benefit, grounding strong duties not to harm or exploit animals.
phil:tillich: Paul Tillich was a German-American theologian and philosopher who sought to interpret Christian faith in dialogue with modern existential thought. He described God not as a being among beings but as "the ground of being" itself, and defined faith as "ultimate concern"—the orientation of one's whole life toward what matters unconditionally. Through works such as The Courage to Be and his Systematic Theology, he used a "method of correlation" to answer the questions posed by human existence with the symbols of religious tradition.
phil:tolstoy: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was the great Russian novelist of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, and in later life a radical Christian moralist. He renounced violence, property, and institutional church alike, developing an ethic of nonresistance to evil that deeply influenced Gandhi and, through him, the theory of nonviolent civil disobedience.
phil:vann-inwagen: Peter van Inwagen is an American philosopher who has made influential contributions to metaphysics, free will, and philosophy of religion. In An Essay on Free Will he articulated the "consequence argument," a widely discussed case for incompatibilism holding that free will is inconsistent with determinism. He is also known for a distinctive view in the metaphysics of material objects, according to which the only composite things that exist are living organisms, and for careful work on the problem of evil.
phil:vico: Giambattista Vico (1668–1744) was a Neapolitan philosopher who challenged Descartes' model of certain knowledge, arguing that we truly understand only what we ourselves have made — above all, history and institutions. His New Science pioneered a philosophy of history in which cultures cycle through ages of gods, heroes, and human beings.
phil:appiah: Kwame Anthony Appiah is a British-born, Ghanaian-raised philosopher known for his work on identity, race, and moral obligation across cultures. He has argued that "race" lacks a biological basis and that identities are best understood as social scripts we neither wholly choose nor should let wholly define us, while defending a rooted cosmopolitanism that balances loyalty to the local with duties to all humanity. His accessible books, including Cosmopolitanism and The Ethics of Identity, have brought these questions to a wide public.
phil:ayn-rand: Ayn Rand (1905-1982) was a Russian-American novelist and self-taught philosopher whose 'Objectivism' defends rational self-interest, ethical egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism. Through novels like The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged she argued that selfishness, rightly understood, is a virtue; academic philosophers have largely kept her at arm's length, but her cultural influence remains enormous.
phil:bernard-suits: Bernard Suits (1929-2007) was a Canadian philosopher of sport and games whose playful classic The Grasshopper defines game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles. He speculated that in a utopia freed from necessity, playing games might be the only thing left worth doing.
phil:bostrom: Nick Bostrom (b. 1973) is a Swedish-born philosopher known for his work on existential risk, the ethics of emerging technology, and the long-term future of humanity. He is widely associated with the simulation argument, which contends that if advanced civilizations could run many detailed ancestor simulations, we may well be living in one, and with the analysis of risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence in his book Superintelligence. His writing on transhumanism and human enhancement has made him a prominent voice in debates about how technology may reshape human life.
phil:clausewitz: Carl von Clausewitz (1780-1831) was a Prussian general and military theorist whose unfinished masterpiece On War made him the West's most quoted strategist. He argued that war is 'the continuation of politics by other means,' and that real war is inherently chaotic, shaped by chance, friction, and the passions of nations.
phil:crenshaw: Kimberlé Crenshaw is an American legal scholar and a leading figure in critical race theory who coined the term intersectionality. She showed how anti-discrimination law, by treating race and gender as separate categories, failed to capture the compounded disadvantages faced by Black women at their intersection. Her framework has become central to analyses of overlapping systems of oppression across law, feminism, and the social sciences.
phil:edmund-burke: Edmund Burke (1729-1797) was an Irish-born British statesman and philosopher, often called the father of modern conservatism for his scathing defense of tradition and gradual reform against the French Revolution. His early Philosophical Enquiry also popularized the aesthetics of the sublime: terrifying vastness that awes rather than pleases.
phil:empedocles: Empedocles (c. 494-434 BC) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher, poet, and physician from Sicily who taught that everything is composed of four eternal 'roots' - earth, water, air, and fire - mixed and separated by two cosmic forces, Love and Strife. He is also credited with an early theory of evolution by survival of the fittest.
phil:gaston-bachelard: Gaston Bachelard (1884-1962) was a French philosopher who wrote on both science and poetry. In philosophy of science he showed how progress demands an 'epistemological break' with past errors, while in The Poetics of Space he explored how attics, cellars, and nests carry our imagination and daydreams.
phil:georges-bataille: Georges Bataille (1897-1962) was a French novelist and philosopher who wrote from the edges - eroticism, sacrifice, the sacred - at once a profound influence on postwar French thought and a scandal to it. His economics of excess held that societies must waste surplus in festival and destruction, defying the sober logic of utility.
phil:goffman: Erving Goffman (1922-1982) was a Canadian-American sociologist who studied face-to-face life as theater. In The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life he showed how we perform roles, manage impressions, and follow subtle stage directions in every interaction - work later drawn on by gender theorists such as Judith Butler.
phil:graham-priest: Graham Priest (born 1948) is a British-born logician and philosopher, now at the City University of New York, famous for defending dialetheism: the view that some contradictions are actually true. Using 'paraconsistent' logics that keep such truths from exploding into chaos, he has reopened questions most logicians considered settled since Aristotle.
phil:huizinga: Johan Huizinga (1872-1945) was a Dutch historian whose 1938 classic Homo Ludens argued that play is older than culture and creates it: law, war, poetry, and philosophy all begin in play. His idea of the 'magic circle' - games as temporary worlds with their own rules - is now central to game studies.
phil:iris-murdoch: Iris Murdoch (1919-1999) was a British novelist and philosopher who made the moral life a matter of attention: the difficult, loving effort to see other people as they really are rather than through the fog of our own ego. Drawing on Plato and Simone Weil, she saw this 'unselfing,' not rules or choices, as the heart of goodness.
phil:josiah-royce: Josiah Royce (1855-1916) was an American absolute idealist at Harvard, a colleague of William James, who argued that individuals become fully themselves only through loyalty to genuine communities. His philosophy of loyalty anticipated later communitarianism, and he made lasting contributions to the problem of error and the nature of community.
phil:mcluhan: Marshall McLuhan (1911-1980) was a Canadian media theorist and literary critic whose aphorism 'the medium is the message' argued that communication technologies reshape human life more than their content does. He foresaw the 'global village' created by electronic media and became a posthumous guru of the internet age.
phil:montaigne: Michel de Montaigne was a French Renaissance thinker and statesman who is widely regarded as the inventor of the personal essay. Writing in the late sixteenth century, he turned self-examination into a philosophical method, using his own habits, doubts, and inconsistencies as material for reflection on the human condition. His skeptical motto, "What do I know?", captured a temperament wary of dogma and confident only in the difficulty of knowing anything for certain. The candor and range of his Essais made him a lasting influence on later writers and philosophers of skepticism and everyday ethics.
phil:naess: Arne Naess was a Norwegian philosopher who coined the term "deep ecology" to distinguish a radical environmental outlook from the merely "shallow" management of pollution and resources. He argued that all living things have intrinsic value independent of their usefulness to humans, and that flourishing requires a widened sense of self that identifies with the larger living world. Drawing on Spinoza and Gandhi, he combined technical work in logic and semantics with a lifelong commitment to ecological activism.
phil:plotinus: Plotinus was a philosopher of the Roman era and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose lectures were collected by his student Porphyry into the six sets of treatises known as the Enneads. Building on Plato, he described reality as a hierarchy emanating from a single ineffable source he called the One, from which proceed Intellect and Soul, and ultimately the material world. He held that the human soul can ascend back toward its origin through contemplation, culminating in a mystical union with the One, an idea that deeply influenced later Christian, Islamic, and Jewish thought.
phil:schelling: F.W.J. Schelling (1775-1854) was a German idealist philosopher who, alongside Fichte and Hegel, transformed post-Kantian thought. He gave nature an active role philosophy had denied it, made art the supreme revelation of the absolute, and posed the problem of evil and human freedom with a darkness that anticipates existentialism.
phil:simone-weil: Simone Weil (1909-1943) was a French philosopher, mystic, and political activist who died at thirty-four, weakened by self-imposed austerity in solidarity with occupied France. Her scattered writings on attention, affliction, and the 'gravity' of the world - later collected as Gravity and Grace - influence theology, ethics, and political thought alike.
phil:voltaire: Voltaire (1694-1778), pen name of Francois-Marie Arouet, was the sharpest wit of the French Enlightenment - a playwright, historian, and crusader for toleration against tyranny and superstition. His satire Candide mercilessly mocked Leibniz's claim that ours is 'the best of all possible worlds' in the face of human suffering.
phil:walzer: Michael Walzer is an American political theorist associated with communitarian and pluralist approaches to justice. In Spheres of Justice he argued for "complex equality," the view that different social goods—money, office, health care, political power—should be distributed according to their own distinct meanings and criteria, so that dominance in one sphere does not translate into dominance in others. He is also a leading figure in just war theory, whose Just and Unjust Wars revived a rights-based moral analysis of when and how wars may legitimately be fought.
phil:zeno-elea: Zeno of Elea was a fifth-century BC Greek philosopher and student of Parmenides, celebrated for a series of paradoxes designed to defend his teacher's claim that reality is single and unchanging. In arguments such as Achilles and the tortoise and the flying arrow, he tried to show that motion and plurality lead to contradiction and are therefore illusory. Whether or not his conclusions convince, his paradoxes sharpened questions about infinity, continuity, and the structure of space and time. Aristotle credited him with inventing dialectic, and his puzzles still occupy philosophers and mathematicians today.
phil:averroes: Averroes, known in Arabic as Ibn Rushd and living from 1126 to 1198, was an Andalusian philosopher, jurist, and physician celebrated for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle. He defended the compatibility of philosophy and revelation, arguing that they are two paths to the same truth, and criticized what he saw as the anti-philosophical excesses of earlier thinkers. Through Latin translations his commentaries profoundly influenced medieval European Scholasticism, where he was known simply as the Commentator.
phil:avicenna: Avicenna, known in Arabic as Ibn Sina and living from 980 to 1037, was a Persian polymath who ranks among the greatest philosophers and physicians of the medieval Islamic world. Building on Aristotle and Neoplatonism, he developed an influential metaphysics centered on the distinction between essence and existence and an argument for a Necessary Being as the ground of all contingent things. His encyclopedic works, especially The Book of Healing and The Canon of Medicine, shaped philosophy and medical teaching in both the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.
phil:benatar: David Benatar is a contemporary South African philosopher at the University of Cape Town, best known for anti-natalism: the provocative argument that coming into existence is always a serious harm, so it is wrong to create new people. He is a leading voice in contemporary philosophical pessimism.
phil:byung-chul-han: Byung-Chul Han is a South Korean-born German philosopher known for short, sharp diagnoses of digital life. He argues that the disciplinary society Foucault described, built on surveillance and prohibition, has given way to an achievement society where people exploit and monitor themselves voluntarily.
phil:derrick-bell: Derrick Bell was an American legal scholar and civil rights lawyer, the first Black professor tenured at Harvard Law School, and a founding figure of Critical Race Theory. He argued that racial equality advances only when it converges with white interests, and his work laid the groundwork for later intersectional analysis of race and law.
phil:fichte: Johann Gottlieb Fichte was a German philosopher and a founding figure of German Idealism who developed the critical philosophy of Kant in a more systematically idealist direction. In his Wissenschaftslehre, or Doctrine of Science, he sought to derive all knowledge from the self-positing activity of the "I," making the free, active subject the starting point of philosophy. His emphasis on will, striving, and the moral vocation of the self influenced later idealists and Romantic thinkers. He also became a prominent public voice, notably in his Addresses to the German Nation, delivered during the Napoleonic occupation.
phil:firestone: Shulamith Firestone was a Canadian-born American radical feminist and a key organizer of the early women's liberation movement. In The Dialectic of Sex she reinterpreted Marx and Engels to argue that the fundamental division in society is not class but sex, rooted in the biological facts of reproduction. She provocatively proposed that liberation would require freeing women from childbearing through technology, aiming to abolish the sex-based structure of the family.
phil:fricker: Miranda Fricker is a British philosopher who introduced the influential concept of "epistemic injustice"—wrongs done to people specifically in their capacity as knowers. In her 2007 book of that title she distinguished testimonial injustice, in which prejudice leads a hearer to discount a speaker's credibility, from hermeneutical injustice, in which gaps in shared concepts leave some people unable to make sense of their own experience. Her work connects the theory of knowledge to ethics and social power, and has shaped debates well beyond philosophy.
phil:friedan: Betty Friedan was an American writer and activist whose 1963 book The Feminine Mystique helped launch second-wave feminism in the United States. She named the pervasive dissatisfaction of mid-century housewives—the 'problem that has no name'—and criticized a cultural ideal that confined women to domestic roles. A co-founder and first president of the National Organization for Women, she pressed for equal opportunity in work, education, and public life.
phil:gadamer: Hans-Georg Gadamer (1900–2002) was a German philosopher and the leading figure of philosophical hermeneutics, the study of how understanding and interpretation are possible. In his major work Truth and Method he argued that understanding is always shaped by our historical situation and inherited prejudices, which he treated not as mere obstacles but as the enabling conditions of interpretation. His notions of the fusion of horizons and the dialogical character of understanding influenced fields ranging from literary theory to law and theology.
phil:gramsci: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist theorist and political activist who reshaped Marxist thinking about culture and power while imprisoned under Mussolini's Fascist regime. In his Prison Notebooks he developed the concept of hegemony to explain how a ruling class maintains dominance not merely through force but by winning consent through cultural, moral, and intellectual leadership. He emphasized the role of civil society, ideology, and "organic intellectuals" in both sustaining and contesting the existing order, giving lasting impetus to cultural and political analysis on the left.
phil:guy-debord: Guy Debord was a French Marxist theorist and filmmaker who led the Situationist International. In The Society of the Spectacle (1967) he argued that modern life has become mediated by images: social relations are replaced by the representation of commodities, a critique that influenced the 1968 Paris protests.
phil:hierocles: Hierocles was an ancient Stoic philosopher, probably of the second century AD, known only from surviving fragments. His image of concentric circles of concern holds that we should progressively draw distant strangers inward, treating them more like family, one of antiquity's clearest arguments for cosmopolitan concern.
phil:jameson: Fredric Jameson is an American Marxist literary critic, one of the most influential theorists of postmodernism. He famously analyzed postmodern culture as the cultural logic of late capitalism, connecting pastiche and the waning of historicity to the economic transformations of the contemporary world.
phil:jung: Carl Jung (1875–1961) was a Swiss psychiatrist who, after an early collaboration with Freud, developed his own school of analytical psychology. He is best known for the ideas of the collective unconscious—a stratum of inherited symbolic material shared across humanity—and of archetypes, recurring images such as the shadow, the anima, and the self that structure myth, dream, and religion. Jung also introduced the notions of psychological types and introversion and extraversion, and framed the goal of psychic development as individuation, the integration of the personality into a coherent whole.
phil:korsgaard: Christine Korsgaard is an American philosopher and a leading contemporary interpreter and defender of Kantian ethics. Her work argues that moral obligations arise from the reflective nature of human agency: because we can step back from our impulses and ask whether to act on them, we must confer value on ourselves and, in turn, on others, a view she develops in The Sources of Normativity. She has also written extensively on personal identity, practical reason, and the moral standing of animals.
phil:maimonides: Maimonides, who lived from 1138 to 1204, was a Jewish philosopher, physician, and legal scholar working in the Islamic world of medieval Spain and Egypt. In his Guide for the Perplexed he sought to reconcile the teachings of the Hebrew Bible with Aristotelian philosophy, developing a rigorously negative theology in which God can be described only by what he is not. His codification of Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah remains authoritative, and his thought influenced later Jewish, Islamic, and Christian philosophers alike.
phil:mencius: Mencius was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period regarded as the most important early interpreter of Confucius. He is best known for arguing that human nature is inherently good, illustrated by the spontaneous alarm anyone feels on seeing a child about to fall into a well, and that moral virtues grow from innate sprouts that education and reflection can nurture. He also developed influential political ideas, holding that rulers govern by a mandate contingent on the people's welfare and that a tyrant forfeits his right to rule.
phil:plumwood: Val Plumwood was an Australian philosopher and prominent voice in ecofeminism and environmental thought. She argued that Western culture is structured by a web of dualisms—reason over nature, human over animal, mind over body, male over female—that license domination, and she sought to overcome these hierarchies without denying real differences. Her book Feminism and the Mastery of Nature (1993) linked the oppression of women, colonized peoples, and the natural world as expressions of the same logic of mastery.
phil:sandel: Michael Sandel is an American political philosopher known for his communitarian critique of liberalism and for his enormously popular Harvard course on justice. In Liberalism and the Limits of Justice he challenged the Rawlsian idea of a self that exists prior to its ends, arguing instead that our identities are partly constituted by community attachments and shared conceptions of the good. Much of his later work, including What Money Can't Buy and The Tyranny of Merit, examines the moral limits of markets and the corrosive effects of a purely meritocratic society on solidarity and the common good.
phil:shankara: Shankara (also Adi Shankara) was an Indian philosopher of the early eighth century and the most influential systematizer of Advaita Vedanta, the school of non-dualism within Hindu thought. He argued that ultimate reality (Brahman) is a single, undivided consciousness, and that the individual self (atman) is identical with it, so that the apparent multiplicity of the world is a product of ignorance (avidya) and appearance (maya). Through commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras, and through the monastic orders he is traditionally credited with founding, he shaped the course of later Indian philosophy and religious practice.
phil:umberto-eco: Umberto Eco was an Italian medievalist, semiotician, and novelist, best known for The Name of the Rose. His scholarly work examined signs, interpretation, and the limits of how far texts can mean, and in his essays he analyzed mass culture, spectacle, and the recurring features of fascist movements.
phil:wolf: Susan Wolf is an American moral philosopher known for questioning whether being perfectly moral is a coherent or desirable ideal. In her essay "Moral Saints" she argued that a life devoted wholly to morality would be strangely impoverished, lacking the personal passions and pursuits that make a life good. She has also written influentially on free will and moral responsibility and on the sources of meaning in life, contending that meaning arises when subjective engagement meets objective worth.
phil:xunzi: Xunzi was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period who offered a rigorous, systematic defense and revision of Confucian thought. In sharp contrast to Mencius, he argued that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, and that goodness is a deliberate achievement produced by education, ritual, and social institutions that reshape our raw desires. He gave a naturalistic account of Heaven as impersonal nature rather than a moral agent, and his emphasis on order through cultivation influenced later Chinese thought, including his students associated with Legalism.
phil:addams: Jane Addams was an American social reformer, activist, and philosopher associated with the pragmatist tradition and a co-founder of Hull House, a pioneering settlement house in Chicago. She developed a distinctive ethics rooted in sympathetic knowledge, cooperation, and lived democratic practice, insisting that social reform required entering into the experience of others. A leading figure in the peace and women's movements, she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931.
phil:al-ghazali: Al-Ghazali, who lived from about 1058 to 1111, was a Persian theologian, jurist, and mystic whose work reshaped Islamic thought. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers he mounted a searching critique of the Aristotelian rationalism of thinkers like Avicenna, challenging their claims about causation and the eternity of the world, while his later writings integrated Sufi mysticism with orthodox theology. His spiritual autobiography and his synthesis of law, philosophy, and inner experience made him one of the most influential figures in the history of Islam.
phil:audre-lorde: Audre Lorde (1934–1992) was an American poet, essayist, and Black feminist thinker who described herself as "black, lesbian, mother, warrior, poet." She argued that racial, sexual, and class differences should be acknowledged and used as sources of power rather than suppressed, and sharply criticized the silence and tokenism within mainstream feminism.
phil:cavell: Stanley Cavell (1926–2018) was an American philosopher, long at Harvard, who extended ordinary language philosophy into readings of skepticism, literature, and film. He treated skeptical doubt not merely as an epistemological problem but as a condition of human relationships, and wrote influentially on Shakespeare, Hollywood comedy, and Emerson and Thoreau.
phil:girard: René Girard (1923–2015) was a French-American philosopher and literary critic who taught at Stanford. He is best known for the theory of mimetic desire — the claim that we learn what to want by imitating others — and for the scapegoat mechanism, in which communities discharge their internal rivalries through collective violence.
phil:h-richard-niebuhr: H. Richard Niebuhr (1894–1962) was an American Christian theologian and ethicist at Yale, brother of the better-known Reinhold Niebuhr. He is remembered for his typology of how Christ relates to culture, for the idea of "radical monotheism," and for an ethics of responsible, relational response to God and to other people.
phil:irigaray: Luce Irigaray (born in Belgium in 1930 or 1932) is a French feminist philosopher trained in psychoanalysis, associated with the French feminist movement of the 1970s. In works like Speculum of the Other Woman she argues that Western philosophy has built its accounts of reason and subjectivity on an implicitly masculine model, leaving woman as the unthought other.
phil:kendall-walton: Kendall Walton (b. 1939) is an American philosopher of art, long at the University of Michigan, known for the make-believe theory of representation. On his view artworks work as props in games of imagination, an approach he famously applied to the paradox of fiction — how we can genuinely feel for characters we know do not exist.
phil:kropotkin: Pyotr Kropotkin (1842–1921) was a Russian geographer and naturalist turned revolutionary, and the leading theorist of anarcho-communism. Drawing on his observations of Siberian wildlife, he argued in Mutual Aid that cooperation, no less than competition, is a driving force of evolution and the foundation for a society without the state.
phil:max-scheler: Max Scheler (1874–1928) was a German phenomenologist and the leading figure of the early phenomenology movement after Husserl. He developed a rich ethics of values and emotional life, studied love and sympathy, and — extending Nietzsche — gave the classic phenomenological analysis of ressentiment as the resentful self-deception of the powerless.
phil:p-f-strawson: P.F. Strawson (1919–2006) was a British philosopher at Oxford, among the most important analytic philosophers of the twentieth century. His landmark essay "Freedom and Resentment" grounded moral responsibility in our everyday reactive attitudes — resentment, gratitude, forgiveness — while his book Individuals defended "descriptive metaphysics" against skeptical puzzles about persons and bodies.
phil:warren: Karen J. Warren is an American philosopher who helped define ecofeminism as a distinct field. She argued that the domination of women and the domination of nature are conceptually and historically connected, sustained by a shared "logic of domination" that ranks some beings above others to justify their subordination. Through works such as Ecofeminist Philosophy, she developed a care-based, context-sensitive environmental ethic attentive to the ways gender, race, and class shape our relations to the natural world.
averroes-reason-revelation: The Concord of Reason and Revelation is the position, developed by the Andalusian philosopher Averroes, that philosophical demonstration and religious scripture cannot ultimately conflict because both issue from the same truth. Where a literal reading of scripture appears to contradict what reason establishes, Averroes held that the text should be interpreted allegorically, since the two are simply different routes to a single reality. Responding to theologians who attacked philosophy as impious, he argued that rational inquiry is not only permitted but obligatory for those capable of it, and that religion addresses different audiences through different modes of speech.
modern-moral-philosophy: In her 1958 essay 'Modern Moral Philosophy,' Elizabeth Anscombe made three provocative claims that helped reshape twentieth-century ethics. She argued that moral philosophy should be set aside until an adequate philosophy of psychology, including a workable account of action and intention, was available; that the notions of moral obligation and moral duty are survivals from an earlier framework of divine law and are incoherent once detached from a lawgiver; and that this legalistic vocabulary should be abandoned in favor of concepts like virtue and human flourishing. She also coined the term 'consequentialism' as a critical label. The essay is widely credited with helping to inaugurate the modern revival of virtue ethics.
darshana: In Indian philosophy, a darshana is a systematic school of thought, a comprehensive 'view' of reality that combines doctrine with a path of practice aimed at liberation. Classical usage counts six orthodox darshanas — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta — which accept the authority of the Vedas, while Buddhist, Jain, and materialist Carvaka schools stand outside that group as rival views. The Sanskrit word derives from a root meaning 'to see,' so each darshana is in effect a distinct way of seeing and organizing experience.
vedic-sacrifice: Yajna, the ritual sacrifice, was the central religious act of Vedic India (roughly 1500-500 BCE): offerings of ghee, grain, and the pressed soma juice poured into the sacred fire by specially trained Brahmin priests. The rite was believed to sustain the gods and thereby uphold cosmic and social order, and elaborate manuals prescribed its correct performance down to each gesture and utterance. Later philosophical reflection transformed it: the Upanishads reinterpreted sacrifice inwardly, while the Mimamsa school made Vedic ritual the very foundation of dharma and held its efficacy to be eternal and self-sufficient.
dependent-origination: Pratityasamutpada, the principle of dependent origination, is the Buddha's central causal teaching: every phenomenon arises only in dependence on other conditions and ceases when those conditions cease, so nothing exists as an independent, self-standing thing. The classic formulation traces twelve links (nidanas), beginning with ignorance, that explain how craving, clinging, and rebirth produce suffering. Because all things are conditioned in this way, the principle grounds the Buddhist doctrines of no-self and, in later Madhyamaka thought, emptiness.
abhidharma: The Abhidharma is the scholastic literature, developing from about the third century BCE, in which Buddhist thinkers analyzed the Buddha's discourses into their ultimate constituents: impermanent, momentary events called dharmas, such as particular instances of color, feeling, or consciousness. On this analysis a person is not a substantial self but a causally connected stream of such dharmas, which explains continuity without positing a soul. Schools such as the Sarvastivada and the Theravadins built rival taxonomies of dharmas, producing the systematic metaphysics that later Buddhist philosophy, including Yogacara, both developed and contested.
yogacara-mind-only: Yogacara, the Buddhist school that flourished from about the fourth century CE and is associated with the half-brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, is known for its doctrine of 'mind-only' (cittamatra) or 'representation-only.' It holds that the objects we experience are constructions of consciousness: we never encounter a world outside our mental representations, which arise from seeds stored in a subconscious 'storehouse consciousness' (alaya-vijnana). The doctrine was meant less as a denial that experience occurs than as an account of how the mistaken belief in an independent external world sustains suffering.
classical-yoga: Classical Yoga is the system codified in the Yoga Sutras, traditionally attributed to the compiler Patanjali and dated somewhere between the second century BCE and the fourth century CE. It prescribes an eight-limbed path (ashtanga) running from ethical restraints and observances through posture, breath control, and sensory withdrawal to progressively deeper states of concentration, meditation, and absorption (samadhi). Sharing the dualist metaphysics of Samkhya, it holds that suffering comes from misidentifying conscious spirit with nature, and that disciplined practice leads to kaivalya, the liberation of the seer from the seen.
samkhya-dualism: Samkhya, often regarded as the oldest of the classical Indian schools and traditionally ascribed to the sage Kapila, is a dualism of purusha and prakriti. Purusha designates the plurality of conscious selves, pure witnesses that are never agents, while prakriti is primordial material nature, composed of three strands (sattva, rajas, and tamas) and capable of evolving into mind, senses, and the physical world. Suffering arises because the self mistakenly identifies with nature's products; liberation comes through discriminating knowledge that separates the witness from what is witnessed, a position classically stated in Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika.
vaisheshika-categories: The Vaisheshika school, traditionally founded by the sage Kanada, developed an atomistic realism organized around an enumeration of the padarthas, the categories into which everything that can be named falls. The classic list has seven members: substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and, added in later systematization, non-existence or absence. Particularity (vishesha) is the category that individuates ultimate atoms, which the school held to be eternal, indivisible particles of earth, water, fire, and air, making Vaisheshika one of the earliest sustained atomic theories.
nyaya-five-limb-inference: The Nyaya school, whose foundational sutras are attributed to Aksapada Gautama, analyzed inference (anumana) into five members, a schema that functions both as a proof and as a fully explicit argument. A standard example: the mountain has fire (thesis); because it has smoke (reason); whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen and unlike a lake (example stating the universal concomitance); this mountain has smoke (application); therefore it has fire (conclusion). The five-membered form remained central to Indian logic and formal debate and was later adapted by Buddhist logicians such as Dignaga and Dharmakirti.
mimamsa: Mimamsa, or Purva Mimamsa, is the Indian school devoted to interpreting the ritual portions of the Vedas, founded on Jaimini's sutras in roughly the last centuries BCE. It defines dharma as what the Vedic injunctions prescribe and defends the Vedas as eternal and unauthored, hence an infallible source of knowledge. In developing its hermeneutics the school produced sophisticated work on language, meaning, and sentence interpretation, and its later masters Kumarila and Prabhakara became major philosophers in their own right, with an epistemology that strongly influenced Vedanta.
semiotics-signifier-signified: Semiotics is the general theory of signs and of how they convey meaning, developed along two main lines: Ferdinand de Saussure's linguistics and Charles Sanders Peirce's logic of signs. Saussure modeled the sign as a union of signifier (the sound-pattern or written mark) and signified (the concept it expresses), insisting that the link between them is arbitrary and that signs mean what they do only through their differences from other signs within a system. That framework underlay structuralist and post-structuralist analyses of culture, in which everything from myth to fashion could be read as a system of signs.
anti-psychologism: Anti-psychologism is the thesis, argued most influentially by Gottlob Frege, that the laws of logic and mathematics are objective truths about concepts, numbers, and validity, not generalizations about how human minds happen to think. The opposing psychologism, prominent in nineteenth-century empiricism, treated logical laws as empirical laws of thought, a view Frege attacked for confusing the grounds of a truth with the psychological causes of holding it. Edmund Husserl delivered a parallel critique in his Logical Investigations, and the resulting separation of logic from psychology became a cornerstone of both analytic philosophy and phenomenology.
intrinsic-vs-instrumental-value: Value theorists distinguish things that are good for their own sake from things that are good as means to something else: pleasure or happiness is often held to be intrinsically valuable, while money or medicine is instrumentally valuable, worth having only because of what it leads to. The distinction, sharpened in the early twentieth century by G. E. Moore's 'isolation test' for intrinsic value, structures debates in ethics about what makes a life or an action ultimately worthwhile. Borderline cases, such as knowledge, achievement, and the value of persons, have kept the analysis of the distinction a live topic.
sorites-paradox: The sorites paradox — from the Greek soros, 'heap' — was posed by the ancient philosopher Eubulides of Miletus: one grain of sand is not a heap, and adding a single grain to what is not a heap cannot make a heap; iterating the reasoning yields that a million grains do not make a heap, which is plainly absurd. The puzzle exposes the problem of vague predicates like 'heap,' 'bald,' and 'tall,' which admit borderline cases and appear to lack sharp boundaries. Contemporary responses include epistemicism, which holds that there are hidden sharp boundaries, and supervaluationism, which preserves ordinary speech while denying that 'heap' has a precise extension.
maternal-thinking: Maternal thinking is the account developed by the American philosopher Sara Ruddick in her 1989 book Maternal Thinking, which presents mothering not merely as labor or feeling but as an intellectual practice that generates its own characteristic ways of thought. The demands of keeping children safe and fostering their growth cultivate attention, humility, and concrete judgment, together with an ethics of preservation, growth, and training that can conflict with abstract principle. Ruddick stressed that 'maternal' names a social practice rather than a biological role, so men can mother, and she argued that the practice carries implications for peace politics as well.
original-sin: Original sin is the Christian doctrine that the transgression of the first human beings, classically Adam's disobedience, wounded human nature itself, so that all descendants are born with an inherited condition inclining them to sin and death. Augustine of Hippo gave the Western church its definitive account, arguing that Adam's guilt and corruption are transmitted to every person and can be remedied only by grace; Pelagius, who denied that Adam's sin damaged his descendants in this way, was condemned as a heretic. Eastern Orthodox theology, by contrast, has generally understood the inheritance as mortality and corruption rather than shared guilt.
parasocial-relationship: The term parasocial relationship was introduced by the media researchers Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl in 1956 to describe the one-sided intimacy television viewers developed with performers, who felt like familiar friends although the relationship ran entirely in one direction. The concept has since been extended to celebrities, influencers, live streamers, and fictional characters, covering the sense of knowing someone who cannot know you in return. Philosophically, such attachments raise questions about authenticity, the ethics of commercially manufactured intimacy, and whether parasocial bonds are a diminished substitute for, or a genuine form of, friendship.
reputation: In social epistemology, reputation refers to the circulating beliefs and evaluations a community holds about a person, which function as testimony: others rely on a reputation to decide whom to trust, hire, or believe before any direct evidence is available. Because reputations can be inaccurate, slow to correct, and shaped by prejudice, they raise questions of fairness — a person can be treated on the strength of false information — and of epistemic justice, since whose word counts often depends on whose reputation stands. Philosophers study how reputational systems, from honor cultures to online ratings, distribute credibility and how they might be reformed.
repetition-and-difference: In Difference and Repetition (1968), Gilles Deleuze argues that repetition is never the mere return of the same: every genuine repetition produces a difference, because it always occurs under conditions of displacement and disguise. Against the philosophical tradition that treats identity as primary and difference as merely derivative, Deleuze reverses the order, making difference-in-itself the fundamental character of reality and of thought. The book is widely read as a rejection of representation — of thinking modeled on the recognition of the same — in favor of thought that registers the new.
archive-fever: Archive fever (mal d'archive) is the title concept of a 1995 lecture by Jacques Derrida, drawing on Freud, which names the double compulsion at the heart of collecting and preserving: the drive to secure the past in a place of custody, and the destructive 'fever' of forgetting that is inseparable from it. Derrida ties the archive to a founding violence — the authority of those who decide what counts as archivable — and argues that the archive's technology (he wrote amid the rise of email) conditions what future memory and future scholarship can be. The piece became a touchstone for theories of memory, history, and documentation.
philosophy-of-grief: The philosophy of grief examines the nature, rationality, and value of mourning: whether grief involves irrational beliefs, as Freud suggested in the survivor's refusal to accept the death; whether painful emotions over losses can be fitting rather than mere pathology; and what grief reveals about our attachments and identity. Contemporary analytic work often treats grief as a form of love that persists beyond death and reshapes the griever's commitments, asking how one can live well while honoring the dead. The topic draws on the Stoics, Augustine, and Spinoza as much as on current philosophy of emotion.
affective-injustice: Affective injustice names wrongs done to people in their emotional lives — for example, when an emotional culture privileges the feelings of some groups while shaming or silencing the emotions of others, or when emotions apt to one's situation, such as anger at oppression, are dismissed as irrational or unprofessional. The idea builds on feminist work such as Alison Jaggar's account of 'outlaw emotions,' feelings that detect injustice the dominant view misses, and on recent analyses of whose affect is permitted public expression. Philosophers use the concept to argue that justice concerns not only material goods and rights but the fair standing of people's emotional capacities.
philosophy-of-anger: The philosophy of anger asks what anger is, when it is justified, and whether it does moral good or harm. The Stoics, especially Seneca, condemned it as a temporary madness and a desire for revenge; Aristotle, by contrast, counted a fitting anger at real slights as part of virtuous character. The contemporary debate renews both positions: some philosophers defend anger at injustice as apt, communicative, and motivating, while others argue, with Martha Nussbaum, that its retributive element makes a forward-looking 'transitional' anger the better moral instrument.
standpoint-epistemology: Feminist standpoint epistemology holds that knowledge is socially situated: what one can perceive and know depends on one's position in relations of labor and power. Drawing on Marx's account of the proletarian standpoint, theorists such as Nancy Hartsock and Sandra Harding argued that the perspectives of marginalized groups, achieved through collective political struggle, can be epistemically advantaged, because the view from below exposes social relations that the dominant standpoint renders invisible. Harding's slogan of 'strong objectivity' claims that starting inquiry from marginalized lives produces more, not less, rigorous knowledge.
beauty-myth: The beauty myth is the thesis advanced by Naomi Wolf in her 1990 book of that name: that as women won legal and economic equality, a rising ideology of female beauty — thinner, younger, ever more unattainable images — was deployed to keep women anxious, competitive, and preoccupied, functioning as a political and economic constraint where older barriers had fallen. Wolf argued that the ideal is not about beauty itself but about control, operating across work, religion, sex, and violence alike. The book was criticized on points of evidence but became a touchstone of feminist analysis of body norms and the beauty industries.
reproductive-justice: Reproductive justice is a framework formulated in 1994 by a coalition of Black women activists, notably Loretta Ross and the group SisterSong, as an alternative to a politics focused solely on abortion rights. It asserts three human rights: the right to have children, the right not to have children, and the right to parent children in safe and sustainable communities, with access to the conditions — economic security, health care, freedom from violence — that make those choices real. The framework insists that legal access without the social means to act is incomplete, and it centers the experience of women of color and poor women.
race-as-social-construct: The claim that race is a social construct holds that races are not natural divisions of humankind marked by biological essence, but kinds constituted by historical, legal, and political practices — slavery, classification, segregation — that nonetheless make race real in its effects. The position traces to W. E. B. Du Bois and has been elaborated by philosophers such as Kwame Anthony Appiah and Sally Haslanger, who debate whether racial categories are illusions to be eliminated or social identities worth retaining for the sake of justice. The constructivist view explains both why biology finds no racial genes dividing humanity and why racism produces measurable social and bodily harms.
wrongful-discrimination: In philosophy, wrongful discrimination is a term of art for differential treatment on grounds such as race, sex, or religion that is wrong — since not all discrimination is: selecting the more qualified candidate is discrimination of an innocent kind. The central question is what makes the wrongful kind wrong. Deborah Hellman has argued that discrimination wrongs people when it demeans them by denying equal social standing, while Benjamin Eidelson locates the wrong in treating people as inferior in worth; the debate extends to indirect discrimination and statistical profiling.
speech-acts: Speech act theory, founded in J. L. Austin's 1962 lectures How to Do Things with Words, studies utterances that perform actions rather than merely describe the world: saying 'I promise,' 'I apologize,' or 'I now pronounce you married' is doing something, and it succeeds only under felicity conditions such as the right authority and circumstances. Austin distinguished the act of saying something (locutionary), the act performed in saying it (illocutionary), and its effects on hearers (perlocutionary), and John Searle systematized the taxonomy of illocutionary acts. Feminist philosophers such as Rae Langton later used the theory to analyze how pornography can silence women's speech.
mimetic-desire: Mimetic desire is the central idea of the French-American thinker René Girard: human beings do not desire objects spontaneously but imitate the desires of others, learning what to want from models or mediators. Because the model becomes a rival for the same object, imitative desire breeds conflict — mimetic rivalry — so desire is triangular, running from subject through model to object. Girard developed the theory through readings of Cervantes, Stendhal, Proust, and Dostoevsky in Deceit, Desire, and the Novel (1961), and extended it into a general theory of social conflict.
scapegoat-mechanism: The scapegoat mechanism is René Girard's account of how human communities escape the self-destructive spiral of imitative rivalry: when mimetic violence threatens a society with all-against-all conflict, it is resolved by the collective killing or expulsion of a single victim, whose death restores peace. The victim, once the source of disorder, becomes the source of order and hence sacred, generating myth, ritual, and religious sacrifice — a thesis argued in Violence and the Sacred (1972). Girard held that the Hebrew scriptures and the Gospels uniquely expose the mechanism by telling these stories from the point of view of the innocent victim.
becoming-other: Becoming is a central notion in the philosophy of Gilles Deleuze, developed with Félix Guattari in A Thousand Plateaus: processes of transformation in which a being passes into what it is not — becoming-woman, becoming-animal, becoming-molecular — without imitating or resembling its target. A becoming occurs in a 'zone of indiscernibility' where two terms exchange elements and both are changed, producing new possibilities rather than preserving fixed identities. The concept underwrites Deleuze's broader attack on identity as the foundation of thought and politics, and his preference for lines of flight over stable structures.
open-interpretation: Open interpretation is the view, prominent in hermeneutics and literary theory, that a text legitimately admits more than one defensible reading rather than a single correct meaning fixed by its author. Umberto Eco's idea of the 'open work' and Roland Barthes's proclamation of the 'death of the author' gave the view its classic formulations, with Barthes locating meaning in language and the reader rather than authorial intention. The debate then turned on limits: Eco himself later argued against unlimited semiosis, insisting that while texts are plural, interpretations can still be shown to be wrong.
popular-parody: Popular parody is the branch of parody that takes popular culture as its object and addresses a mass audience, as distinct from the 'art parody' of elite tradition. Parody theory, notably Linda Hutcheon's account of parody as 'repetition with critical distance' and Margaret Rose's work on the form, emphasizes that parody ranges from ridicule to reverent homage: a popular parody typically reproduces the conventions of a genre or text with a difference that both honors and comments on the original. The form raises questions about the boundary between critique and mere copying, and about what changes when the source is itself already commercial.
phil:panini: Panini was a Sanskrit grammarian of northern India, conventionally dated to the fourth century BCE, whose Astadhyayi (Eight Chapters) is one of the most remarkable intellectual achievements of the ancient world. The work compresses the grammar of the Sanskrit language into roughly four thousand terse rules (sutras), organized with meta-rules and ordering conventions so that, given a stem and an ending, the correct form can be derived mechanically. Scholars regard it as a generative system comparable in power to modern formal grammars, and it remained the authoritative description of Sanskrit for all later Indian linguistic and philosophical work.
phil:ramanuja: Ramanuja (1017-1137) was a South Indian theologian-philosopher, the greatest exponent of Vishishtadvaita, the 'qualified non-dualism' school of Vedanta. Against Shankara's doctrine that the world of souls and matter is ultimately illusory, Ramanuja held that individual selves and the material world are real, forming the body of a personal God, Vishnu, who is the sole independent reality. He wrote the Sribhashya, an influential commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and made loving devotion (bhakti) to God the path to liberation, shaping the devotional Srivaishnava tradition of South India.
phil:arthur-danto: Arthur Danto (1924-2013) was an American philosopher and art critic who taught for decades at Columbia University. His 1964 essay 'The Artworld,' prompted by Warhol's Brillo Box, argued that what makes an object art is not how it looks but its relation to the artworld's theories and history: two visually indistinguishable objects can differ in that one is art and the other is not. Danto went on to define artworks as embodied meanings — artifacts that are about something and express that meaning in their form — and to argue, after Hegel, that art had entered a post-historical condition of pluralism in which its narrative of progressive development had ended.
phil:linda-zagzebski: Linda Zagzebski is a contemporary American philosopher, long at the University of Oklahoma, best known for developing virtue epistemology, which models intellectual evaluation on virtue ethics: knowledge is understood as arising from acts of intellectual virtue such as conscientiousness and open-mindedness (Virtues of the Mind, 1996). In later work she advanced exemplarism, the theory that moral and epistemic concepts are anchored in our direct admiration of exemplary persons, presented in Exemplarist Moral Theory (2017). She has also written extensively on divine foreknowledge, fatalism, and the nature of epistemic authority.
phil:heather-widdows: Heather Widdows is a British philosopher at the University of Birmingham known for work in global ethics, bioethics, and the philosophy of beauty. In Perfect Me! Beauty as an Ethical Ideal (2018) she argues that the contemporary beauty ideal — thinness, youth, smooth skin — has become a dominant moral ideal demanding work and discipline like other moral projects, so that beauty practices require ethical evaluation rather than dismissal as trivial. She has also written on the ethics of infectious disease, global health, and the methodology of ethics across borders.
phil:paul-ricoeur: Paul Ricoeur (1913-2005) was a French philosopher who worked at the crossing point of phenomenology and hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation. His wide-ranging work included studies of the will and evil, a landmark interpretation of Freud, the philosophy of metaphor in The Rule of Metaphor, and the three-volume Time and Narrative, which examined how humans configure time through stories and developed the notion of narrative identity — the self as told rather than merely found. He placed Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud at the origin of a 'hermeneutics of suspicion,' and also wrote on justice, translation, and personal identity in Oneself as Another.
phil:michael-cholbi: Michael Cholbi is a contemporary American philosopher known as one of the leading philosophers of grief and of suicide. His book Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) argues that grief is a form of love for the departed that reorients the griever's own commitments, and that the pain of grief is rational rather than a malfunction to be cured. He has also written on the ethics of suicide, Kantian ethics, punishment, and bioethics, and has helped establish the philosophy of death and dying as a recognized research field.
phil:edith-stein: Edith Stein (1891-1942) was a German philosopher, a student and later assistant of Edmund Husserl whose dissertation On the Problem of Empathy (1917) remains a classic phenomenological study of how we apprehend the experiences of other subjects. After converting from Judaism to Catholicism in 1922, she sought to integrate phenomenology with Thomist metaphysics in Finite and Eternal Being, while also writing on women's education and social philosophy. She entered a Carmelite convent as Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, was arrested during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, and died at Auschwitz in 1942; she was canonized in 1998.
phil:w-d-ross: W. D. Ross (1877-1971) was a Scottish philosopher at Oxford, an eminent Aristotle scholar whose translation of the Nicomachean Ethics remains widely used. In The Right and the Good (1930) he proposed that morality is a plurality of 'prima facie duties' — fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, and self-improvement — genuine duties that can conflict, with no single master principle to settle the conflicts; judgment must weigh them case by case. This pluralist deontology was a major alternative to utilitarianism and to Kantian monism and remains central to normative ethics.
phil:peter-geach: Peter Geach (1916-2013) was a British analytic philosopher who studied under Wittgenstein at Cambridge and taught at Birmingham and Leeds. He worked on logic, reference, and predication — his Reference and Generality (1962) is a classic study of quantification — and advanced the 'relative identity' thesis that identity statements are always relative to a sortal term. A devout Catholic and Thomist, he and his wife, the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe, wrote Three Philosophers together on Aristotle, Aquinas, and Frege, helping bring scholastic ideas into dialogue with analytic philosophy.
phil:helene-cixous: Hélène Cixous, born in 1937 in Oran, French Algeria, is a French writer and theorist associated with the feminist theory of écriture féminine, or feminine writing. In her 1975 essay 'The Laugh of the Medusa' she called on women to write their bodies and their desire, against a phallocentric literary tradition that had defined them as lacking, and she linked writing, sexuality, and subversion. A prolific novelist and critic, she was among the founders of the experimental University of Paris VIII at Vincennes, and her work spans deconstruction, psychoanalysis, and readings of writers from Clarice Lispector to James Joyce.
phil:ibram-x-kendi: Ibram X. Kendi, born in 1982, is an American historian and public scholar of racism and antiracism, author of Stamped from the Beginning (2016), which won the National Book Award, and How to Be an Antiracist (2019). He defines racism strictly at the level of ideas and policies: a racist idea is any that asserts one racial group is superior or inferior, and a racist policy is one that produces racial inequity, so the relevant divide is between racist and antiracist rather than between racist and 'not racist.' He founded the Center for Antiracist Research at Boston University, and his work has shaped both scholarship and public debate.
phil:reinhold-niebuhr: Reinhold Niebuhr (1892-1971) was an American Protestant theologian and social ethicist, the leading figure of Christian realism. In Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) he argued that individuals may be capable of selflessness but social groups almost always act from self-interest and power, so moral idealism is a poor guide to politics and justice must be pursued through balances of power rather than pure love. Works such as The Nature and Destiny of Man and his influence on postwar American liberalism made him one of the most consequential religious thinkers of the twentieth century; the Serenity Prayer is attributed to him.
phil:axel-honneth: Axel Honneth, born in 1949, is a German philosopher and a third-generation representative of the Frankfurt School of critical theory, directing its Institute for Social Research from 2001 to 2018. His central work, The Struggle for Recognition (1992), grounds social critique in three spheres of recognition — love in intimate relations, rights as a legal person, and solidarity or esteem for one's contributions — arguing that social conflicts and movements are best understood as struggles against recognition withheld in one of these forms. He has since developed a normative reconstruction of freedom in Freedom's Right and written on reification, capitalism, and democracy.
phil:thomas-paine: Thomas Paine (1737-1809) was an English-born pamphleteer and radical political thinker who became one of the intellectual voices of both the American and French revolutions. His pamphlet Common Sense (1776) did much to turn colonial opinion toward independence, while Rights of Man (1791-92), his reply to Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution, defended natural rights and popular sovereignty and proposed social measures such as old-age pensions. In The Age of Reason he set out a deist critique of organized and revealed religion, and in Agrarian Justice he sketched an early argument for universal payments funded by landowners, anticipating the welfare state.
phil:ruth-benedict: Ruth Benedict (1887-1948) was an American cultural anthropologist, a student and close colleague of Franz Boas at Columbia, whose Patterns of Culture (1934) became one of the most influential works of the discipline. Arguing that cultures are integrated wholes — she contrasted the 'Apollonian' Zuni with the 'Dionysian' Dobu — she held that traits and values make sense only within their configuration, and drew from this a case for cultural relativism in ethics: what counts as normal and good is defined differently in different cultures. Her The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), a study of Japanese culture written during the war without fieldwork, shaped both anthropology and American understanding of Japan.
phil:malinowski: Bronislaw Malinowski (1884-1942) was a Polish-born anthropologist working in Britain who is regarded as the founder of modern ethnographic fieldwork. Through extended immersive residence among the Trobriand Islanders, described in Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), he established the method of participant observation: learning the local language, living among the people, and grasping the 'native's point of view' rather than collecting artifacts and reports at a distance. His functionalism explained institutions by the needs — biological, social, and symbolic — they satisfy, and his fieldwork model became the defining method of social anthropology.
phil:graham-greene: Graham Greene (1904-1991) was an English novelist whose fiction, though not academic philosophy, stands among the most serious literary explorations of faith, sin, and moral ambiguity of the twentieth century. In novels such as Brighton Rock, The Power and the Glory, The Heart of the Matter, and The End of the Affair he dramatized flawed and even wicked characters caught between belief and doubt, asking whether pity, love, and conscience can corrupt as well as save. He also wrote fast-paced 'entertainments' such as The Third Man and political novels set in Vietnam, Haiti, and Latin America, and his recurring theme — the shabbiness of devoted belief — made him a lasting reference in discussions of moral psychology.
phil:linda-hutcheon: Linda Hutcheon is a Canadian literary theorist at the University of Toronto whose work has defined the study of parody, postmodernism, and adaptation. In A Theory of Parody (1985) she characterized parody as 'repetition with critical distance,' a form ranging from reverent homage to ridicule that marks difference at the heart of similarity; in A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988) she coined the term 'historiographic metafiction' for fiction that self-consciously rewrites history; and in A Theory of Adaptation (2006) she analyzed adaptation as 'repetition without replication' across media.
phil:langer: Susanne Langer (1895-1985) was an American philosopher of mind and art who, building on Ernst Cassirer's symbolic forms, argued that human feeling is understood through symbolization. In Philosophy in a New Key and Feeling and Form she treated art - especially music - as a non-discursive, presentational symbolism whose meaning cannot be translated into words.
phil:becker-denial-of-death: Ernest Becker (1924-1974) was a cultural anthropologist whose Pulitzer-winning The Denial of Death argued that civilization is an elaborate defense against the terror of mortality: humans repress the knowledge of their own death and build immortality projects - religions, nations, fame, love - to transcend it. His synthesis of psychoanalysis, Kierkegaard, and Otto Rank became a touchstone for existential psychology.
phil:carroll-aesthetics: Noel Carroll (born 1947) is an American philosopher of art best known for his work on film, horror, and suspense. He rejects theories that reduce art to beauty or emotion-matching, analyzing instead how genres orchestrate cognition - why monsters disgust and fascinate, how plots generate curiosity, and how mass art earns the name of art.
phil:warren-personhood: Mary Anne Warren (1946-2010) was an American philosopher whose work on the abortion debate distinguished genetic humanity from personhood, proposing criteria - consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness - that ground moral status. Her seven-criteria account remains one of the most cited positions in bioethics.
